Persistent receiver errors in one direction; equalization not converged; a receiver that never acks (firmware or hardware bug).
How to detect / prove
lspci -vvv CESta "Rollover+"; the Root Port's LnkSta "Link Training" bit or speed/width change; Linux bandwidth notifications from drivers/pci/pcie/bwctrl.c; analyzer: repeated identical TLP retransmissions followed by TS1 ordered sets (Recovery).
Linux v7.2 source
Logged by drivers/pci/pcie/aer.c as a correctable error; no driver recovery. Link speed or width changes are tracked by bwctrl.c.
Test to provoke it
As T-35, with stronger impairment. CAUTION: may cause link down.
T-37Ack latency too long: unnecessary replays and lost bandwidthDegradedPCIe Data Link Layer
In a PEX trace
Visible Interval = end of TLP with sequence N → first Ack DLLP with AckNak_Seq_Num ≥ N; compare with the AckNak latency table; spurious replays follow when it exceeds the partner's replay time.
What happens
The receiver must return an Ack within its AckNak latency limit. A receiver that batches Acks for too long makes the transmitter's replay timer expire although nothing was corrupted.
How it shows up
Correctable Replay Timer Timeouts on the partner (T-35) with no Bad TLP / Bad DLLP on either side; throughput below expectation because the replay buffer fills and the transmitter stalls.
Spec basis
PCIe Base, Data Link Layer: AckNak_LATENCY_TIMER limits (tables by payload size, width, rate); it should be well below the partner's replay limit.
Typical causes
Device Data Link Layer implementation coalescing Acks too aggressively; receive-side backpressure inside the device; L0s entry delaying DLLPs.
How to detect / prove
Analyzer: measure time from TLP end to the covering Ack DLLP; compare with the spec table for the negotiated width, rate and MPS. Throughput test with fio sequential reads at high queue depth.
Linux v7.2 source
Not visible to Linux except via the correctable counters (aer.c).
Test to provoke it
Run maximum-bandwidth sequential I/O and inspect Ack spacing in an analyzer. SAFE.
T-38Flow-control credit starvation (no UpdateFC)Timer onlyPCIe Transaction / Data Link Layer
In a PEX trace
Visible Track UpdateFC DLLPs per type (P/NP/Cpl, header/data); interval between consecutive UpdateFC of a type should be ≤ ~30 µs while credits are finite; a credit counter stuck at zero with TLPs pending on the other side proves starvation.
What happens
A transmitter may send a TLP only when the receiver has advertised credits for it. If the receiver stops returning credits (no UpdateFC DLLPs), traffic of that type stops. No error is defined for "slow credits"; only upper-layer timers notice.
How it shows up
Nothing on the starved link itself, unless the optional flow-control update watchdog retrains the link or a Flow Control Protocol Error (AER uncorrectable bit 13, PCI_ERR_UNC_FCP) is detected for an illegal credit update. Upstream symptoms: Completion Timeouts (T-33), NVMe I/O timeouts (T-22).
Spec basis
PCIe Base: InitFC1/InitFC2/UpdateFC DLLPs per type (Posted, Non-Posted, Completion; header and data credits); UpdateFC sent when credits are freed and periodically (about every 30 µs) while credits are not infinite; an optional 200 µs update watchdog verify.
Typical causes
Device receive buffer stuck (firmware not draining posted writes, e.g. doorbells or CQE writes from the host side); deadlock between posted and non-posted queues violating ordering rules; switch buffer exhaustion.
How to detect / prove
Analyzer: credit tracking view (most analyzers compute available credits): the advertised credit counter stays at zero while the partner has TLPs waiting. lspci cannot show credits.
Linux v7.2 source
No direct visibility. Indirect: aer.c for FCP errors and Completion Timeouts, pci.c:nvme_timeout() for stalled commands.
Test to provoke it
Exerciser endpoint configured to withhold UpdateFC for posted credits while the host writes doorbells. EXPERT.
T-39LTSSM state timeout: training loops, falls back or downshiftsDegradedPCIe Physical Layer
In a PEX trace
Visible LTSSM state entries/exits (TS1/TS2, EIOS, electrical idle) with timestamps: interval = state entry → exit or fallback; e.g. Polling.Active → Detect after 24 ms. Negotiated width/rate visible in TS ordered sets. Requires an analyzer that records the training (start capture before reset).
What happens
Each LTSSM state has a timeout. If the expected ordered sets are not seen in time, the state machine moves on: Detect repeats every 12 ms while no receiver is detected; Polling and Configuration fall back to Detect; Recovery may fall back to Detect (link down). Repeated partial success shows up as a link trained at lower width or speed.
How it shows up
No AER error for a successful downshift. lspci -vvv LnkSta shows "Speed 8GT/s (downgraded), Width x2 (downgraded)" versus LnkCap. Root Port LnkSta2 equalization bits; Link Bandwidth Management Status. In the worst case the link never reaches L0 and the device is missing.
Spec basis
PCIe Base, LTSSM: Detect.Quiet 12 ms timeout verified; Polling.Active 24 ms, Polling.Configuration 48 ms, Configuration.Linkwidth.Start 24 ms, other Configuration substates 2 ms, Recovery.RcvrLock 24 ms, Recovery.RcvrCfg 48 ms, Recovery.Idle 2 ms verify in spec; equalization phase timeouts at 8 GT/s and above verify.
Typical causes
Signal integrity (lane failing receiver detect or symbol lock); lane reversal or polarity issues; equalization failure at 16/32 GT/s; reference clock problems; mis-wired lanes on risers.
How to detect / prove
Compare LnkCap and LnkSta for both ends; analyzer LTSSM view: state durations and which state times out; Linux bwctrl.c link speed change notifications; repeated link-up/down events in dmesg (pciehp: "Link Down"/"Link Up").
Linux v7.2 source
quirks.c:pcie_failed_link_retrain() handles one known case (link stuck in training; retrain at 2.5 GT/s then lift the limit) — "broken device, retraining non-functional downstream link at 2.5GT/s".
Test to provoke it
Disable lanes with a lane-disabling interposer, or force target speed (setpci on Link Control 2 — EXPERT, can drop the link) and retrain.
T-40Link does not come up in time after reset or power-onTimer onlyPCIe Physical / software wait
In a PEX trace
Visible Interval = PERST# deassertion (if the fixture records sideband) or electrical idle exit → first TS1 → L0 (first DLLP/InitFC); and L0 → first CfgRd from the host (must be ≥ 100 ms above 5 GT/s).
What happens
After a reset the downstream component must enter Detect within 20 ms, and software must not send configuration requests until the link is up and a further 100 ms have passed (above 5 GT/s, measured from Data Link Layer Link Active). If the link is not active within the host's wait, software declares the device missing.
How it shows up
Linux: the device does not enumerate, or not ready Nms after bus reset; giving up; for hot-plug ports, no "Link Up" event. Without Data Link Layer Link Active reporting Linux simply sleeps 1000 ms + delay and hopes.
Spec basis
PCIe Base reset and link-up timing rules (as quoted in drivers/pci/pci.c comments: enter Detect within 20 ms; 100 ms minimum before configuration requests; at least 1 s before declaring a non-responding device broken). Link Capabilities DLLLARC; Link Status DLLLA and LT bits.
Typical causes
Slow device PHY start; reference clock or PERST# sequencing errors; LTSSM failures (T-39).
How to detect / prove
dmesg with pci=... debug (dyndbg="file drivers/pci/* +p") shows "waiting N ms for downstream link"; analyzer timestamp of PERST# deassertion vs first TS1 and vs L0.
Linux v7.2 source
pci.c:pci_bridge_wait_for_secondary_bus(), pcie_wait_for_link_delay() (20 ms then poll DLLLA, timeout PCIE_LINK_RETRAIN_TIMEOUT_MS, then pcie_failed_link_retrain()), pcie_wait_for_link_status() polling every 1 ms.
Test to provoke it
Delay the device's PERST# release with a controllable fixture; secondary bus reset via /sys/bus/pci/devices/BDF/reset (CAUTION: resets the device).
T-41Device not ready after reset: RRS beyond 1 s or no response at allTimer onlyPCIe configuration / readiness
In a PEX trace
Visible CfgRd0 → Cpl with status RRS (Configuration Request Retry) repeated; interval = reset (or L0) → first CplD with a valid Vendor ID; compare with 1 s. DRS/FRS messages, if sent, are visible as Msg TLPs.
What happens
After a Conventional Reset or D3cold→D0, a function must accept configuration requests within 1 s, but may answer with Request Retry Status (RRS, formerly CRS) to ask for more time. A function that keeps answering RRS, or answers with all-ones, is "not ready".
How it shows up
Linux: pci BDF: not ready 1023ms after FLR; waiting, then ready Nms after ... or, after 60 s, not ready 65535ms after ...; giving up. During enumeration: not ready after Nms; giving up from pci_bus_wait_rrs(). NVMe probe never starts.
Spec basis
PCIe Base: device readiness 1 s after Conventional Reset; RRS completions; Root Control "Configuration RRS Software Visibility Enable" (with it, a Vendor ID read returns the special value 0001h); Readiness Time Reporting extended capability; Device Readiness Status (DRS) and Function Readiness Status (FRS) messages; Immediate Readiness bit in the Status register.
Typical causes
Firmware boot slower than 1 s (large drives loading internal tables); firmware stuck in a boot loop; failed link retrain.
How to detect / prove
dmesg lines above; lspci -s BDF -vvv returning "Unknown header type 7f" (all-ones); analyzer: CfgRd0 answered by Cpl with status RRS repeatedly.
Linux v7.2 source
pci.c:pci_dev_wait() (uses Vendor ID with RRS SV, otherwise the Command register; PCI_RESET_WAIT 1000 ms, caller timeout PCIE_RESET_READY_POLL_MS 60000 ms); probe.c:pci_enable_rrs_sv(), pci_bus_wait_rrs(), pci_bus_read_dev_vendor_id(..., 60*1000); probe.c:pci_imm_ready_init() reads Immediate Readiness. The local v7.2 subset showed no consumer of Readiness Time Reporting, DRS or FRS verify.
Test to provoke it
Trigger FLR via echo 1 > /sys/bus/pci/devices/BDF/reset (CAUTION: unbind the NVMe driver first, data in flight is lost) and time the "ready Nms" message.
T-42D3hot→D0 transition: access before the 10 ms recovery timeTimer onlyPCIe power management
In a PEX trace
Visible Interval = CfgWr to PMCSR setting D0 → next config/memory request to that function; must be ≥ 10 ms (or the device's value); its completion shows whether the device was ready.
What happens
After writing PowerState=D0 in the PM capability of a function that was in D3hot, software must wait 10 ms before accessing it (unless the function reports otherwise). Accessing earlier, or a function that needs longer, gives undefined results.
How it shows up
Config reads return garbage or all-ones; MMIO reads time out (T-33); the NVMe driver sees CSTS=0xffffffff on resume. Linux increases the delay for known-bad devices (quirks 20 ms or 120 ms).
Spec basis
PCI Power Management: D3hot→D0 recovery time 10 ms; "No Soft Reset" bit determines whether state is preserved.
Typical causes
Device firmware needs longer than 10 ms; platform-specific slowness; driver skipping the wait.
How to detect / prove
dmesg with PM debug; analyzer: CfgWr to PMCSR (D0) followed by CfgRd sooner than 10 ms, answered badly.
Linux v7.2 source
pci.c:pci_dev_d3_sleep() (max of dev->d3hot_delay and global pci_pm_d3hot_delay; default PCI_PM_D3HOT_WAIT = 10 ms, defined in drivers/pci/pci.h); then pci_dev_wait(dev, "power up D3hot->D0uninitialized", PCIE_RESET_READY_POLL_MS). quirks.c:quirk_d3hot_delay() raises it to 20 ms for some devices; quirk_intel_pcie_pm() sets the global delay to 120 ms; quirk_remove_d3hot_delay() sets 0 for some Intel chipset functions.
Test to provoke it
Runtime PM: echo auto > /sys/bus/pci/devices/BDF/power/control and idle the device; measure resume. SAFE.
T-43Function Level Reset not complete in 100 msTimer onlyPCIe reset
In a PEX trace
Visible Interval = CfgWr to Device Control with Initiate FLR (bit 15) → first CfgRd that completes successfully; must be ≥ 100 ms (unless Immediate Readiness); outstanding non-posted requests at FLR time are visible.
What happens
After Initiate FLR, a function must complete the reset within 100 ms; it may silently drop requests during that time. Software also should wait for outstanding transactions to drain before initiating FLR.
How it shows up
Linux: timed out waiting for pending transaction; performing function level reset anyway (Transaction Pending bit still set after about 700 ms of polling), then readiness messages from pci_dev_wait() (T-41).
Spec basis
PCIe Base: FLR (Device Capabilities FLR bit, Device Control Initiate FLR bit 15); 100 ms completion requirement; Device Status Transactions Pending bit.
Typical causes
DMA engine stuck (completions never returned); firmware slow to reinitialise after FLR.
How to detect / prove
dmesg; lspci -vvv DevSta "TransPend+" before reset; time between CfgWr setting Initiate FLR and the first successful CfgRd.
Linux v7.2 source
pci.c:pcie_flr(): pci_wait_for_pending_transaction() (polls 4 times with 0, 100, 200, 400 ms sleeps), sets PCI_EXP_DEVCTL_BCR_FLR, msleep(100) unless dev->imm_ready, then pci_dev_wait(dev, "FLR", PCIE_RESET_READY_POLL_MS).
Test to provoke it
echo flr > /sys/bus/pci/devices/BDF/reset_method then echo 1 > .../reset with the driver unbound. CAUTION.
T-44Surprise link down / hot removal while I/O is in flightReportedPCIe link / hot-plug
In a PEX trace
Partly visible The link drop is visible (traffic stops, electrical idle, Detect) and outstanding tags never complete; the Surprise Down AER bit and hot-plug slot events are in the port's registers, visible only if read by software over a probed link.
What happens
The link drops without warning (cable pull, power fault, failed Recovery). Outstanding requests can never complete; the port may report a Surprise Down error and hot-plug events.
How it shows up
Port AER uncorrectable bit 5 (Surprise Down, PCI_ERR_UNC_SURPDN) if the port supports Data Link Layer Link Active reporting; Slot Status Data Link Layer State Changed / Presence Detect Changed; DPC may contain the port. NVMe: reads of CSTS return all-ones, the controller is removed; I/O fails with a host path error and fails over if multipath.
Spec basis
PCIe Base: Surprise Down error, Data Link Layer State Changed, hot-plug slot registers, Downstream Port Containment (DPC).
Typical causes
Physical removal; power loss on the device; REPLAY_NUM rollover followed by failed Recovery (T-36); deep power state not exiting (T-15).
How to detect / prove
dmesg: pciehp "Link Down", AER "Surprise Down", DPC containment messages, NVMe "controller is down" or removal. lspci -vvv on the port: SltSta DLActive-.
Linux v7.2 source
pci.c:nvme_timeout() checks pci_dev_is_disconnected() and moves the controller to DELETING; pci.c:pci_dev_wait() returns early when disconnected; DPC in drivers/pci/pcie/dpc.c, recovery in err.c. (pciehp itself is not in this atlas's source subset.)
Test to provoke it
Hot-plug capable slot: echo 0 > /sys/bus/pci/slots/N/power during I/O (CAUTION), or pull a U.2 drive in a hot-plug backplane (EXPERT).
T-45ASPM exit latency larger than the endpoint can acceptDegradedPCIe power management
In a PEX trace
Visible Interval = electrical idle (EIOS) → first TLP after exit, i.e. the L0s/L1 exit time; compare with LnkCap exit latency and DevCap acceptable latency (both visible in config CplD payloads if captured).
What happens
Each port reports how long it needs to leave L0s and L1 (Link Capabilities exit latencies); each endpoint reports how much latency it can accept (Device Capabilities acceptable latencies). If exit latency (plus 1 µs per switch for L1) exceeds acceptable latency, enabling that ASPM state can starve the device.
How it shows up
If enabled anyway (by firmware or by forcing a policy): latency spikes, sometimes Completion Timeouts or replay errors after L1 exit. If Linux detects the mismatch it silently does not enable the state (higher power, no error).
Spec basis
PCIe Base: Link Capabilities L0s/L1 Exit Latency, Device Capabilities Endpoint L0s/L1 Acceptable Latency, Link Control ASPM Control.
Typical causes
Under-reported exit latencies; PLLs that take longer than declared; platform BIOS forcing ASPM.
How to detect / prove
lspci -vvv: LnkCap "ASPM L0s L1, Exit Latency L0s <1us, L1 <8us", DevCap "Latency L0s <64ns, L1 <1us", LnkCtl "ASPM L1 Enabled". Compare with /sys/module/pcie_aspm/parameters/policy. Measure fio latency with ASPM on and off (pcie_aspm=off).
Linux v7.2 source
drivers/pci/pcie/aspm.c:pcie_aspm_check_latency() converts encodings (calc_l0s_latency() = 64 ns « encoding, calc_l1_latency() = 1 µs « encoding; encoding 7 means "more than"), adds 1 µs per switch for L1 and clears aspm_capable bits that do not fit. It does not check L1 substates ("We assume that the L1 exit latencies advertised by a device include L1 substate latencies").
Test to provoke it
Compare tail latency with pcie_aspm.policy=performance vs powersupersave. SAFE.
T-46L1 substates / LTR misprogrammed: wake too slow or link lostDegradedPCIe power management
In a PEX trace
Partly visible L1 entry (PM DLLPs / EIOS) and exit timing visible; L1.2 itself turns the PHY off so the analyzer sees only electrical idle and the wake; CLKREQ# is sideband (visible only with a sideband probe). LTR Message TLPs carrying latency values are visible.
What happens
L1.1/L1.2 turn off more of the PHY. Entry depends on the device's Latency Tolerance Reporting (LTR) value versus the LTR_L1.2_THRESHOLD; exit timing depends on T_POWER_ON and Common_Mode_Restore_Time. Wrong values make exit slower than the device tolerates, or make exit fail.
How it shows up
Latency spikes after idle; in bad cases the link fails to retrain after L1.2 and the drive disappears (T-15, T-44). No error is reported for a slow exit.
Spec basis
PCIe Base: L1 PM Substates extended capability (capability ID 1Eh): L1SS capabilities, Control 1 (enables, Common_Mode_Restore_Time, LTR_L1.2_THRESHOLD value/scale), Control 2 (T_POWER_ON scale/value); LTR extended capability (18h): Max Snoop/No-Snoop Latency; Device Control 2 LTR Mechanism Enable.
Typical causes
Inconsistent values programmed on the two ends; T_POWER_ON shorter than the PHY needs; CLKREQ# routing problems; device reporting very large LTR values.
How to detect / prove
lspci -vvv: "L1SubCap", "L1SubCtl1: PCI-PM_L1.2+ ASPM_L1.2+ ... T_CommonMode=..us LTR1.2_Threshold=..ns", "L1SubCtl2: T_PwrOn=..us", "LTR+" in DevCtl2. Compare both ends of the link. Reproduce with L1.2 disabled.
Linux v7.2 source
aspm.c:aspm_calc_l12_info() computes T_POWER_ON, Common_Mode_Restore_Time and LTR threshold from both ends; pcie_encode_t_power_on(); pci_configure_aspm_l1ss(), pci_save_aspm_l1ss_state()/pci_restore_aspm_l1ss_state() across suspend.
Test to provoke it
Toggle L1.2 via the ASPM policy (powersupersave) on a laptop and run idle/burst fio patterns. SAFE.
📭 What the spec does not say

No PCIe timer bounds how long an endpoint may take to process a posted write (such as an NVMe doorbell) or to issue its next request. A drive that accepts a doorbell write and then does nothing for a minute violates no PCIe rule. The only watchdog for "the device forgot to do the work" is the host NVMe timeout.

III.5 Performance-Time Failures: Slow but "Successful"

← III.4 PCIe Timers: Completion Timeout, Replay, Flow Control, Training, Readiness and PowerIII.6 Measuring Time on a PEX Trace →

Some time failures never trip any timer. Every command completes successfully, well inside 30 seconds, yet the system misses its purpose: a database misses its p99.9 latency target, a stream stalls, throughput halves after an hour. These are Degraded failures. They are found only by measuring and comparing against a target that you define, because neither NVMe nor PCIe defines one.

latency(cmd) = t(CQE written) − t(SQ doorbell written)
  • t(SQ doorbell written) — timestamp of the host's MWr to the SQ tail doorbell that made the command visible to the controller (on a PEX trace) or the nvme_setup_cmd tracepoint (on the host).
  • t(CQE written) — timestamp of the device's MWr into the CQ slot holding that CID (trace) or nvme_complete_rq (host; includes interrupt and scheduling delay).

Measure both if you can. The difference between the device-side latency (trace) and the host-side latency (tracepoints, fio clat) is time spent in the host — the part a PEX trace cannot see.

T-47Tail-latency SLA miss (p99 / p99.9 / p99.99)DegradedPerformance / service level
In a PEX trace
Partly visible Per-command latency = doorbell MWr → CQE MWr (match CID and SQID) for every command in the capture; build the distribution and compare p99/p99.9 with the SLA. Host-side latency above the driver is not visible.
What happens
Median latency is fine, but a small fraction of commands take tens or hundreds of times longer. A service with a percentile target fails even though every command succeeded.
How it shows up
No error anywhere. Only the latency distribution shows it: fio clat percentiles, application histograms, blk-mq stats.
Spec basis
None. NVMe and PCIe define no per-command latency limit; the SLA is yours. Contributing spec mechanisms: arbitration (CC.AMS, Arbitration feature 01h), interrupt coalescing (feature 08h), APST and ASPM exit latencies.
Typical causes
Garbage collection (T-48), power-state exits (T-14, T-45, T-46), thermal throttling (T-49), read retries on worn NAND (internal error recovery), queue imbalance or head-of-line blocking behind large commands, host interrupt or scheduling delays (T-32).
How to detect / prove
fio --name=t --rw=randread --bs=4k --iodepth=1 --runtime=600 --time_based --lat_percentiles=1 --percentile_list=50:99:99.9:99.99 --filename=/dev/nvme0n1 (read-only workload); bpftrace on nvme:nvme_setup_cmd/nvme:nvme_complete_rq for per-command latency; correlate outliers with SMART temperature, power state (nvme get-feature -f 0x02) and AER counters.
Linux v7.2 source
Linux v7.2 does not track SLAs; measurement via tracepoints in drivers/nvme/host/trace.c and block-layer statistics.
Test to provoke it
Run a read-latency probe at QD1 while a second job does sustained random writes; compare percentiles with and without the writer. SAFE for the probe; the writer is DESTRUCTIVE to data on the target range.
T-48Garbage-collection stallDegradedDevice internal / performance
In a PEX trace
Partly visible GC itself is internal; visible symptom is a burst of long doorbell → CQE intervals on writes (and reads) under sustained random write, with otherwise normal link behaviour.
What happens
When free blocks run low, the SSD must copy valid pages out of blocks before erasing them. Host commands queue behind this work, producing periodic latency spikes from milliseconds to hundreds of milliseconds.
How it shows up
Latency spikes correlated with sustained writes; no error. The Tiny-Tail Flash study (FAST 2017) reports 5–138× GC-induced slowdowns at the 99–99.99th percentiles for a baseline design.
Spec basis
Not specified. Related host hints exist: Deallocate/TRIM (DSM 09h), Write Zeroes, Streams/Flexible Data Placement, Predictable Latency Mode (I/O determinism windows) where supported.
Typical causes
High write amplification (random small writes, low over-provisioning); no TRIM; full drive.
How to detect / prove
Long sustained random-write test with latency logging (--write_lat_log); plot latency vs time and vs bytes written. If supported, check Predictable Latency Mode logs and Endurance Group logs.
Linux v7.2 source
No driver involvement; Linux sends Discard as DSM Deallocate when the filesystem issues it (core.c:nvme_setup_discard()).
Test to provoke it
Precondition the drive (fill sequentially twice), then 4 KiB random writes at high QD for hours. DESTRUCTIVE to data on the drive; CAUTION wear.
T-49Thermal throttling slowdownDegradedDevice / thermal
In a PEX trace
Partly visible Visible symptom: doorbell → CQE intervals and data throughput dropping over time; temperature and throttling state only in SMART log payloads (Get Log Page 02h data) if the host reads them during the capture.
What happens
As the composite temperature rises past the drive's thermal management thresholds, the controller reduces performance to cool down. Commands still succeed, just slower.
How it shows up
Throughput drops and latency rises after minutes of load. SMART / Health log: Composite Temperature, Warning Composite Temperature Time, Critical Composite Temperature Time, Thermal Management Temperature 1/2 Transition Count and Total Time. An Asynchronous Event (SMART/Health, temperature) may be raised when a threshold is crossed — that part is reported.
Spec basis
NVMe Base: SMART / Health Information log (02h) temperature fields and thermal management counters; Identify WCTEMP/CCTEMP; Host Controlled Thermal Management (feature 10h) with MNTMT/MXTMT; Temperature Threshold feature (04h).
Typical causes
Insufficient airflow or heatsink; sustained writes; host thermal management thresholds set low.
How to detect / prove
Poll nvme smart-log /dev/nvme0 every few seconds during a fio run; correlate throughput with temperature and with the thermal transition counters; /sys/class/hwmon NVMe sensors (Linux drivers/nvme/host/hwmon.c).
Linux v7.2 source
hwmon.c exposes temperatures and thresholds; quirks NVME_QUIRK_NO_TEMP_THRESH_CHANGE, NVME_QUIRK_NO_SECONDARY_TEMP_THRESH exist for devices that misbehave.
Test to provoke it
Run sequential writes with airflow blocked (CAUTION: monitor temperature, stop before the critical threshold).
T-50Write cliff: steady-state write performance far below fresh-out-of-boxDegradedDevice internal / performance
In a PEX trace
Partly visible Visible as write CQE latency rising and throughput falling after a capacity-sized amount of written data (sum of NLB in Write SQEs); the cause (free-block exhaustion) is internal.
What happens
A new or freshly sanitized drive writes into free blocks (and often an SLC cache). After roughly a drive capacity of writes (or once the cache fills), throughput drops sharply to the steady-state rate.
How it shows up
No error. Throughput vs time graph shows a step down; latency rises. Benchmarks run on an empty drive overstate performance.
Spec basis
Not specified. SNIA Solid State Storage Performance Test Specification defines preconditioning methods (external standard).
Typical causes
SLC cache exhaustion; free-block pool exhaustion leading to GC (T-48).
How to detect / prove
Write the whole drive while logging bandwidth once per second (--bwavg_time=1000 --write_bw_log); find the knee; compare with datasheet steady-state numbers.
Linux v7.2 source
No driver involvement.
Test to provoke it
Sanitize or format, then sequential write 2× capacity. DESTRUCTIVE.
T-51Flush or FUA write takes far longer than expectedDegradedNVMe command / volatile cache
In a PEX trace
Visible Interval = Flush SQE (opcode 00h) doorbell MWr → its CQE MWr; compare with your SLA; whether data was really made durable is not visible.
What happens
With a volatile write cache, a Flush (or a write with Force Unit Access) must wait until cached data is on non-volatile media. On some drives this takes hundreds of milliseconds or more; databases that fsync often stall.
How it shows up
No error; fsync latency spikes. If it exceeds io_timeout, it becomes T-22.
Spec basis
NVMe NVM Command Set: Flush (00h), FUA bit in Write; Identify Controller VWC; Volatile Write Cache feature (06h).
Typical causes
Large dirty cache; flush serialised behind GC; firmware flushing the mapping table too.
How to detect / prove
fio with --fsync=1 or --fdatasync=1 and latency percentiles; tracepoints for opcode 0x00 latency; check VWC with nvme id-ctrl | grep vwc and nvme get-feature -f 0x06.
Linux v7.2 source
Linux issues Flush for REQ_PREFLUSH when the device reports a volatile cache (core.c sets the queue write-cache flag from VWC).
Test to provoke it
Mixed write + fsync workload; compare with write cache disabled (nvme set-feature -f 0x06 -v 0, CAUTION: changes drive behaviour until reset/power cycle).

III.6 Measuring Time on a PEX Trace

← III.5 Performance-Time Failures: Slow but "Successful"IV.1 The deallocate that didn't: a full worked case →

A PEX trace (a Teledyne LeCroy PCIe protocol-analyzer capture) records every TLP, DLLP and ordered set on the probed link with a timestamp. That makes it the best tool there is for time failures on that link — with three limits:

  • A timeout is visible only as an absence. The trace shows a request and then no completion; you prove the violation by measuring the time from the request to the end of the capture (or to the recovery action) and comparing it with the limit.
  • Only the probed link. A Completion Timeout on a different link, a network capsule for NVMe over Fabrics, or a host CPU stall are not on the trace.
  • Registers are visible only when read. CAP, CSTS, CRTO, AER status and Device Control 2 appear only as payloads of configuration or memory reads the host performs during the capture. Read them deliberately at the start and the end of a capture (e.g. nvme show-regs, lspci -vvv) so their values are in the trace.

Each NVMe interval is bounded by two packets that both cross the link: a host write (doorbell or register) and a device write (CQE, MSI-X) or a completion of a host read (CSTS). Each PCIe interval is bounded by a request and its completion, a TLP and its Ack, or two LTSSM state entries.

III.6.2 Example: proving a timeout with timestamps

Synthetic trace — Read on QID 3 that never completes, then Abort and reset (generic columns; not an analyzer export)
TimeDirPacketDecoded
0.000000 sHost→DevMWr 4 B, BAR0+1018hSQ3 tail doorbell = 0x22
0.000001 sDev→HostMRd 64 B, tag 0x11Fetch SQ3 slot 0x21
0.000002 sHost→DevCplD 64 B, tag 0x11SQE: opcode 02h Read, CID 0x0011, NSID 1
0.000002 s – 30.0 s—(no CQE MWr for CID 0x0011)Command outstanding; other CIDs complete normally
30.0012 sHost→DevMWr 4 B, BAR0+1000hSQ0 tail doorbell (Abort)
30.0013 sDev→HostMWr 16 B to ACQAbort CQE, DW0 = 00000001h (not aborted)
60.0025 sHost→DevMWr 4 B, BAR0+14hCC.EN = 0 (reset)
60.0026 s –Host→Dev / Dev→HostMRd BAR0+1Ch / CplDCSTS polling until RDY = 0

The proof is the pair "SQE fetched at 0.000002 s" and "no CQE for CID 0x0011 before the reset at 60.0025 s". Together with the Abort result, it shows the drive accepted the command and never completed it. What the drive was doing internally is not on the trace; collect a telemetry log next.

🧪 Lab III.1 — Measure your drive's real time limits SAFE

Objective: compare advertised limits with measured times on a test machine.

Setup: a non-production NVMe drive; root shell; optionally a PCIe analyzer on the drive's link.

  1. Record advertised values: nvme show-regs /dev/nvme0 (CAP.TO, CRTO), nvme id-ctrl /dev/nvme0 (rtd3e, rtd3r, mtfa, edstt, crdt1–3, kas, anatt, acl, power-state table).
  2. Record host values: cat /sys/module/nvme_core/parameters/{io_timeout,admin_timeout,max_retries,shutdown_timeout,default_ps_max_latency_us}, cat /sys/class/nvme/nvme0/{io_timeout,admin_timeout}.
  3. Measure enable time: unbind and rebind the driver (echo 0000:01:00.0 > /sys/bus/pci/drivers/nvme/unbind, then bind) — CAUTION: unmount first — and read the timestamps in dmesg -T, or on the analyzer the CC EN=1 → RDY=1 interval.
  4. Measure idle-exit latency: fio --rw=randread --bs=4k --iodepth=1 --thinktime=500ms --runtime=120 --time_based --lat_percentiles=1 --readonly with APST on and with default_ps_max_latency_us=0.
  5. Check PCIe settings: lspci -vvv -s 01:00.0 DevCtl2 (Completion Timeout), LnkCap/LnkCtl (ASPM), L1SubCtl1/2.

Observations: fill a table of advertised versus measured values.

Questions: Is CAP.TO generous or tight compared with your measurement? Does the first-I/O-after-idle latency exceed EXLAT of the deepest state Linux enabled?

Solution notes

Typical drives become ready in well under CAP.TO after a clean shutdown and closer to it after an unsafe one. If idle-exit latency exceeds the sum of EXLAT and the PCIe L1 exit latency, either the drive under-reports EXLAT or the platform adds latency (L1.2, clock request); repeat with pcie_aspm=off to separate them.

Extension: repeat step 3 after an unsafe power cut (CAUTION: risk to data on that drive) and compare.

Quiz

  1. CAP.TO reads 28h. How long should the host wait for CSTS.RDY, and how long does Linux v7.2 wait?

    Answer

    28h = 40 units × 500 ms = 20 s. Linux uses (CAP.TO + 1) / 2 seconds in integer arithmetic = 20 s (or the larger CRWMT if CRTO is supported).

  2. Why does Linux send no Abort for a timed-out admin command?

    Answer

    The Abort itself would be an admin command on the same queue that is apparently not progressing; v7.2 resets the controller directly when nvmeq->qid == 0.

  3. The drive's Completion Timeout is set to Range D. What do you expect to see when a host memory read is lost?

    Answer

    An NVMe I/O timeout at 30 s (and probably a reset) before any AER Completion Timeout is logged, because the PCIe timer (4–64 s) may be longer than the NVMe timer.

  4. Which interval on a PEX trace proves a missed interrupt?

    Answer

    A CQE MWr with no following MSI-X MWr (or one to the wrong address), followed only much later by the CQ head doorbell; dmesg shows "completion polled".

  5. CRD=2 and CRDT2=5. How long should Linux wait before resubmitting?

    Answer

    5 × 100 ms = 500 ms (nvme_retry_req()), provided ACRE was enabled.

Interview questions

  1. Beginner Why is a command timeout considered an error even though no status code is returned?
    Model answerBecause the host no longer knows the state of the request: it may or may not have executed. Recovery (abort, reset, retry) is required, exactly as for an error status, and often with a bigger impact.
  2. Intermediate Describe the Linux v7.2 escalation for an NVMe/PCIe I/O timeout.
    Model answerblk-mq timeout work calls nvme_timeout(): check disconnect/offline/CFS, poll the CQ, then send Abort (if Abort credits remain) and re-arm; on a second expiry, or for admin commands, disable and reset the controller; cancelled commands are retried up to max_retries.
  3. Senior How would you design timer values across PCIe, NVMe and the application?
    Model answerNest them: lower layers must fire first with margins of at least an order of magnitude (CTO in ms, NVMe command timeout in tens of seconds, application or cluster failover above that), and make sure device-advertised limits (CAP.TO, MTFA, RTD3E, ANATT) are below the corresponding host waits.
✅ Mastery gate
  • I can name the unit of CAP.TO, CRTO, MTFA, CRDT, KATO, KAS, RTD3E, EDSTT and ANATT without looking.
  • I can explain which timer fires first for a lost device DMA read and why.
  • I can read a Linux timeout message and tell whether it was polled, aborted or reset.
  • I can measure CC.EN→RDY, doorbell→CQE and MRd→CplD intervals on a PEX trace.
  • I can separate a slow device from a slow host using trace and tracepoint timestamps.

PART IV

Silent Failures: Success That Isn't

The worst failures are the ones that never show up anywhere. The command is sent, the device accepts it, it posts a completion with status 0 (Success), and the analyzer, the kernel log and the SMART log all look clean. But the drive did not do the job: blocks that should be deallocated are still there, a flush did not reach the NAND, a write went to the wrong place, an erase left data behind. This part starts with a full worked chapter on the case you raised: "I wrote 10 GB, trimmed the last 5 GB, the drive said Success, and nothing changed." Then it lists every other kind of silent or semantic failure as an error card (D-01 to D-33), and ends with a chapter on how to catch them. The main idea of this part: a Success completion only means the controller accepted the command. To know the command did its job, you need a separate check that reads the result back.

IV.1 The deallocate that didn't: a full worked case

← III.6 Measuring Time on a PEX TraceIV.2 Deallocate, Write Zeroes and allocation accounting: the error cards →
📌 The question this chapter answers

After writing 10 GiB to a namespace, the host deallocates (trims/discards) the last 5 GiB. The drive completes the command with Success, but it does not actually deallocate. The PEX trace (the Teledyne LeCroy PCIe analyzer capture) looks normal, dmesg shows nothing, and nvme error-log is empty. How do you find out what really happened, and how do you prove it either way?

IV.1.1 Why this chapter exists

Deallocate is the clearest example of a command whose acceptance is visible but whose effect is not. Every step you can see on the wire happens normally: the Dataset Management (DSM) command, the fetch of its range list, the completion queue entry (CQE) and the MSI-X interrupt. The step that matters, the flash translation layer (FTL) dropping the logical-to-physical mapping entries, happens inside the controller and never crosses the PCIe link. So a trace can never prove that deallocation happened. It can only prove that it was requested correctly. Proof has to come from somewhere else: what a later read returns, an error that only appears when a feature is turned on, the namespace utilization counter, or a performance signature.

There is a second, less obvious point. In many cases the NVMe specification allows the drive to "not deallocate" without being wrong. Before calling a drive broken, you must work out which guarantee it actually made. The Identify Namespace fields DLFEAT and NSFEAT tell you that, and this chapter shows how to read them.

  • Trace a discard from fstrim/blkdiscard/file truncate through the Linux v7.2 block layer and nvme_setup_discard() down to the DSM command and its 16-byte range descriptors.
  • Know what Linux v7.2 sends in each case: DSM with the Attribute – Deallocate (AD) bit, or Write Zeroes with the Deallocate (DEAC) bit. Know the quirks that change this (NVME_QUIRK_DEALLOCATE_ZEROES, NVME_QUIRK_DISABLE_WRITE_ZEROES).
  • Say exactly what the NVMe specification promises for deallocated blocks (DLFEAT read behaviour, DULBE, NUSE), and what it does not promise.
  • Explain why the analyzer trace, the kernel log and the error log all look normal.
  • Prove whether deallocation happened, using five independent kinds of evidence, and run the procedure as a CAUTION lab on a spare drive.
📭 What the spec does not say

The spec does not define the drive's internal mapping table, when garbage collection runs, or how fast deallocated space is reclaimed. Deallocation is described by its visible effects: what a read of a deallocated block returns (DLFEAT), whether a read can be made to fail (DULBE), and how the Namespace Utilization (NUSE) count behaves. If a drive gives none of these guarantees, "it didn't deallocate" may be impossible to see from outside, and may not even count as a failure.

IV.1.2 The story, the analogy, and where the analogy breaks

A validation engineer runs a simple script on a 1 TB drive formatted with 4096-byte logical blocks. The script writes a known pattern over LBAs 0 to 2,621,439 (10 GiB), then runs blkdiscard --offset 5GiB --length 5GiB /dev/nvme0n1. The command returns 0. The analyzer captured one DSM command and a Success completion. Then the engineer reads LBA 2,000,000 and gets the original pattern back, not zeroes. Is the drive broken? That depends on DLFEAT. If DLFEAT says reads of deallocated blocks return zeroes (read behaviour 001b), the drive has broken its promise: it either did not deallocate, or it deallocated and then returned stale data. If DLFEAT says 000b ("not reported"), old data is an allowed result and the read-back proves nothing.

🌍 Analogy

You tell a warehouse to "throw away everything on shelves 50 to 99". The clerk signs the form and hands it back. The signed form is the CQE. Whether the shelves are actually empty, you only find out by walking over and looking (a read), by asking for the inventory count (NUSE), or by noticing that the warehouse suddenly has room for new deliveries (better write performance).

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

In a real warehouse an empty shelf always looks empty. In an SSD, the drive may be allowed to show you the old content of a "thrown away" shelf (DLFEAT read behaviour 000b), so looking is not always proof. Also, the drive may legally throw things away later (in the background). The only thing it must get right immediately is what a read returns, and only when it has promised a value.

IV.1.3 The host path in Linux v7.2: who turns "free these blocks" into NVMe commands

There are three common ways the request starts. All of them end in the block layer as a REQ_OP_DISCARD (or REQ_OP_WRITE_ZEROES) request, which the NVMe driver turns into an NVMe command in nvme_setup_cmd().

Where it startsWhat happens before the NVMe driverEasy-to-miss trap
blkdiscard -o 5GiB -l 5GiB /dev/nvme0n1BLKDISCARD ioctl on the raw block device → blkdev_issue_discard() (in block/blk-lib.c; that file is not in the local source snapshot used for this atlas, so the name comes from general kernel knowledge) → discard bios.Fails with EOPNOTSUPP if the queue's discard_max_bytes is 0. This is the one case where you are told something.
fstrim -v /mntFITRIM ioctl → the filesystem walks its free-space map and issues discards for free extents only.The "N GiB trimmed" number is what the filesystem asked for, not what the drive did. Some filesystems report the whole free space every run.
File truncate / rm on a filesystem mounted with -o discardThe filesystem issues discards for freed extents, usually after the journal transaction commits (online discard).Without -o discard, a truncate sends nothing to the drive. The blocks are freed only in the filesystem's map until the next fstrim (often a weekly timer). File LBAs are also not "the last 5 GiB of the device".

Discard limits: how big pieces can be

drivers/nvme/host/core.c:nvme_update_disk_info() sets the queue limits from Identify data (v7.2, around lines 2123–2170):

  • Maximum discard size: if the controller reports DMRSL (Dataset Management Range Size Limit, from the I/O Command Set specific Identify Controller structure, read in nvme_init_non_mdts_limits()), then max_hw_discard_sectors is DMRSL converted to 512-byte sectors. Otherwise, if ONCS bit 2 (DSM supported) is set, it is UINT_MAX. If ONCS.DSM is clear, it is 0 and discard is disabled.
  • Maximum number of ranges: max_discard_segments = DMRL (Dataset Management Ranges Limit) if non-zero, else NVME_DSM_MAX_RANGES = 256.
  • Granularity: discard_granularity comes from NPDG/NPDGL and NPDA/NPDAL (preferred deallocate granularity and alignment) when the OPTPERF bits say they are valid, otherwise the logical block size. The block layer uses this to round discards, so a discard smaller than the granularity, or not aligned to it, may be trimmed or dropped on the host side before it is ever sent.

You can see all of this in sysfs: /sys/block/nvme0n1/queue/discard_max_bytes, discard_max_hw_bytes, discard_granularity, max_discard_segments, write_zeroes_max_bytes.

Building the DSM command: nvme_setup_discard()

drivers/nvme/host/core.c:nvme_setup_discard() (v7.2 line 840) does four things:

  1. It allocates a range buffer sized for all 256 ranges (sizeof(*range) * NVME_DSM_MAX_RANGES = 4096 bytes), even if only one range is used. The source comment says why: "Some devices do not consider the DSM 'Number of Ranges' field when determining how much data to DMA." This is a real device bug that the driver works around silently (see card D-32). If the allocation fails, it falls back to a per-controller discard_page.
  2. It fills one struct nvme_dsm_range per bio: cattr = 0 (context attributes), nlb = length in logical blocks, slba = starting LBA. Each descriptor is 16 bytes.
  3. It checks that the number of ranges built equals blk_rq_nr_discard_segments(). If not, it does WARN_ON_ONCE and fails the request with BLK_STS_IOERR. This is a host-side error you would see.
  4. It builds the 64-byte command: opcode nvme_cmd_dsm (09h), nr = segments − 1 (a 0's based count in CDW10), attributes = NVME_DSMGMT_AD (bit 2 of CDW11), and attaches the range buffer as a "special payload" (RQF_SPECIAL_PAYLOAD), so the PRP entries point at it.
/* Linux v7.2 drivers/nvme/host/core.c, nvme_setup_discard() (excerpt) */
	memset(cmnd, 0, sizeof(*cmnd));
	cmnd->dsm.opcode = nvme_cmd_dsm;
	cmnd->dsm.nsid = cpu_to_le32(ns->head->ns_id);
	cmnd->dsm.nr = cpu_to_le32(segments - 1);
	cmnd->dsm.attributes = cpu_to_le32(NVME_DSMGMT_AD);

	bvec_set_virt(&req->special_vec, range, alloc_size);
	req->rq_flags |= RQF_SPECIAL_PAYLOAD;

Note that Linux never sets IDR or IDW (Integral Dataset for Read/Write, bits 0 and 1). It sends only AD. Context attributes are always 0.

Write Zeroes and the DEAC bit: nvme_setup_write_zeroes()

REQ_OP_WRITE_ZEROES (from blkdev_issue_zeroout(), blkdiscard -z, fallocate zero-range, or filesystems) is handled by nvme_setup_write_zeroes() (v7.2 line 949):

  • If the controller has NVME_QUIRK_DEALLOCATE_ZEROES, the function simply calls nvme_setup_discard(): a "write zeroes" request is sent as a DSM deallocate. The quirk's comment says the controller "deterministically returns 0's on reads to logical blocks that deallocate was called on". In drivers/nvme/host/pci.c v7.2 this quirk is set for Intel device IDs 0953h (750/P3500/P3600/P3700) and 0A53h (P3520). With this quirk and ONCS.DSM set, max_write_zeroes_sectors becomes UINT_MAX.
  • Otherwise it builds a real Write Zeroes command (opcode 08h) with SLBA and NLB. It sets NVME_WZ_DEAC (bit 9 of the control word, so CDW12 bit 25) only if the request does not have REQ_NOUNMAP and the namespace has NVME_NS_DEAC.
  • NVME_NS_DEAC is set in nvme_update_ns_info_block() (v7.2 around line 2483) only when (dlfeat & 0x7) == 0x1 (deallocated blocks read as zeroes) and dlfeat bit 3 is set (Write Zeroes supports the Deallocate bit). The comment explains: the DEAC bit itself does not require zeroes, "it must be a no-op if reads from deallocated data do not return zeroes".
  • If PI is enabled, it also sets PRACT so the controller generates protection information.

Write Zeroes can also be turned off: nvme_init_non_mdts_limits() sets max_zeroes_sectors to 0 if ONCS bit 3 (Write Zeroes) is clear or the controller has NVME_QUIRK_DISABLE_WRITE_ZEROES ("Broken Write Zeroes"). Many entries in the v7.2 nvme_id_table carry that quirk, including the Intel 600P/P3100 (F1A5h) and the QEMU emulated controller (Intel ID 5845h). When Write Zeroes is off, the block layer falls back to writing real zero-filled buffers, which is slower but cannot fail silently in the same way.

💡 Senior insight: the quirk table is a list of drives that lied

Each entry in nvme_id_table is a drive that once failed silently or behaved against the spec, and someone found out the hard way. NVME_QUIRK_DEALLOCATE_ZEROES goes the other way: the drive guaranteed more than it said in Identify, so Linux trusts it more. When a new drive behaves strangely, read the quirk list first. If your drive's vendor already has entries, look at what they were for.

🔧 What Linux v7.2 does after the CQE

When the DSM completes with status 0, nvme_complete_rq() finishes the request with BLK_STS_OK and nvme_cleanup_cmd() frees the range buffer (or releases discard_page). Nothing checks the result. There is no read-back, no NUSE check, nothing. If the DSM fails, nvme_error_status() maps the status: Invalid Field / Invalid Opcode → BLK_STS_NOTSUPP, LBA Out of Range → BLK_STS_TARGET, others → BLK_STS_IOERR, and nvme_log_error() prints a rate-limited line such as nvme0n1: Dataset Management(0x9) @ LBA …, … blocks, … (sct 0x0 / sc 0x2). So you only get a log line when the drive refuses. A drive that accepts and then does nothing leaves no trace at all.

IV.1.4 What the specification actually promises

The table separates what can be checked in the local sources (Linux headers, libnvme types.h, the QEMU model) from what you should read in the NVM Command Set specification yourself. Field names are reliable. Exact normative wording is paraphrased, so verify in spec before quoting it in a bug report.

ItemWhereWhat it means for "did it deallocate?"Confidence
ONCS bit 2 (DSM) / bit 3 (Write Zeroes) / bit 11 (Write Zeroes Deallocate size limit, MAXWZD)Identify Controller, ONCSSays only that the commands are supported. Nothing about what deallocation does.verified (bit names in include/linux/nvme.h, libnvme enum nvme_id_ctrl_oncs)
DSM CDW11.AD (bit 2), CDW10.NR (0's based, up to 256 ranges), 16-byte range: Context Attributes, Length (NLB), Starting LBANVM Command Set, Dataset ManagementAD expresses the host's intent. It is generally understood to let the controller deallocate, without requiring it. Older base-spec text said the NVM subsystem "may" deallocate, and that a read of a deallocated LBA returns zeroes, ones, or the last data written. Newer specs tie read results to DLFEAT.Layout verified; "may" wording verify in spec
DLFEAT bits 2:0 read behaviour: 000b not reported, 001b reads return all 00h, 010b reads return all FFhIdentify Namespace, DLFEATThe key field. With 001b or 010b the drive promises a value, and a read-back can prove a failure. With 000b old data on read-back is allowed.verified (libnvme enum nvme_id_ns_dlfeat)
DLFEAT bit 3: Write Zeroes supports the Deallocate bit. Bit 4: Guard field of deallocated blocks with PI is the CRC of the returned data.Identify Namespace, DLFEATBit 3 together with RB = 001b is what makes Linux set DEAC. Bit 4 matters for PI namespaces: otherwise reading a deallocated block may raise a Guard error, or PI checks may be skipped for it verify in spec.verified (libnvme; Linux nvme_update_ns_info_block)
NSFEAT bit 2: DULBE supported. Feature 05h (Error Recovery) CDW11 bit 16: DULBE enable.Identify Namespace NSFEAT; Set Features FID 05hWhen supported and enabled, reads (and Compare/Verify) of deallocated or unwritten blocks fail with status 287h, "Deallocated or Unwritten Logical Block" (SCT 2h Media and Data Integrity). This turns deallocation into something you can observe as an error.Bits verified (libnvme NVME_FEAT_ERROR_RECOVERY_DULBE_SHIFT = 16; Linux NVME_SC_UNWRITTEN_BLOCK = 0x287); exact command coverage verify in spec
NSZE, NCAP, NUSE; NSFEAT bit 0 (THIN)Identify NamespaceNUSE = "current number of logical blocks allocated". If deallocation works and the drive tracks allocation, NUSE should go down by about the number of blocks deallocated (rounded to the internal granularity). Many drives report NUSE = NCAP all the time, and QEMU does exactly that (hw/nvme/ns.c: "no thin provisioning", nuse = ncap). In that case NUSE tells you nothing.Definition verified (libnvme comment); whether your drive tracks it is impl
NPDG/NPDA, NPDGL/NPDAL (preferred deallocate granularity / alignment)Identify Namespace / NVM CS Identify NamespaceDeallocating less than this, or misaligned, may have only partial effect inside the drive. It is a preference, not an error condition.verified (Linux comment cites NVM CS 1.1)
DMRL, DMRSL, WZDSLI/O Command Set specific Identify Controller (NVM)Limits on number of ranges, size of one range, and Write Zeroes size. What a controller does when a host exceeds them varies, see the QEMU note below.verified (Linux nvme_init_non_mdts_limits)
Get LBA Status (admin opcode 86h), OACS bit "GLSS"Admin commandMainly reports Potentially Unrecoverable LBAs (action types 10h/11h). libnvme also lists action type 02h "Return tracked allocated LBAs status", a newer addition. Do not assume Get LBA Status shows deallocation on a given drive. It does so only if action type 02h is supported, and its meaning should be verified in spec.Opcode verified; ATYPE 02h semantics version
Write ZeroesNVM Command SetUnlike DSM, Write Zeroes is a write: after it completes, reads must return zeroes (and PI as specified). With DEAC the controller may implement it by deallocating, but the read result is still mandatory. So Write Zeroes failing to zero is a clear spec violation, while DSM failing to deallocate often is not.derived from Linux DEAC comment + spec semantics; verify in spec
🏭 Implementation-dependent: the QEMU model skips ranges silently

The QEMU NVMe controller in the local snapshot (hw/nvme/ctrl.c:nvme_dsm_cb()) processes each range in turn. A range whose nlb is larger than n->dmrsl is skipped with only a trace event (pci_nvme_dsm_single_range_limit_exceeded, then goto next). A range that is out of bounds is also skipped (pci_nvme_err_invalid_lba_range, goto next). The command still completes with Success. QEMU also sets dlfeat = 0x9 (reads of deallocated blocks return zeroes, Write Zeroes supports DEAC) in nvme_ns_init(), and passes the discard to its block backend with blk_aio_pdiscard(). If that backend ignores discards (an option of the QEMU drive configuration, verify the default for your QEMU version), you get exactly the case in this chapter: DSM Success, DLFEAT promises zeroes, and a read-back returns old data. That makes QEMU a safe place to practise the proof procedure before using real hardware.

IV.1.5 What the PEX trace contains, and why it looks perfect

A PEX trace is a Teledyne LeCroy PCIe protocol-analyzer capture of the link between the root port (or switch) and the SSD. It records every TLP and DLLP that crosses that link, with timestamps, and the analyzer software decodes the NVMe structures inside the payloads: the 64-byte SQE in the completion data of the device's fetch, the DSM range list, the 16-byte CQE, and data buffers. For the trim of the last 5 GiB, this is everything the capture holds. Every packet is correct. A drive that deallocated and a drive that did nothing produce the same sequence, byte for byte, apart from timestamps.

Synthetic PEX-style trace — DSM deallocate of LBA 1,310,720 + 1,310,720 blocks (4 KiB LBA format), I/O queue 3, CID 0x1047. The good drive and the lying drive produce the SAME trace.
#Time (µs)DirTLPDecoded contentWhat it proves
10.000H→DMWr 32b, 4 BBAR0+0x1018 (SQ3 tail doorbell) = 0x0000_0012Host submitted one command
20.410D→HMRd 64b, 64 B, tag 0x21Address = SQ3 base + 0x11×64Device saw the doorbell and fetched the SQE
30.980H→DCplD 64 B, tag 0x21, SCSQE: OPC=09h (Dataset Management), CID=0x1047, NSID=1, PRP1=0x0_7F3A_1000, CDW10=0000_0000h (NR=0 → 1 range), CDW11=0000_0004h (AD=1)The command is a deallocate, not only an IDR/IDW hint
41.350D→HMRd 64b, 16 B, tag 0x22Address = 0x0_7F3A_1000 (range list)Device fetched the ranges. Length matters: 16 B for NR=0 is correct. A 4096-B read means it ignores NR (D-32). Less than 16×(NR+1) means it never saw some ranges (D-02).
51.910H→DCplD 16 B, tag 0x22, SCRange 0: CATTR=0000_0000h, NLB=0014_0000h (1,310,720), SLBA=0000_0000_0014_0000h (1,310,720)The exact LBAs requested: LBA 1,310,720 … 2,621,439 = the last 5 GiB. This is the only place they appear on the wire.
—1.9 … 9.6—(no TLPs)FTL updates its mapping table, or doesn'tInvisible. The link is idle either way.
69.640D→HMWr 64b, 16 BCQE to CQ3: DW0=0, SQHD=0x12, SQID=3, CID=0x1047, P=1, Status=0000h (SCT 0 / SC 0 = Success)Command accepted and finished without reported error
79.700D→HMWr 32b, 4 BMSI-X vector 4 message (address 0xFEE0_xxxx)Interrupt
811.200H→DMWr 32b, 4 BBAR0+0x101C (CQ3 head doorbell) = 0x12Host consumed the CQE. The trim is "done" for the host.

Why it looks perfect. The analyzer's protocol checks (TLP format, ordering, completion timeouts, credit flow, NVMe field decoding) all pass, because nothing here breaks a rule. The SQE is well-formed, the range list is fetched with the right length, the CQE matches the CID, the phase bit is right, and the interrupt follows the CQE. NVMe has no status code that means "accepted but I will not deallocate". The FTL change, which is the thing that failed, happens in controller memory and never produces a TLP. Timing does not help either: a drive that only logs the request and unmaps later in the background (legal) completes as fast as a drive that does nothing.

What the trace does tell you. (a) The deallocate was sent, which rules out the host-side drops in D-04. (b) It carried the LBAs you expected; wrong LBAs point to host bugs such as partition offsets, dm-crypt, LVM or granularity rounding. (c) It was fetched completely and accepted. It cannot tell you (d): did the FTL change.

The extra evidence, and how much of it can be put into the same capture

The proof comes from later commands whose results are visible as payloads. If you keep the analyzer running while you run the checks from section IV.1.7, the same PEX file can contain the proof. That is the best bug report you can hand a drive vendor: one capture with the promise, the trim and the broken result.

Synthetic PEX-style trace — the proof sequence captured after the trim (lying drive, DLFEAT = 09h, NSFEAT bit 2 = 1)
#DirTLPDecoded contentMeaning
9D→HMWr, 4096 B (in several MPS-sized TLPs)Identify Namespace data (admin CNS 00h, NSID 1): bytes 16–23 NUSE = 0x0000_0000_0028_0000 (2,621,440); byte 24 NSFEAT = 05h; byte 33 DLFEAT = 09hThe promise (zeroes after deallocate, DULBE supported) is on the wire. NUSE did not drop by 1,310,720.
10H→D / D→HSQE fetch + CQERead: OPC=02h, SLBA=2,000,000 (0x1E8480), NLB=0 (1 block), CID=0x1050 → Status 0The read is accepted
11D→HMWr, 4096 BData payload to the read buffer: A5 A5 A5 A5 … 4c 1e 00 … (the fio verify header and pattern written before the trim)Visible proof: DLFEAT RB = 001b promises 00h, and the drive returned the old data
12H→D / D→HAdmin SQE + CQESet Features FID=05h, CDW11=0001_0000h (DULBE=1) → SuccessError for deallocated/unwritten blocks enabled
13D→HMWr 4096 B + CQERead SLBA 2,000,000 → data payload returned, CQE Status = 0Expected CQE Status SCT 2h / SC 87h (287h, Deallocated or Unwritten Logical Block). Success means the drive still treats the block as allocated.
14D→HCQE onlyRead SLBA 2,621,440 (never written) → CQE Status SCT 2h / SC 87h, no data MWrControl: DULBE works, so step 13 is meaningful
EvidenceIn the PEX trace?Where to look
Deallocate requested, which LBAsVisibleSQE CplD (OPC 09h, CDW11 bit 2) and range-list CplD
Deallocate acceptedVisibleCQE MWr, Status 0
FTL unmapped the LBAsNot visibleOnly indirectly, through the rows below
DLFEAT/NSFEAT promiseVisible if Identify is capturedIdentify Namespace data MWr, bytes 24 and 33
Read after trim returns old dataVisibleRead data MWr payload. It is proof only if DLFEAT RB = 001b/010b.

🔍 Host-side trace without an analyzer

Linux tracepoints show the command but not the ranges: nvme_setup_cmd for a DSM prints nr=…, attributes=… via drivers/nvme/host/trace.c:nvme_trace_dsm(), and attributes=4 means AD. The LBAs live in the payload, so to see them use blktrace/blkparse (discard requests show RWBS containing D with sector and size), or a bpftrace probe on nvme_setup_discard. The PEX trace is the only view that shows the range list as the device fetched it.

IV.1.6 The discard path and where the evidence is: interactive figure

Click a step to follow one deallocate from the filesystem to the FTL, and then the probes you use afterwards to get evidence. Grey dashed arrows are inside the SSD and never appear on PCIe. Those are exactly the steps an analyzer cannot show you. synthetic

Software / host starts itDevice starts it (visible on PCIe)Inside the SSD (NOT visible on PCIe)PCIe link
  1. The filesystem or tool asks the block layer to discard

    blkdiscard (BLKDISCARD ioctl), fstrim (FITRIM) or a filesystem mounted with -o discard after a truncate creates discard bios. If the filesystem is not mounted with discard, a truncate stops here and nothing is ever sent.

    Where: kernel, block layer entryPCIe: No
    blkdiscard -o 5368709120 -l 5368709120 /dev/nvme0n1 → REQ_OP_DISCARD, sector 10485760, 10485760 sectors (512 B units)
  2. The block layer splits the discard; the driver builds the DSM command and range list

    The block layer cuts the request to discard_max_bytes, granularity and max_discard_segments. nvme_setup_discard() writes one 16-byte range per bio into a 4096-byte buffer and builds the 64-byte SQE with opcode 09h, NR = ranges − 1, and AD set.

    Where: host memory (SQ slot + range buffer)PCIe: No. The CPU writes its own RAM.
    SQE: OPC=09h CID=0x1047 NSID=1 CDW10=0 (NR=0 → 1 range) CDW11=4 (AD) Range[0]: CATTR=0 NLB=0x140000 SLBA=0x140000 (Large requests may become several ranges or several DSM commands: check with blktrace.)
  3. The driver rings the SQ tail doorbell

    A 4-byte posted write to the SQ3 tail doorbell. Only the new tail index crosses the link.

    Where: BAR0 + 1000h + (2·3)·(4<<DSTRD)PCIe: Yes, host → device · MWr 4 B
    With DSTRD=0: offset 0x1018, value 0x12
  4. The controller fetches the SQE

    A memory read of the 64-byte slot. An analyzer that decodes NVMe shows "Dataset Management, AD".

    Where: host memory, SQ3 slot 0x11PCIe: Yes · MRd 64 B + CplD
    First evidence point: the command IS a deallocate (CDW11 bit 2 = 1).
  5. The controller fetches the range list

    The controller reads the range descriptors from PRP1. This is the only place on the wire where the LBAs appear. Check that the read length matches 16 × (NR+1). A 4096-byte read when NR=0 shows the device ignores NR, the bug Linux allocates around.

    Where: host memory, range bufferPCIe: Yes · MRd 16 B (expected) + CplD
    Second evidence point: SLBA 0x140000, NLB 0x140000 → exactly LBAs 1,310,720 … 2,621,439
  6. Internal: the FTL unmaps the LBAs (or doesn't)

    A correct drive marks the mapping entries invalid (often lazily, in a journal or bitmap). A lying drive does nothing, or only part of it. The old NAND pages stay physically present until garbage collection either way. This is the step in question, and it is invisible.

    Where: controller SRAM/DRAM, FTL metadataPCIe: No. Nothing differs on the link.
    Good: 1,310,720 map entries → UNMAPPED (NUSE −1,310,720 if tracked) Bad: 0 map entries changed; same CQE, same timing
  7. The controller posts a Success CQE

    A 16-byte completion with status 0. This means the command was accepted and processed without an error the controller chose to report. It does not mean the blocks are now deallocated.

    Where: host memory, CQ3PCIe: Yes, device → host · MWr 16 B
    DW2: SQHD=0x12 SQID=3 DW3: CID=0x1047 P=1 Status=0x0000
  8. MSI-X interrupt; Linux completes the request

    The handler calls nvme_handle_cqe(), the request ends with BLK_STS_OK, the range buffer is freed, blkdiscard exits 0. No log line is printed.

    Where: CPU, nvme_irq → nvme_handle_cqePCIe: Yes · MWr 4 B to MSI-X address
    dmesg: (nothing) nvme error-log: (no new entry)
  9. Evidence queries: Identify Namespace, log pages, and Reads

    The host sends normal admin and I/O commands to measure the result: Identify Namespace (NUSE, DLFEAT, NSFEAT), Get Features 05h (DULBE), SMART log, Get LBA Status if supported, and Reads of sample LBAs from inside, at the edges of, and outside the range.

    Where: admin and I/O queuesPCIe: Yes · normal command traffic
    nvme id-ns /dev/nvme0n1 -H | grep -iE 'nuse|dlfeat|nsfeat' nvme read /dev/nvme0n1 -s 2000000 -c 0 -z 4096 -d out.bin
  10. Read-back data or a DULBE error comes back: this is the evidence

    The NAND→controller step is internal. The data (or error status) the controller returns is on the wire and in your buffer. Compare it with the DLFEAT promise: zeroes, FFh, an error 287h (DULBE enabled), or the old pattern.

    Where: host memory, read buffer / CQE statusPCIe: Yes · MWr data + CQE
    DLFEAT RB=001b and data = old pattern → PROVEN failure DLFEAT RB=000b and data = old pattern → allowed; use DULBE / NUSE instead

IV.1.7 How to prove it: the evidence ladder

Use the strongest evidence the drive supports. Each rung says what it proves, what it cannot prove, and when it applies. Rung 0 always comes first. Most reported cases of "the drive ignored my trim" turn out to be a discard that never left the host.

RungMethodProvesCannot prove / caveatsNeeds
0blktrace / tracepoint / analyzer: DSM with AD sent, ranges as expected, Success CQEThe host asked correctly and the device accepted itAnything about the FTLAlways possible
1Read-back of sample LBAs, compared with the DLFEAT read behaviourWith RB = 001b/010b: any old data = violation proven. All zeroes/FFh = consistent with deallocation (or with a Write Zeroes-like implementation).With RB = 000b old data is legal. Data matching the promised pattern does not prove the space was reclaimed internally.DLFEAT RB ≠ 000b
2DULBE: enable Feature 05h bit 16, then read sample LBAs with passthroughStatus 287h (Deallocated or Unwritten Logical Block) for blocks in the range = the controller's own metadata says they are deallocated. Success with old data = not deallocated.Only if NSFEAT bit 2 = 1. Affects every reader of the namespace (Linux returns BLK_STS_MEDIUM, so filesystems will see I/O errors).NSFEAT.DULBE
3NUSE before/after (Identify Namespace)A drop of about NLB (± granularity) = allocation accounting changedMany drives report NUSE = NCAP always. NUSE may update lazily. It counts the whole namespace, so other writers skew it.Drive that tracks NUSE (test: does NUSE drop after a Format? after a known-good DSM?)
4Get LBA Status with action type 02h (tracked allocated), where supportedPer-range allocation view from the controllerNewer feature. Action types 10h/11h report potentially unrecoverable LBAs, not deallocation. versionOACS.GLSS + ATYPE 02h support
5Performance / write amplification signatureAfter real deallocation of half the drive, sustained random writes over the other half run faster and with lower write amplification than a control run without deallocateIndirect and statistical. Needs a preconditioned drive and a control. Some drives reclaim slowly.Hours of drive time; vendor NAND-write counter helps
6SMART / vendor logs: host vs NAND writesData Units Written should not change from DSM. A vendor "NAND bytes written" counter lets you compute write amplification for rung 5.SMART has no "deallocated" counter. Vendor log formats are vendor- or OCP-specific impl.Vendor/OCP log support
7Vendor debug (FTL dump, internal trace)Direct view of the mapUnder NDA, firmware-specificVendor engagement
🐞 Decision procedure
  1. Did it leave the host? If there is no DSM/Write Zeroes in blktrace or the analyzer, the bug is host-side (D-04). Stop and fix the mount option, dm layer or discard_max_bytes.
  2. Were the ranges right? Decode the range list. If the LBAs are wrong, it is a partition/LVM/offset bug, not a drive bug.
  3. Was it rejected? A non-zero status shows in dmesg via nvme_log_error() and in nvme error-log. Not silent.
  4. What did the drive promise? nvme id-ns -H: DLFEAT RB, NSFEAT DULBE/THIN, NPDG/NPDA. nvme id-ctrl -H: ONCS, OACS.GLSS. NVM Identify Controller (nvme nvm-id-ctrl, if your nvme-cli has it): DMRL, DMRSL.
  5. Pick the strongest rung (1 > 2 > 3 > 4 > 5) the promises allow, and repeat with a known-good reference drive or the QEMU model as a control.
  6. Classify: promise broken (RB=001b, old data back) → D-01/D-03, a spec violation. Partial (edges or some ranges only) → D-02. No promise, accounting unchanged → "deallocate not effective", a quality or performance issue for the vendor, not a conformance failure.

IV.1.8 Worked example with numbers synthetic

Drive: 1.0 TB, one namespace, LBA format 4096 + 0 (lba_shift 12). Identify Namespace: NSZE = NCAP = 244,190,646. NSFEAT = 05h (THIN + DULBE). DLFEAT = 09h (RB 001b + Write Zeroes DEAC). NPDG = NPDA = 7 (0's based → 8 blocks = 32 KiB). NVM Identify Controller: DMRL = 0, DMRSL = 0.

LBAs written = 10 GiB / 4096 = 2,621,440 (LBA 0 … 2,621,439)
Range to deallocate = LBA 1,310,720 (0x140000), NLB = 1,310,720 (0x140000)
Granularity check: 1,310,720 mod 8 = 0 and 1,310,720 mod 8 = 0 → aligned
  • NUSE expected — before: ≥ 2,621,440 (plus any earlier data); after: before − 1,310,720, within one granule (8 blocks) per range edge.
  • DLFEAT 09h — reads of deallocated blocks must return 00h, and Linux will set DEAC on Write Zeroes for this namespace.

Observations on the "lying" drive: DSM completes in 11 µs with status 0. nvme id-ns NUSE before = 2,621,440, after = 2,621,440 (unchanged, even after 60 s idle). Reads of LBA 1,310,720, 2,000,000 and 2,621,439 return the original pattern. With DULBE enabled, reading LBA 2,000,000 returns Success, not 287h. Reads of LBA 2,621,440 (never written) do return 287h, which proves DULBE works and the drive tracks unwritten blocks. Conclusion: the drive promised zeroes (RB 001b) and returned old data. Its own allocation tracking (DULBE, NUSE) shows the range is still mapped. The deallocate was accepted and not performed. This is a conformance failure, card D-01, and the evidence package is: the trace (rungs 0), Identify before/after, read-back dumps, and the DULBE control read.

🧪 Lab IV.1 — Prove or disprove a deallocate on a spare drive CAUTION LAB
⚠️ Destroys data

Every write, discard and Set Features below acts on the whole namespace. Use a spare drive or a QEMU NVMe device with nothing mounted, and double-check the device name (nvme list, lsblk). Enabling DULBE makes reads of unwritten blocks fail for all users of the namespace. Turn it off again at the end. Never run this on a disk holding a filesystem you care about.

Objective. Write 10 GiB of verifiable data, deallocate the last 5 GiB, and collect at least three independent kinds of evidence about whether deallocation took effect.

Setup. Linux with nvme-cli, fio, util-linux (blkdiscard), optionally blktrace. Note the namespace's LBA size (nvme id-ns -H, "in use" LBA format). The example assumes 4096-byte LBAs; recompute LBA numbers for 512.

# 0. What does the drive promise?  (read-only)
DEV=/dev/nvme0n1; CTRL=/dev/nvme0
nvme id-ctrl $CTRL -H | grep -iE 'oncs|oacs|vwc'
nvme id-ns   $DEV  -H | grep -iE 'nsze|ncap|nuse|nsfeat|dlfeat|npdg|npda|in use'
cat /sys/block/nvme0n1/queue/{discard_max_bytes,discard_granularity,max_discard_segments,write_zeroes_max_bytes}
nvme get-feature $CTRL -f 0x05 -n 1 -H          # Error Recovery (TLER, DULBE)

# 1. Write 10 GiB of self-verifying data (header with offset + checksum per block)
fio --name=fill --filename=$DEV --rw=write --bs=128k --size=10G --direct=1 \
    --verify=crc32c --do_verify=0 --ioengine=libaio --iodepth=16
nvme id-ns $DEV | grep -i nuse            # record NUSE_1

# 2. Optional: start blktrace in another shell to capture the discard
#    blktrace -d $DEV -o - | blkparse -i - | grep ' D '

# 3. Deallocate the last 5 GiB (LBA 1310720, 1310720 blocks)
blkdiscard --offset 5GiB --length 5GiB $DEV ; echo "exit=$?"
sleep 30
nvme id-ns $DEV | grep -i nuse            # record NUSE_2

# 4. Read-back: inside, both edges, and just outside the range
for L in 1310719 1310720 2000000 2621439; do
  nvme read $DEV -s $L -c 0 -z 4096 -d /tmp/lba_$L.bin
  echo "LBA $L:"; od -A d -t x1 /tmp/lba_$L.bin | head -2
done

# 5. DULBE (only if NSFEAT bit 2 = 1): enable, read, disable
nvme set-feature $CTRL -f 0x05 -n 1 -v 0x10000
nvme read $DEV -s 2000000 -c 0 -z 4096 -d /dev/null   # expect status 0x287 if deallocated
nvme read $DEV -s 2621440 -c 0 -z 4096 -d /dev/null   # never written: control, expect 0x287
nvme set-feature $CTRL -f 0x05 -n 1 -v 0x0

# 6. fio verify of the first half must still pass (deallocate must not touch it)
fio --name=check --filename=$DEV --rw=read --bs=128k --size=5G --direct=1 \
    --verify=crc32c --verify_only --ioengine=libaio

Observations to record: DLFEAT RB, NSFEAT bits, NUSE_1 and NUSE_2, the first bytes of each read-back, DULBE statuses, the fio verify result for the first half, and (if captured) the discard line from blkparse with its sector and size.

Questions. (1) If LBA 1,310,719 (just outside) reads back as zeroes, what went wrong? (2) If NUSE does not change but read-backs are zero, is the drive failing? (3) Why is the never-written LBA a necessary control for step 5?

Solution

(1) The deallocate covered too much. Either the host rounded the range out (granularity or offset error, check blkparse) or the drive deallocated outside the range. Both are serious, see D-02. (2) Not necessarily. NUSE may be reported as NCAP on drives that do not track allocation, or update lazily. Zero read-back with RB=001b means the promise was kept. (3) It proves DULBE is really enabled and implemented. Without it, "Success" on LBA 2,000,000 could mean "DULBE is ignored" rather than "block still allocated".

Extension. Repeat with blkdiscard -z (Write Zeroes; with DLFEAT 09h Linux sets DEAC) and compare. Repeat in QEMU with a backend that ignores discards to reproduce a "lying" controller, and with one that honours them as a control.

IV.1.9 Common mistakes

  • Treating the Success CQE as proof. It shows acceptance. For DSM it is not even a promise of action.
  • Calling old data on read-back a failure when DLFEAT RB = 000b. That is allowed. Use DULBE or NUSE instead.
  • Testing through a filesystem. File extents are not device LBAs, discard may be deferred or not sent at all, and the filesystem may never read freed blocks again. Test on the raw namespace.
  • Ignoring granularity. Ranges not aligned to NPDA/NPDG may be partly deallocated by design. Test aligned and misaligned cases separately.
  • Measuring right after the CQE only. Background unmapping is legal for the internal space accounting. Check NUSE again after idle time. Read results must be correct immediately.
  • Leaving DULBE enabled. A filesystem reading never-written metadata areas will see I/O errors.

Quiz

  1. Which Identify Namespace field decides whether a read-back of old data after a deallocate is a spec violation?

    Answer

    DLFEAT bits 2:0 (read behaviour). 001b promises zeroes, 010b promises FFh, 000b promises nothing.

  2. Under what exact condition does Linux v7.2 set the DEAC bit in Write Zeroes?

    Answer

    When (dlfeat & 7) == 1 and dlfeat bit 3 is set (so NVME_NS_DEAC is set), and the request does not carry REQ_NOUNMAP. With NVME_QUIRK_DEALLOCATE_ZEROES it sends a DSM instead of Write Zeroes at all.

  3. Where in a PCIe trace do the LBAs of a deallocate appear?

    Answer

    Only in the CplD that returns the range list to the device's MRd at PRP1. They are not in the SQE.

  4. Why does nvme_setup_discard() always allocate 4096 bytes for ranges?

    Answer

    Some devices ignore the NR field and DMA-read the maximum of 256 ranges. A small buffer would make them read past its end (card D-32).

  5. Which status code does a DULBE-enabled read of a deallocated LBA return, and what does Linux turn it into?

    Answer

    287h "Deallocated or Unwritten Logical Block" (SCT 2h). nvme_error_status() maps it to BLK_STS_MEDIUM.

Interview questions

  1. Beginner Why can't a protocol analyzer show whether a trim worked?
    Model answerThe analyzer sees the PCIe link. The DSM command, its range list and the completion are on the link, but the FTL change is inside the controller. A drive that unmaps and one that does nothing produce identical traffic.
  2. Intermediate A customer says "fstrim says 400 GiB trimmed but performance never recovers." Walk through your investigation.
    Model answerFirst confirm discards reach the device (blktrace for D requests, tracepoint nvme_setup_cmd with attributes=4, dm layers' discard passthrough, discard_max_bytes). Then check promises (DLFEAT, NSFEAT, NPDG), then do a raw-device controlled test: write, deallocate, read-back per DLFEAT, DULBE probe, NUSE delta. Finally a performance A/B with a control. fstrim's number is the request size, not the effect.
  3. Senior When is "deallocate not performed" a conformance bug and when is it a quality issue?
    Model answerConformance: when an observable promise is broken: DLFEAT RB 001b/010b with old data returned, DULBE enabled and supported but a deallocated block reads Success, Write Zeroes (with or without DEAC) not returning zeroes. Quality: with RB 000b and no DULBE/NUSE tracking, nothing observable is promised, so a no-op deallocate only costs space and performance. That is a vendor-qualification problem, and you prove it with performance and write-amplification A/B tests.
✅ Mastery gate
  • I can name the Linux v7.2 functions from discard request to SQE, and the limits that apply.
  • I can read DLFEAT/NSFEAT and state what a read-back can prove for this drive.
  • I can explain to a manager why a clean trace is not evidence.
  • I have run Lab IV.1 on QEMU or a spare drive and recorded three independent kinds of evidence.

Summary. A deallocate is visible on the wire only as a request and an acceptance. Whether it took effect is visible only through promised read behaviour (DLFEAT), errors you can turn on (DULBE), allocation accounting (NUSE, Get LBA Status 02h), or long-term performance. Rule out host-side drops first, then use the strongest evidence the drive supports. The next chapter turns each variant of this problem into an error card.

IV.2 Deallocate, Write Zeroes and allocation accounting: the error cards

← IV.1 The deallocate that didn't: a full worked caseIV.3 Durability and data-integrity failures: acknowledged but not true →

This chapter turns the worked case into cards you can look up. Each card says what the failure is, what is (and is not) reported, the spec basis, how to prove it, and how to provoke it. "Silent" means the command completes with Success and nothing appears in dmesg, nvme error-log or the SMART log. The cards share one rule: check the drive's promises first (DLFEAT, NSFEAT, ONCS, granularity), because they decide whether the observed behaviour is a spec violation or only a quality problem.

OperationLinux v7.2 sendsWhat must be true afterwardsCan a silent failure be proven by read-back?
blkdiscard, fstrim, online discardDSM 09h, CDW11.AD=1 (nvme_setup_discard)Only what DLFEAT/DULBE promiseYes if DLFEAT RB ≠ 000b or DULBE supported, otherwise only indirectly
blkdiscard -z, BLKZEROOUT, zero-rangeWrite Zeroes 08h (+DEAC if NVME_NS_DEAC), or DSM if NVME_QUIRK_DEALLOCATE_ZEROES, or plain zero-filled Writes if Write Zeroes is disabledReads return zeroes (Write Zeroes is a write)Yes, always
Sanitize / Format (Part IV.4)Admin 84h / 80h via passthroughPer action (block erase, crypto erase, overwrite)Partly: read-back proves the logical view only, not the physical media
D-01Deallocate accepted but not performed SilentNVMe command
In a PEX trace
Partly visible The DSM SQE (OPC 09h, CDW11=4), the range-list fetch with SLBA/NLB, the Success CQE and MSI-X are all visible and look perfect. The failure itself is not. Partial clue: if the capture also holds the Identify Namespace data (DLFEAT RB=001b/010b) and a later Read of the range, a non-zero data payload in that Read proves it. Detail: Identical to a good deallocate: doorbell MWr, MRd of the 64-byte SQE (OPC 09h, CDW11 = 4), MRd of 16×(NR+1) bytes of ranges, MWr of a CQE with status 0, MSI-X. The DSM exchange itself never shows the failure; only the absence of a later effect does.
What happens
The host sends DSM with AD=1 for a range. The controller fetches the range list, completes with status 0, and leaves every LBA in the range mapped. Old data, space accounting and garbage-collection load stay as if nothing happened.
How it shows up
Nothing is reported: CQE status 0, no dmesg line, no Error Information log entry, no AER. blkdiscard/fstrim exit 0. Over time sustained write performance and endurance are worse than expected, because the drive keeps moving data the host no longer needs.
Spec basis
NVM Command Set: Dataset Management, Attribute – Deallocate. Identify Namespace DLFEAT (read behaviour bits 2:0), NSFEAT bit 2 (DULBE), NUSE; Feature 05h DULBE bit. Whether doing nothing is a violation depends on these promises. AD is widely described as advisory verify in spec.
Typical causes
