Firmware treats AD as a hint and drops it under load or when the queue of unmap work is full. Ranges smaller than the internal mapping unit are ignored. Firmware feature disabled in a SKU. A bug where a multi-range DSM processes only range 0.
How to detect / prove

1) Confirm the DSM and its ranges on the wire or with blktrace (rule out D-04). 2) If DLFEAT RB = 001b/010b: read back sample LBAs; old data = proven. 3) If NSFEAT.DULBE: enable Feature 05h bit 16 and read; Success instead of status 287h = not deallocated (control: a never-written LBA must give 287h). 4) NUSE before/after (if the drive tracks it). 5) Performance A/B against a run without deallocate.

Linux v7.2 source
drivers/nvme/host/core.c:nvme_setup_discard() builds the command; nvme_update_disk_info() sets discard limits; nvme_cleanup_cmd() frees the range buffer. No code path verifies the effect.
Test to provoke it
Lab IV.1 CAUTION: write a pattern, deallocate an aligned range, read back per DLFEAT, DULBE probe, NUSE delta. Vary the range size (1 granule, 1 GiB, whole namespace), number of ranges (1, 2, 256), and queue depth of concurrent writes. In QEMU, a backend that ignores discards reproduces it on purpose.
D-02Deallocate partially performed: ranges or edges silently skipped SilentNVMe command
In a PEX trace
Partly visible The range descriptors and the length of the range-list MRd are visible, so a device that fetched fewer than 16×(NR+1) bytes is caught. Which ranges took effect is not visible, except through later Read payloads at range edges. Detail: Decode every range descriptor in the range-list CplD. Confirm that NR+1 descriptors were fetched (the MRd length). If the device fetched fewer bytes than 16×(NR+1), it cannot have processed the later ranges. That is the one case where the trace does show a partial deallocate.
What happens
Only part of the request takes effect: the first range of a multi-range DSM, only fully-aligned granules (the unaligned head and tail are kept), or every range except the ones larger than an internal limit. The CQE is still Success.
How it shows up
Silent. Read-back gives zeroes in the middle of the range and old data near the edges, or in whole sub-ranges. NUSE drops by less than NLB.
Spec basis
NPDG/NPDA and NPDGL/NPDAL are preferred granularity and alignment. Unaligned deallocates are allowed, and how much is deallocated is implementation-dependent unless DLFEAT promises a read value for each deallocated LBA. DMRL/DMRSL are limits the host should honour. What a controller must do when they are exceeded: verify in spec.
Typical causes
Internal mapping unit larger than the LBA size (for example 4 KiB map on 512-byte LBAs). Range-count or range-size limits handled with a silent "skip". The QEMU model does exactly this: hw/nvme/ctrl.c:nvme_dsm_cb() skips a range with nlb > dmrsl or out-of-bounds LBAs, emits only a trace event, and completes Success.
How to detect / prove
Read back the first and last LBA of every range, plus one LBA either side of each. With DLFEAT RB = 001b, any non-zero LBA inside a range is a violation, whatever the alignment. Check NUSE delta against Σ NLB. For multi-range, use distinct patterns per range so you can tell which range was skipped.
Linux v7.2 source
core.c:nvme_update_disk_info() (discard_granularity from NPDG/NPDA/NPDGL/NPDAL; max_discard_segments from DMRL or 256; max_hw_discard_sectors from DMRSL); core.c:nvme_init_non_mdts_limits() reads DMRL/DMRSL.
Test to provoke it
CAUTION With nvme dsm passthrough (bypasses the block layer's rounding): issue ranges that start or end off the NPDA boundary, 256-range DSMs, and a range just above DMRSL. Check every edge LBA. Run on QEMU first to see the skip behaviour in its trace events.
D-03Read after deallocate returns old data (DLFEAT promise broken) SilentData integrity
In a PEX trace
Visible If the capture includes the Identify Namespace payload (DLFEAT), the DSM, and the later Read, the Read data payload carrying the old pattern instead of the promised 00h/FFh is direct proof on the wire. Detail: The later Read's data MWr TLPs carry the old pattern. This is one of the few silent failures where the proof itself is visible on the wire, in the read data payload.
What happens
The namespace reports DLFEAT read behaviour 001b (zeroes) or 010b (FFh). After a successful deallocate, a Read returns the previous contents of the block. Either the FTL did not unmap it, or it unmapped and a cache (read buffer, write cache, read-ahead) still returns the old page.
How it shows up
Read completes Success with stale data. With PI enabled, the stale PI may still be valid for the old data, so even PI checks pass.
Spec basis
Identify Namespace DLFEAT bits 2:0. With 001b/010b the read result is defined. Returning old data is a conformance failure. Linux relies on this promise: nvme_update_ns_info_block() enables DEAC only when RB = 001b and DLFEAT bit 3 is set.
Typical causes
Deallocate not performed (D-01). Unmap applied to the map but not invalidated in an internal read cache. A race between a write still in the volatile cache and the deallocate (ordering bug). Unmap lost across a power cycle (the unmap journal was not persisted, so after power-on the old mapping comes back). The last case is the nastiest: data deleted for security reasons reappears.
How to detect / prove
Read-back right after the CQE, again after idle, and again after a clean power cycle (nvme subsystem-reset or a real power cycle). Any non-promised value at any point is proof. Collect: Identify Namespace (DLFEAT), trace of the DSM, and a hex dump of the read.
Linux v7.2 source
core.c:nvme_update_ns_info_block() (DEAC condition), core.c:nvme_setup_write_zeroes(); quirk NVME_QUIRK_DEALLOCATE_ZEROES in nvme.h and pci.c:nvme_id_table.
Test to provoke it
CAUTION Write pattern → deallocate → read immediately → idle 10 min → read → power cycle → read. Also overlap: issue a Write and a DSM to the same LBAs back to back at high queue depth, then read. The result must be either the new data or the promised value, consistent with the completion order.
D-04Discard never reaches the device (host-side silent drop) SilentHost / block layer
In a PEX trace
Visible Visible as an absence: no SQE with OPC 09h (or 08h) in a capture window long enough to cover the journal commit or fstrim. That proves the drive was never asked. Detail: Nothing: no OPC 09h SQE in the capture window. Note that discards may come long after the truncate (journal commit, periodic fstrim), so capture long enough.
What happens
The user believes the space was trimmed, but no DSM was ever sent. Common reasons: filesystem not mounted with -o discard and no fstrim run; dm-crypt without discard passthrough; LVM/MD layers or a virtual disk that do not forward discards; discard_max_bytes = 0 because ONCS.DSM is clear or the queue limit was changed; the discard was smaller than discard_granularity and rounded away.
How it shows up
Mostly silent. blkdiscard on a device without discard support does fail (EOPNOTSUPP), but filesystem truncate and many stacked layers just drop the request. The drive is blamed for keeping data it was never told about.
Spec basis
Not a device issue. Identify Controller ONCS bit 2 decides whether Linux enables discard at all.
Typical causes
Mount options, dm/LVM configuration, virtualization layers, misread fstrim output (its byte count is what it asked for), discards rounded away by granularity.
How to detect / prove
lsblk --discard on every layer of the stack (non-zero DISC-GRAN/DISC-MAX needed on each). blktrace -d /dev/nvme0n1 while truncating or trimming: look for discard requests (RWBS with D). Enable the nvme:nvme_setup_cmd tracepoint and look for DSM with attributes=4. Analyzer: no SQE with OPC 09h means nothing was sent.
Linux v7.2 source
core.c:nvme_update_disk_info(): max_hw_discard_sectors = 0 when ONCS.DSM is clear and DMRSL is 0. core.c:nvme_setup_cmd() is the single point where REQ_OP_DISCARD becomes a DSM, so a probe there catches every discard that leaves the block layer.
Test to provoke it
SAFE on a scratch filesystem: mount without discard, write and delete a file, trace for 2 minutes and observe no DSM. Remount with discard and repeat. Repeat on dm-crypt with and without discard passthrough.
D-05Write Zeroes completes but blocks are not zero SilentNVMe command
In a PEX trace
Visible The Write Zeroes SQE (OPC 08h, DEAC in CDW12 bit 25) and Success CQE, followed by a Read whose data payload is non-zero, are both on the wire, which proves the failure. Detail: SQE OPC 08h with SLBA/NLB in CDW10-12 and DEAC in CDW12 bit 25. No data transfer for the command itself. The later Read data TLPs show the non-zero content.
What happens
Write Zeroes (08h), with or without DEAC, returns Success, but later reads return old data, garbage, or zeroes for only part of the range. Filesystems and databases that rely on zero-out for allocation (for example, unwritten extents converted to written, or BLKZEROOUT used to clear metadata) then see stale structures.
How it shows up
Silent at the NVMe level. Upper layers may later report corruption (filesystem check errors, database page checksum failures) far away from the cause.
Spec basis
NVM Command Set Write Zeroes: after completion the LBAs read as zeroes (and PI per PRACT/PRINFO). DEAC allows the controller to deallocate instead, but the zero read result is still required. Linux's comment in nvme_update_ns_info_block() says DEAC "must be a no-op if reads from deallocated data do not return zeroes".
Typical causes
Firmware implementing DEAC as "deallocate" on a drive whose deallocated read value is not zero. Size-limit handling (WZSL, or WZDSL when ONCS bit 11 applies) silently truncating long commands. Bugs the Linux quirk NVME_QUIRK_DISABLE_WRITE_ZEROES ("Broken Write Zeroes") exists for: in v7.2 it is set for many device IDs in pci.c:nvme_id_table, including the Intel 600P/P3100 and the QEMU 5845h controller.
How to detect / prove
Write a non-zero pattern, Write Zeroes the range (both DEAC=0 and DEAC=1 via nvme write-zeroes … --deac), read every block back, compare with zeroes. Test sizes around WZSL/WZDSL and MDTS. Any non-zero byte is proof, independent of DLFEAT.
Linux v7.2 source
core.c:nvme_setup_write_zeroes(), core.c:nvme_init_non_mdts_limits() (WZSL, NVME_QUIRK_DISABLE_WRITE_ZEROES), core.c:nvme_update_disk_info() (max_write_zeroes_sectors, NVME_QUIRK_DEALLOCATE_ZEROES).
Test to provoke it
CAUTION On a spare namespace: pattern-fill 1 GiB; nvme write-zeroes in sizes 1 block, WZSL−1, WZSL, WZSL+1 (expect an error, not silent truncation), with and without --deac. Read back and compare. Also run blkdiscard -z and confirm with blktrace which command Linux actually used.
D-06Deallocate reaches too far: live data outside the range lost SilentData integrity
In a PEX trace
Partly visible The range descriptors in the range-list CplD show whether the host asked for the right LBAs. Lost guard blocks show up only if the capture also holds the guard writes and a later read of the guards. Detail: Range descriptor values in the CplD. If they are right and guards are still lost, the device is at fault. If they are already wrong, the host is.
What happens
Blocks outside the requested range read back as zeroes/FFh or fail with 287h. The drive rounded the range out to its internal unit, mis-parsed the descriptor (for example, read NLB as 0's based, which adds one block), or the host sent the wrong range.
How it shows up
Silent until the data is read. Filesystems see corrupted files or metadata long after the trim. Host-side cases have happened in practice: a 2019 dm-devel thread reports fstrim discarding too many or the wrong blocks on Linux 5.1 with dm-crypt/LVM, which led to data loss.
Spec basis
Range descriptor: Length in logical blocks (a 1's based count, unlike CDW12 NLB in Read/Write, which is 0's based). Deallocating LBAs not listed in any range is never permitted.
Typical causes
Firmware treating Length as 0's based; rounding unaligned ranges outward instead of inward; host stacking layers translating offsets wrongly; a DSM processed against the wrong namespace (NSID bug).
How to detect / prove
Guard pattern: write distinct "guard" blocks right before and after each range, deallocate, and verify the guards with a checksumming read (fio --verify=crc32c over the guard areas). Decode the range list in the trace to tell host error from device error.
Linux v7.2 source
core.c:nvme_setup_discard(): nlb = blk_rq_sectors(req) >> (lba_shift - 9) (single segment) or bi_size >> lba_shift per bio, written as a 1's based count.
Test to provoke it
CAUTION For N in {1, 7, 8, 9, 4095, 4096, 4097} blocks: guard–range–guard layout, deallocate the range via nvme dsm, verify guards. Repeat with 2- and 256-range DSMs and with ranges in a second namespace to catch NSID mix-ups.
D-07Allocation accounting wrong: NUSE frozen, DULBE not reported SilentIdentify / features
In a PEX trace
Visible The Identify Namespace data payload (NUSE at bytes 16–23) before and after, and the CQE status of a DULBE-enabled Read (287h expected, 0 observed) are on the wire, provided the test commands are captured. Detail: Identify Namespace data (4 KiB CplD/MWr to the host) shows NUSE at bytes 16–23. Compare captures before and after. The DULBE read's CQE carries SCT 2h / SC 87h when it works.
What happens
The namespace advertises thin provisioning (NSFEAT bit 0) or DULBE (NSFEAT bit 2), but NUSE never changes after writes or deallocates, or DULBE is enabled and reads of never-written/deallocated blocks still return Success. Management software that relies on NUSE for capacity planning or thin-provisioning alerts gets wrong numbers.
How it shows up
No error. NUSE stays equal to NCAP (or at its value from the factory), and Get Features 05h shows DULBE=1 while reads of unwritten LBAs succeed.
Spec basis
Identify Namespace NUSE ("current number of logical blocks allocated", ≤ NCAP), NSFEAT THIN/DULBE, Feature 05h DULBE bit 16. A drive without thin provisioning may legitimately report NUSE = NCAP. The QEMU model does so on purpose (hw/nvme/ns.c: "no thin provisioning").
Typical causes
NUSE computed once at format time; DULBE accepted by Set Features but not wired to the read path; DULBE checked for never-written blocks but not for deallocated ones (or the reverse).
How to detect / prove
After a Format (NUSE should drop to about 0 on a tracking drive), write N blocks (NUSE +N), deallocate them (NUSE −N). For DULBE: read a never-written LBA (expect 287h), write it (expect Success), deallocate it (expect 287h). The QEMU controller's nvme_check_dulbe() is a reference: it returns NVME_DULB when the block-status query says the range holds no data.
Linux v7.2 source
Linux does not use NUSE for block I/O. core.c:nvme_error_status() maps NVME_SC_UNWRITTEN_BLOCK (287h) to BLK_STS_MEDIUM; constants.c names it "Deallocated or Unwritten Logical Block".
Test to provoke it
CAUTION Format the test namespace, then run the NUSE/DULBE state table above: never-written → written → deallocated → written again, at both 1-block and 1 GiB scale. Disable DULBE afterwards.
🐞 Reading the cards together

D-01, D-02 and D-03 are the same mechanism seen at different strengths: nothing, part, or "something done but the read path not updated". D-04 is the false positive to rule out first. D-06 is the dangerous opposite of D-01: too much deallocated, which destroys data instead of wasting space. When a customer reports "trim doesn't work", check D-04 first, then D-01/D-02. When a customer reports "files corrupted after trim", check D-06 first.

Quiz

  1. A drive has DLFEAT = 00h and returns old data after a deallocate. Which card applies, and is it a spec violation?

    Answer

    Possibly D-01, but with RB = 000b old data is allowed, so the read-back is not proof and not a violation. Use DULBE (if NSFEAT bit 2) or NUSE, or a performance A/B, to decide.

  2. What is the one partial-deallocate case that a trace alone can prove?

    Answer

    The device fetched fewer than 16×(NR+1) bytes of range list, so it never saw the later ranges.

  3. Why is D-05 always provable by read-back but D-01 is not?

    Answer

    Write Zeroes defines the read result (zeroes) for every drive. DSM deallocate defines it only when DLFEAT says so.

IV.3 Durability and data-integrity failures: acknowledged but not true

← IV.2 Deallocate, Write Zeroes and allocation accounting: the error cardsIV.4 Erase, protection, identity, completion and firmware: more successes that aren't →

These failures break the most basic contract of a storage device: what I wrote and was told is safe, I will read back unchanged, from the place I wrote it. Every card here is silent at the moment it happens. The drive returned Success for the Write, the Flush, or the Read. The damage shows up later, often far from the cause: a database refuses to start, a filesystem check finds orphaned blocks, a checksum mismatch appears months later. Field studies show these are not theoretical:

  • Power faults: Zheng, Tucek, Qin and Lillibridge (FAST '13) cut power to 15 commodity SSDs from five vendors over more than 3,000 fault-injection cycles. 13 of the 15 showed failures such as bit corruption, shorn writes, unserializable writes, metadata corruption and total device failure. The extended ACM TOCS 2016 version reports 14 of 17 SSDs from six vendors failing, including devices sold as enterprise-class.
  • Corruption in production: Bairavasundaram et al. (FAST '08) analysed corruption across 1.53 million disk drives in NetApp systems over 41 months and found more than 400,000 checksum mismatches, which were not independent within a disk or a system. That study is about hard disks, but its taxonomy (checksum mismatches, lost writes, misdirected writes) applies to any block device. Krioukov et al. (FAST '08, "Parity Lost and Parity Regained") analysed how lost and misdirected writes defeat RAID parity schemes.
  • Drives that ignore flushes: Rajimwale et al. (DSN 2011, "Coerced Cache Eviction and Discreet-Mode Journaling") built a file-system technique specifically for disks that do not honour cache flushes correctly.
  • Flash in the field: Schroeder, Lagisetty and Merchant (FAST '16, Google) found that 20–63% of drives saw at least one uncorrectable error within four years, and that raw bit error rate does not predict uncorrectable errors well. Meza et al. (SIGMETRICS '15, Facebook) found that SSD failure rates do not rise steadily with wear but go through distinct periods. Maneas et al. (FAST '20, 1.4 million enterprise SSDs at NetApp) studied factors including firmware versions.

These studies count detected errors. The silent ones in this chapter are, by definition, under-counted. They are only found where an end-to-end checksum exists.

📘 The contracts involved
MechanismField / commandContract
Volatile write cacheIdentify Controller VWC bit 0 (present); Feature 06h WCE; Linux also reads NSFEAT bit 5 (NVME_NS_VWC_NOT_PRESENT) from the I/O-command-set-independent Identify NamespaceIf present and enabled, a Write completion does not mean the data is on non-volatile media.
FlushNVM opcode 00hOn completion, all data and metadata previously completed for the namespace is on non-volatile media. With no volatile cache present or enabled, Flush has no effect and completes Success.
Force Unit AccessRead/Write CDW12 bit 30 (Linux NVME_RW_FUA = control bit 14)That write is on non-volatile media before completion, regardless of cache.
AtomicityAWUN, AWUPF (Identify Controller), NAWUN, NAWUPF, NABSPF (Identify Namespace, when NSFEAT bit 1)Writes up to this size (and not crossing the boundary) are all-or-nothing in normal operation (AWUN) and across power fail (AWUPF).
Power-loss behaviourNo single field. Vendor "PLP" claims. Shutdown notification via CC.SHN and CSTS.SHSTWithout a volatile cache, or with power-loss protection, completed writes survive power loss. An orderly shutdown (SHN, wait for SHST = complete) must persist everything.
D-08Flush ignored / volatile write cache that lies SilentNVMe command
In a PEX trace
Partly visible Flush SQE (OPC 00h) and its CQE are visible, so you can show the host flushed. A Flush that always completes in microseconds after many MiB of writes is a clue, not proof. With VWC=0 you see no Flushes at all. The data loss needs a power-cut ledger test. Detail: Flush SQE (OPC 00h, NSID) and its Success CQE. How long the Flush took is the only clue: a Flush after many MiB of cached writes that completes in microseconds every time is suspicious, but not proof (the drive may have PLP). With VWC = 0 you will see no Flush commands at all.
What happens
Either (a) Flush completes Success before the cached data is on NAND, or (b) the drive reports VWC = 0 (no volatile cache) while it really buffers writes in DRAM or SRAM without power-loss protection. In case (b) Linux never sends a Flush at all, because the queue is set up without a write cache.
How it shows up
Nothing until an unexpected power loss. Then data that fsync()/fdatasync() reported as durable is missing or old, and journals replay inconsistent states.
Spec basis
NVM Command Set Flush; Identify Controller VWC; Set/Get Features 06h (Volatile Write Cache, WCE bit 0). A completed Flush is a durability promise for all previously completed writes.
Typical causes
Firmware completing Flush early for benchmark scores; a flush that only drains the controller's front-end buffer, not the FTL metadata; a missing VWC report; capacitors (PLP) degraded or absent on a SKU that shares firmware with a PLP model. A widely reported informal 2022 test (by Russ Bishop, covered in the press) claimed that two of four consumer NVMe SSDs lost flushed data on power cuts uncertain (not peer-reviewed; details not independently verified here).
How to detect / prove
Power-cut test with a host-side ledger (see Lab IV.3): write records, fsync/Flush, log the acknowledged sequence number to a different machine, cut power at random points, power up, check that every acknowledged record is present. Any acknowledged-but-missing record after Flush = proof. Check nvme id-ctrl -H VWC and nvme get-feature -f 6. On Linux, /sys/block/nvme0n1/queue/write_cache shows "write back" or "write through". "write through" on a drive you suspect caches is case (b).
Linux v7.2 source
core.c:nvme_update_ns_info_block() sets BLK_FEAT_WRITE_CACHE | BLK_FEAT_FUA only if ctrl->vwc & NVME_CTRL_VWC_PRESENT and not info->no_vwc; core.c:nvme_setup_flush() builds the Flush; core.c:nvme_ns_info_from_id_cs_indep() reads NVME_NS_VWC_NOT_PRESENT.
Test to provoke it
EXPERT: controlled power interruption (programmable PSU or a PCIe slot power switch / interposer) during a write+fsync workload, hundreds of cycles, varied timing relative to the Flush completion. Compare with the same drive with WCE disabled (nvme set-feature -f 6 -v 0) as a control.
D-09FUA not honoured SilentNVMe command
In a PEX trace
Partly visible The FUA bit (Write CDW12 bit 30) and the completion latency are visible. FUA writes as fast as cached writes on a drive without PLP is a clue. Proof needs a power-cut test. Detail: Write SQE CDW12 bit 30 = 1. FUA writes that complete exactly as fast as non-FUA writes on a drive without PLP are a strong hint.
What happens
A Write with FUA = 1 completes while its data is still only in volatile cache. Filesystems and databases use FUA for journal commit blocks (Linux turns REQ_FUA into NVME_RW_FUA), so a lost FUA write loses the commit record of a transaction the application already saw as complete.
How it shows up
Only after power loss: the last committed transactions are missing even though the commit write completed.
Spec basis
Read/Write command Force Unit Access bit (CDW12 bit 30). Durable at completion, independent of the write cache.
Typical causes
Firmware treating FUA as a hint, or making the data durable but not the mapping-table update that points to it (after power-up the LBA maps to the old page).
How to detect / prove
Power-cut ledger test using only FUA writes and no Flush (use a small program that writes with O_DIRECT|O_DSYNC; Linux can then mark the write REQ_FUA when the queue advertises FUA. Confirm with the nvme_setup_cmd tracepoint that the control field has bit 14 set before trusting the test). Any acknowledged FUA write missing after power-up = proof.
Linux v7.2 source
core.c:nvme_setup_rw(): if (req->cmd_flags & REQ_FUA) control |= NVME_RW_FUA;. FUA is advertised to the block layer only with a write cache (BLK_FEAT_FUA in nvme_update_ns_info_block()). Otherwise the block layer never sets it.
Test to provoke it
EXPERT: as D-08 but with O_DSYNC writes. Compare the FUA write latency distribution with WCE on and off: if they are the same and the drive has no PLP, investigate.
D-10Acknowledged writes lost on power loss (PLP failure) SilentDevice internal
In a PEX trace
Not visible Not visible: the trace before the cut is normal, and after power-up you see only a normal (possibly slower) initialization. Use a power-cut ledger and the SMART Unsafe Shutdowns counter. Detail: Nothing before the cut. After power-up: normal initialization, possibly a longer time to CSTS.RDY = 1 (the drive rebuilding its map), then Reads returning old or wrong data.
What happens
On a drive that claims power-loss protection, or with the cache disabled, writes that completed before the power cut are missing or old after power-up. Also includes losing data written long before the cut, when an FTL metadata update in flight corrupts the mapping of older data. Zheng et al. classify this as metadata corruption.
How it shows up
Nothing at power-up in most cases. Sometimes the SMART log Unsafe Shutdowns counter increments (it should on every unexpected power loss), and sometimes Media and Data Integrity Errors rise if the drive notices. A drive that comes back with no namespace, read-only mode, or a Critical Warning bit set is the "total device failure" end of the range.
Spec basis
No single NVMe field promises PLP. Durability rests on Flush/FUA and the VWC report. SMART / Health log: Unsafe Shutdowns, Critical Warning bits (including "volatile memory backup device has failed"), Media and Data Integrity Errors.
Typical causes
Hold-up capacitors aged or out of tolerance; firmware not finishing the dump within the hold-up time; mapping table checkpoint corruption; power cut during an internal operation (GC, wear levelling) that moved live data.
How to detect / prove
Power-cut ledger test with verification of all previously written data, not just the latest records, because older data can be lost too. nvme smart-log before and after each cycle: Unsafe Shutdowns must increase by exactly one per cut (if it does not, the drive's power-loss detection itself is broken). Check the critical warning bits.
Linux v7.2 source
Linux has no visibility. On orderly shutdown it sets CC.SHN and waits for CSTS.SHST (see the shutdown timeout parameter shutdown_timeout in core.c). An unexpected power loss skips this entirely.
Test to provoke it
EXPERT: hundreds to thousands of randomized power cuts (the FAST '13 study used more than 3,000 cycles across devices) with mixed sequential, random and flush-heavy workloads, including cuts during idle (background GC). Record temperature, as hold-up energy varies with it.
D-11Torn (shorn) write: atomicity broken SilentData integrity
In a PEX trace
Not visible Not visible: the write traffic is normal and the tear happens inside the drive at the cut. After power-up, Read payloads show mixed old/new blocks only if you read them back and know the expected content. Use record checksums. Detail: Normal Writes. The torn state is visible only in later Read payloads.
What happens
A write that should be atomic persists only partly: some logical blocks new, some old, or even part of one logical block new (a "shorn write" in Zheng et al.'s terms). Databases that rely on atomic 4 KiB or 16 KiB page writes (to skip double-write buffers) then see half-written pages.
How it shows up
After power loss (or after an error/reset during the write), reads return a mix. Page checksums in the application fail, but the drive reports nothing.
Spec basis
AWUN/AWUPF (Identify Controller, 0's based in logical blocks), NAWUN/NAWUPF/NABSPF (Identify Namespace, valid when NSFEAT bit 1 is set). A write ≤ NAWUPF that does not cross an NABSPF boundary must be all-or-nothing even across power failure. A single logical block is always expected to be atomic.
Typical causes
NAND page programming interrupted; firmware splitting a host write across two internal units with separate mapping updates; advertising NAWUPF larger than really guaranteed.
How to detect / prove
Write records of exactly NAWUPF size, aligned to NABSPF, each carrying a sequence number and checksum in every logical block (so a mix is detectable). After a power cut every record must be entirely old or entirely new. Also test records of NAWUPF + 1 blocks to confirm the boundary (tearing is allowed there).
Linux v7.2 source
core.c:nvme_configure_atomic_write() uses NAWUPF (and NABSPF as the boundary) only when NSFEAT has the atomics bit. Otherwise it logs "AWUPF ignored, only NAWUPF accepted" and uses one logical block. nvme_update_disk_info() limits physical_block_size to the atomic size, because "Linux filesystems assume writing a single physical block is an atomic operation".
Test to provoke it
EXPERT: power-cut loop with atomic-size records. Also CAUTION: controller reset (nvme reset) or an FLR in the middle of large writes, then verify the records, because tearing can also follow resets, not only power loss.
D-12Unserializable persistence: write order not preserved across a power cut SilentData integrity
In a PEX trace
Partly visible The trace proves the host side of the contract (Writes completed, Flush SQE/CQE, then the commit Write), which is half the evidence. The out-of-order persistence itself is not visible. Detail: Correct ordering on the host side: Writes completed, Flush SQE/CQE, then the commit Write. Capturing the trace proves the host kept its side of the contract.
What happens
After power loss, a later write (acknowledged and followed by Flush) is present, but an earlier one, also flushed before it, is missing. The persisted state matches no order in which the host could have seen the writes complete. Zheng et al. call these "unserializable writes".
How it shows up
Silent. Journaling and log-structured software break, because they assume "if the commit record is there, the data blocks before the flush are there too".
Spec basis
NVMe does not order independent commands, so writes in flight together may persist in any order. But Flush is a barrier: everything completed before it must be durable when it completes. A state with post-flush data present and pre-flush data missing violates the Flush contract.
Typical causes
Flush implemented per internal channel or die rather than globally. Mapping journal entries written out of order. The flush-ignoring behaviour of D-08 combined with a cache that evicts out of order.
How to detect / prove
Ledger with epochs: epoch N data → Flush → commit record N → Flush → epoch N+1. After a cut, if commit record N is present, every block of epoch N must verify. Note the distinction: missing data from an epoch whose Flush had not completed is legal.
Linux v7.2 source
Block layer flush machinery generates REQ_OP_FLUSH → core.c:nvme_setup_flush(). Linux does not wait for anything beyond the Flush CQE.
Test to provoke it
EXPERT: power-cut loop with the epoch ledger. Run it with high queue depth and many concurrent streams so the drive's internal parallelism is busy.
D-13Lost write (dropped write) without any power event SilentData integrity
In a PEX trace
Visible If the Write and the later Read are both captured: the device fetched the new data (MRd/CplD of the write buffer), posted Success, and later returned the old version in the Read data payload. That is proof on the wire. Detail: Write SQE, data MRd/CplD (the device fetched the new data), Success CQE. The later Read returns the old payload. The trace proves the device received the new data, which pins the fault inside the device.
What happens
A Write completes Success, no power event or reset follows, and a later Read returns the previous content of the block. The write was dropped (never programmed, or programmed but the mapping not updated).
How it shows up
Silent. A per-block checksum stored with the block cannot catch it, because the old block is self-consistent. Only a checksum or version stored elsewhere (in the parent pointer, as in ZFS/Btrfs, or in an application index) catches it. This is the case Krioukov et al. analysed for RAID.
Spec basis
Write command semantics. With PI Type 1, the reference tag only checks the LBA, not the version, so PI does not detect lost writes either.
Typical causes
FTL mapping-update race (two writes to the same LBA in flight, the older one's mapping update applied last); write-cache bugs on overlapping writes; firmware error recovery that retries a failed program and silently gives up.
How to detect / prove
Write a version number into each block and keep the expected version in host memory (fio --verify with --verify_header-style headers, or a custom tool that stores per-LBA generation counters). Read back after overwrites. Old version = lost write. Stress overlapping writes to the same LBA at high queue depth.
Linux v7.2 source
No detection in the driver. Linux allows overlapping writes in flight (the block layer does not serialize them), so an application that issues them must not depend on order.
Test to provoke it
CAUTION: fio --rw=randwrite --bs=4k --size=1G --iodepth=64 --verify=crc32c --verify_backlog=1024 with --norandommap (allows overwrites) plus a custom generation-counter checker. Long runs (hours), near-full drive to force GC.
D-14Misdirected write: data written to the wrong LBA SilentData integrity
In a PEX trace
Partly visible The Write SQE SLBA shows where the host asked to write. The misdirection is visible only if you also capture a Read of the wrong destination returning that data (with an LBA header inside the payload). Detail: The Write SQE's SLBA shows what the host asked for. If the SLBA is already wrong, it is a host bug. If it is right and the data shows up elsewhere, it is the device.
What happens
The data for LBA X lands at LBA Y. Two corruptions result: X keeps old data (a lost write), and Y is overwritten with data that belongs elsewhere. Zheng et al. describe "flying writes" after power faults, data appearing at an unexpected location, which is the power-fault version of this.
How it shows up
Silent at the device. Detectable by checksums that embed the block's own address (a header containing the LBA, or PI reference tag with Type 1/2).
Spec basis
Write semantics; End-to-end Data Protection: with PI Type 1 the Reference Tag must match the lower bits of the LBA and the controller checks it when PRCHK includes the reference tag. A misdirected write then fails with Reference Tag Check Error (status 284h) on the read, or at write time if the controller re-checks.
Typical causes
FTL mapping corruption; namespace offset bugs (multi-namespace); bit flips in internal address paths without parity; on the host side, wrong SLBA from a stacking-driver bug.
How to detect / prove
Write blocks whose content includes their own LBA (fio verify headers include the offset). On read, check that the header offset equals the LBA read. A block containing another block's header = misdirected write, and the header tells you the intended destination.
Linux v7.2 source
core.c:nvme_set_ref_tag() fills the reference tag for PI Type 1/2 (16-bit and 64-bit guard formats); core.c:nvme_error_status() maps NVME_SC_REFTAG_CHECK to BLK_STS_PROTECTION.
Test to provoke it
CAUTION: full-drive fio write with --verify=crc32c (headers carry the offset), then a full read-verify, repeated after GC-heavy random overwrites and after power cuts (EXPERT). On a PI-formatted namespace, also confirm that a deliberately wrong SLBA via passthrough is caught.
D-15Stale data returned on read SilentData integrity
In a PEX trace
Visible With timestamps: the Write CQE MWr is earlier than the Read SQ doorbell MWr, and the Read data payload carries the old version. An analyzer capture gives exactly that ordering proof. Detail: Write CQE MWr timestamp earlier than the Read's SQ doorbell MWr timestamp, and the Read data payload carries the old version. An analyzer with timestamps gives exactly that proof.
What happens
A Read returns an older version of a block although a newer Write to that LBA has completed (no power event). Unlike D-13, the new data may be on media: a later Read, after a cache eviction or a reset, returns the correct new data. So the error comes and goes.
How it shows up
Silent, intermittent, and very hard to reproduce. Applications see "my write disappeared, then came back".
Spec basis
A Read that starts after a Write's completion must return that Write's data (or newer). NVMe does not order commands that are in flight at the same time, so a Read issued before the Write completed may legally return either version.
Typical causes
Read cache / read-ahead buffer not invalidated by a write to the same LBA; multi-queue race in firmware (write on one SQ, read on another); with multi-path/multi-controller subsystems, a second controller serving from a stale cache.
How to detect / prove
Write–complete–read loops with version numbers on the same LBAs from different queues (different CPUs) and, for multi-controller subsystems, via different controllers. Record the completion time of the write and the submission time of the read to show the read started after the write completed. That ordering is what turns "odd" into "proven".
Linux v7.2 source
Requests are spread over per-CPU hardware queues by blk-mq (block/blk-mq.c), so cross-queue read-after-write is normal Linux traffic.
Test to provoke it
CAUTION: small hot set (for example 64 LBAs), one thread per CPU, each doing write(version)→wait for completion→read from another CPU→compare. Run with the drive both near-empty and full.
D-16Wrong data / bit flips returned without an error SilentData integrity
In a PEX trace
Partly visible The Read data payload with the wrong bytes is visible, and LCRC protected the hop, so the trace proves the device sent them. Recognising them as wrong needs the expected data (a captured earlier Write or a checksum). Detail: The Read data MWr payload already contains the wrong bytes, which proves the device sent them (PCIe LCRC protected the hop). If the trace shows correct data and the buffer is wrong, the fault is in host memory or an IOMMU/DMA mapping problem.
What happens
A Read completes Success but the data differs from what was written by a few bits or by a whole chunk. The drive's ECC either miscorrected (decoded to a wrong but valid codeword), or the corruption happened outside the ECC-protected path: controller SRAM/DRAM without parity, a firmware buffer handling bug, or the PCIe/host side (very unlikely to be undetected on PCIe because of LCRC, but possible in host memory).
How it shows up
Silent at the drive: no media error status, no SMART Media Errors increment. Only an end-to-end checksum catches it.
Spec basis
Read semantics. SMART/Health log Media and Data Integrity Errors counts only errors the controller detected. End-to-end Data Protection (PI guard CRC) covers the whole path from host buffer to media and back when PRCHK guard is enabled.
Typical causes
ECC miscorrection at high raw bit error rates; DRAM bit flips in the drive's buffer without ECC; firmware bugs in buffer management or in compression/encryption engines; host memory errors (rule out with ECC RAM and EDAC counters).
How to detect / prove
Checksummed reads: fio --verify=crc32c or sha256, a checksumming filesystem (ZFS/Btrfs scrub), PI with guard checking. Keep the bad buffer and compare it bit by bit with the expected one: a few scattered bit flips point to media/ECC, a block-sized chunk of other valid data points to D-14/D-15. Check host memory EDAC counters to rule out the host.
Linux v7.2 source
With a PI namespace and CONFIG_BLK_DEV_INTEGRITY, core.c:nvme_init_integrity() registers the profile so the block layer generates and verifies guard tags. Without it, Linux sets PRACT and the controller handles PI alone (core.c:nvme_setup_rw()), so host-to-controller transfer is not covered.
Test to provoke it
CAUTION: long fio verify runs at high temperature, after many P/E cycles (endurance tests), and with data retention bakes (write, power off, store warm, read-verify). Compare the detected-error counters with the verify failures: every verify failure without a matching Media Errors increment is a silent corruption.
D-17Retries mask failing media DegradedDevice + host
In a PEX trace
Partly visible Device-internal retries are visible only as longer gaps between SQE fetch and data MWr. Host retries are visible as an error CQE (no DNR) followed by re-submission of the same SLBA/NLB. The media wear itself is not visible. Detail: Device-internal retries: only longer gaps between the Read SQE fetch and the data MWr. Host retries: the same command (same SLBA/NLB, new CID or same tag) re-submitted after an error CQE without DNR.
What happens
Data is returned correctly, but only after many internal read retries (read-level shifts, soft decoding) or after the host retried a failed command. Every layer reports success, while the media is wearing out and latency tails grow. Eventually it becomes an uncorrectable error. Schroeder et al. found uncorrectable errors in 20–63% of drives within four years, and that raw bit error rate is a poor predictor of them, so you cannot rely on a single "health" number.
How it shows up
Higher p99/p99.9 read latency on specific LBA ranges. SMART Percentage Used and Available Spare change slowly. On the host side, Linux retries a non-DNR error up to max_retries (default 5) times. A request that eventually succeeds produces no error to the application, and only the per-namespace command_retries_count in sysfs counts it.
Spec basis
CQE status Do Not Retry (DNR) bit and Command Retry Delay (CRD, with CRDT1–3 in Identify Controller). SMART/Health log Media and Data Integrity Errors, Available Spare, Percentage Used. Vendor or OCP logs may expose internal retry and ECC-correction counts impl.
Typical causes
Wear-out, read disturb, retention loss (data written long ago or at temperature extremes); host-visible retries also come from transient link or controller issues.
How to detect / prove
Latency heat map per LBA region (fio with --write_lat_log/--log_avg_msec, or bpftrace on block completion latency by sector). Read the per-path namespace counters in the diag sysfs group, …/diag/command_retries_count and …/diag/command_error_count (Linux v7.2 sysfs.c, nvme_ns_diag_attr_group; with native multipath they appear on the hidden path disk such as nvme0c0n1, not on the head nvme0n1). Track SMART over time. Compare Verify-command latency (opcode 0Ch, reads media without transfer) across regions.
Linux v7.2 source
core.c:nvme_decide_disposition() (RETRY unless DNR set, blk_noretry_request(), or retries >= nvme_max_retries); core.c:nvme_retry_req() (honours CRD via ctrl->crdt[], increments ns->retries); sysfs.c:command_retries_count_show(); module parameter nvme_core.max_retries.
Test to provoke it
SAFE to observe: periodic full-drive read scans with latency logging. CAUTION: use the kernel's NVMe fault injection (drivers/nvme/host/fault_inject.c, debugfs fault_inject) to inject retryable status codes and confirm that only the retry counter shows them.
🧪 Lab IV.3 — Power-cut durability ledger EXPERT LAB
⚠️ Hardware risk

Cutting power to a running SSD can corrupt or kill it, and switching slot power can harm the host if done wrongly. Use a spare drive, a dedicated test host, and a power-switching method designed for it (a programmable supply feeding a powered riser or interposer, or a controllable slot-power switch). Never cut the host's own power while the system disk is the device under test.

Objective. Prove or disprove D-08 to D-12 for one drive.

Setup. Device under test (DUT) on a separately powered riser. The test host writes; a second machine (the ledger) receives acknowledgements over the network, because the ledger must survive the cut.

loop forever:
    rec = {seq, epoch, lba, crc32c(payload), payload}
    write(rec) to LBA; on completion:
        if mode == FUA:   use O_DSYNC write              # D-09
        if mode == FLUSH: every K records: fdatasync()   # D-08 / D-12
        send(seq, lba, "durable") to ledger  ONLY after the durability point
    at random time T: ledger tells power controller: CUT
power on, wait for CSTS.RDY, read nvme smart-log (Unsafe Shutdowns must be +1)
verify:
    for every seq the ledger marked durable: record present, crc ok      # D-08/09/10
    every record either fully old or fully new (atomic-size records)    # D-11
    if commit(N) present then all of epoch N present                     # D-12
    no record found at an LBA other than its own                         # D-14

Observations. For each cycle: time from last durability point to cut, number of missing durable records, torn records, Unsafe Shutdowns delta, time to CSTS.RDY.

Solution / interpretation

Zero missing durable records over hundreds of cycles is a pass for that workload. One missing record after a completed Flush or FUA is a proven durability failure. Report it with the ledger extract, the power-cut timestamp and the SMART log. Torn records only above NAWUPF are allowed. Unsafe Shutdowns not incrementing is a separate bug in power-loss detection.

Extension. Repeat with WCE disabled (Feature 06h = 0) as a control, at high and low ambient temperature, and with the drive nearly full so GC runs during the cut.

IV.4 Erase, protection, identity, completion and firmware: more successes that aren't

← IV.3 Durability and data-integrity failures: acknowledged but not trueIV.5 How to catch silent failures →

The previous chapter was about user data. This one covers commands whose job is to destroy data (Sanitize, Format, crypto erase), to protect it (PI), to describe the device (Identify, SMART, firmware slots, zone state), and the queue mechanics that tell the host a command finished (CQE, CID, DMA). For each one the trace shows a well-formed exchange, and the problem is in what the content means. Many of these cards are partly visible in a PEX trace, because the misleading information (an Identify payload, a CQE with the wrong CID, a DMA to a strange address) does cross the link. You only need to know what to compare it with.

⚠️ Host-side false positive for every erase test

After a Sanitize or Format sent through passthrough (nvme sanitize, nvme format), the Linux page cache of /dev/nvme0n1 may still hold blocks read before the erase. A buffered dd or hexdump can then show "old data" that is not on the drive at all. The v7.2 driver marks Format and Sanitize with the LBCC (logical block content change) effect in core.c:nvme_init_known_nvm_effects(), and Format also with NCC (namespace capability change) so the namespace is rescanned. But verify with O_DIRECT reads or nvme read passthrough, and drop caches (echo 3 > /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches) before concluding anything.

IV.4.1 Erase and protection

D-18Sanitize reports success but user data remains SilentAdmin command
In a PEX trace
Partly visible The Sanitize SQE (admin OPC 84h, SANACT in CDW10), its quick Success CQE, the Get Log Page 81h polling and the Sanitize Status payload (SPROG, SSTAT) are visible. Read data payloads after the sanitize showing old patterns are visible proof that the logical view still has data. Remaining data in NAND blocks that are no longer mapped is not visible.
What happens
A Sanitize (Block Erase, Overwrite or Crypto Erase) runs to completion. The Sanitize Status log reports the most recent sanitize as completed successfully, but some user data can still be read: from LBAs (an incomplete pass), from areas outside the user LBA space (over-provisioning, retired blocks, caches), or by reading the raw NAND.
How it shows up
SSTAT says success (value 1, or 4 for the No-Deallocate variant), and no error is logged. Only a read-back audit or forensic analysis of the NAND finds the leftovers.
Spec basis
Base spec Sanitize command (84h) and Sanitize Status log (81h). libnvme defines SSTAT status values 0 never sanitized, 1 completed successfully, 2 in progress, 3 failed, 4 completed successfully with No-Deallocate, plus the Global Data Erased bit (bit 8) and completed-passes count. Identify Controller SANICAP (CES, BES, OWS, NDI, NODMMAS). Sanitize is meant to affect all user data, including caches and unallocated media verify exact scope wording in spec.
Typical causes
Firmware erasing only mapped blocks; skipping retired or bad blocks that still hold readable data; host-memory-buffer or controller cache not cleared; a power loss during sanitize followed by a wrong recovery. Wei, Grupp, Spada and Swanson (FAST '11) found that built-in sanitize commands worked on drives where they were implemented correctly, but some implementations were incorrect.
How to detect / prove
Fill the whole namespace with a recognizable, LBA-tagged pattern (including writes over the full capacity several times, so over-provisioned blocks also hold the pattern), sanitize, poll the log to completion, then read every LBA with O_DIRECT and search for the pattern. For the media-level claim, only a lab chip-off/raw-NAND read (as in Wei et al.) or a vendor-supported verification can prove it.
Linux v7.2 source
Linux never issues Sanitize itself. It arrives via the passthrough ioctls; core.c:nvme_init_known_nvm_effects() forces the LBCC and CSE effects for nvme_admin_sanitize_nvm, and core.c:nvme_passthru_end() unfreezes queues afterwards.
Test to provoke it
CAUTION (destroys all data): pattern-fill ×2, nvme sanitize /dev/nvme0 -a 2 (block erase; check nvme sanitize --help for your version), nvme sanitize-log /dev/nvme0 until done, full O_DIRECT read audit. Repeat for each SANACT the drive supports, and once with a power cut mid-sanitize (EXPERT): the drive must resume or report failure, never report success.
D-19Crypto erase leaves data readable SilentAdmin command
In a PEX trace
Partly visible The command (Sanitize SANACT=100b, or Format NVM with SES=010b) and its Success CQE are visible. A later Read whose data payload contains the old plaintext is visible proof. A key that was not really replaced (data still decryptable with the old key, but reads return garbage) is not visible.
What happens
The drive reports a successful cryptographic erase but did not change the media encryption key, or changed it for some ranges only, or kept a copy. Reads either return old plaintext (key unchanged) or random-looking data (key changed). The second case looks correct even if a copy of the old key remains.
How it shows up
Silent. The user's only check, "reads now return something other than my data", passes even when the erase is not cryptographically effective.
Spec basis
Sanitize Crypto Erase (SANICAP.CES) and Format NVM Secure Erase Setting 010b (cryptographic erase), supported when the Identify Controller FNA field says so verify FNA bit. NVMe defines the command, not the key management. TCG Opal/Ruby specs cover encryption ranges.
Typical causes
Drive not actually encrypting media (no self-encryption despite the claim); key wrapped by a constant; per-range keys with one range forgotten; firmware bug that rewrites the old key after power cycle.
How to detect / prove
Read-back immediately after the erase and after a power cycle: old plaintext anywhere = proof. Strong assurance needs vendor documentation, a certification report (for example FIPS 140 validation of the drive's crypto module), or raw-NAND analysis showing ciphertext that changes between two writes of the same plaintext.
Linux v7.2 source
Passthrough only; Format gets LBCC|NCC|CSE effects in core.c:nvme_init_known_nvm_effects(), so the namespace is rescanned after it.
Test to provoke it
CAUTION: write pattern, crypto erase, O_DIRECT read audit, power cycle, audit again. Compare against the DLFEAT read behaviour: many drives deallocate after crypto erase, so reads return zeroes. A drive returning ciphertext is fine, and one returning plaintext has failed.
D-20Format NVM leaves old data SilentAdmin command
In a PEX trace
Visible The Format SQE (admin OPC 80h) shows the SES field in CDW10, so the trace proves which erase was requested. If SES=001b or 010b was requested, a later Read data payload with old data is visible proof. With SES=000b the trace also shows that no secure erase was asked for.
What happens
After Format NVM completes, reads return the data written before. Two different situations: (a) SES = 000b (no secure erase) was used. Then the spec does not require the data to be destroyed, only the LBA format to change, and with DLFEAT 000b the old data may still read back. That is a misunderstanding, not a drive failure. (b) SES = 001b (user data erase) or 010b was requested and data remains. That is a real failure.
How it shows up
Silent. Format may complete in milliseconds in either case.
Spec basis
Format NVM CDW10: LBAF, MSET, PI, PIL, SES (000b none, 001b user data erase, 010b cryptographic erase). FNA in Identify Controller says whether Format applies to all namespaces and whether crypto erase is supported verify bit layout.
Typical causes
Tools defaulting to SES=0 (users assume "format = wipe"); firmware implementing SES=1 as "deallocate all" on a drive with DLFEAT 000b, so reads still return old content.
How to detect / prove
Check the SES actually sent (PEX trace, or nvme format … --ses=1 on the command line). Pattern-fill, format, O_DIRECT read audit. With SES ≥ 1, any old pattern = proof. Check the Format completion time against Identify Controller's estimate, if reported.
Linux v7.2 source
Passthrough. After the command, nvme_passthru_end() runs a namespace rescan (NCC effect), which also catches LBA-format changes.
Test to provoke it
CAUTION: run the same audit for SES=0, 1 and 2. Expect possible old data only for SES=0 with DLFEAT 000b.
D-21Metadata / protection information not checked SilentData integrity
In a PEX trace
Partly visible The PRINFO bits (PRACT, PRCHK guard/app/ref in CDW12 bits 29:26) of every Read/Write, and the reference/application tags in CDW14–15, are visible, so you can prove checking was not requested. With separate metadata (MPTR) or extended LBAs the PI bytes themselves cross the link and can be checked offline. Whether the controller really checked is not visible, unless a deliberately bad PI comes back with Success.
What happens
The namespace is formatted with PI, but corrupted data passes because: PI checking was not requested (PRCHK = 0); the host uses PRACT = 1 so the controller generates and strips PI and the host-to-controller path is not covered; the PI type is 0 (metadata only, never checked); application tag FFFFh disables checking for that block (an escape value verify per PI type); or the controller ignores PRCHK.
How it shows up
No Guard/App/Reference Tag Check Error (282h/283h/284h) even though data or LBA is wrong.
Spec basis
NVM Command Set End-to-end Data Protection: Identify Namespace DPC/DPS, FLBAS/LBA format MS, PRINFO in Read/Write. Status codes Guard Check Error 282h, Application Tag Check Error 283h, Reference Tag Check Error 284h (Linux NVME_SC_GUARD_CHECK etc.).
Typical causes
Kernel without CONFIG_BLK_DEV_INTEGRITY; integrity profile not registered; the user assuming "formatted with PI" means "protected end to end"; firmware skipping checks for performance.
How to detect / prove
Write with a deliberately wrong guard or reference tag via passthrough (nvme write … --prinfo with a wrong --ref-tag) and confirm the error. A Success here proves the check is not done. Check /sys/block/nvme0n1/integrity/ (format, read_verify, write_generate) to see what Linux does.
Linux v7.2 source
core.c:nvme_init_integrity() (returns PI-capable only if the namespace has PI when integrity support is missing); core.c:nvme_setup_rw() sets PRACT when no integrity payload exists, and PRCHK bits from BIP_CHECK_GUARD/REFTAG/APPTAG; core.c:nvme_set_ref_tag(); core.c:nvme_error_status() maps 282h–284h and Invalid PI to BLK_STS_PROTECTION.
Test to provoke it
CAUTION on a test namespace formatted with PI Type 1: wrong ref tag write; correct write then wrong expected ref tag on read; corrupt guard. Each must fail. Repeat with app tag FFFFh to see the documented escape.

IV.4.2 Identity, accounting and health reporting

D-22Bogus or duplicate namespace identifiers (NGUID / EUI64 / UUID) SilentIdentify
In a PEX trace
Visible The Identify payloads (Identify Namespace NGUID/EUI64, and the Namespace Identification Descriptor list for CNS 03h) cross the link as MWr data. All-zero, all-FFh, or identical values across namespaces or across drives of the same model can be read straight from the capture.
What happens
The drive reports identifiers that are not unique: the same NGUID for every unit of a model, garbage, or the same ID for two namespaces. Multipath software and /dev/disk/by-id links may then merge two different namespaces into one, or point to the wrong disk.
How it shows up
Silent unless Linux detects the duplicate. Linux v7.2 then prints "clearing duplicate IDs for nsid N" and "use of /dev/disk/by-id/ may cause data corruption" (or "ignoring nsid N because of duplicate IDs" for fabrics or shared multi-controller namespaces) and sets NVME_QUIRK_BOGUS_NID at runtime.
Spec basis
Identify Namespace NGUID/EUI64, Namespace Identification Descriptor list (CNS 03h), NSFEAT bit 3 (identifiers never reused).
Typical causes
Firmware with a constant ID from the reference design; manufacturing step that never programs a unique value. v7.2 pci.c:nvme_id_table has many NVME_QUIRK_BOGUS_NID entries, including Intel 0A54h (P4500/P4600) and both QEMU device IDs.
How to detect / prove
nvme id-ns /dev/nvme0n1 | grep -iE 'nguid|eui64' and nvme ns-descs /dev/nvme0n1 on several units and namespaces; compare. dmesg | grep -i "duplicate IDs\|bogus".
Linux v7.2 source
core.c:nvme_process_ns_desc() (ignores IDs under the quirk), core.c:nvme_identify_ns() ("Ignoring bogus Namespace Identifiers"), core.c:nvme_init_ns_head() (duplicate detection, runtime quirk), core.c:nvme_subsys_check_duplicate_ids().
Test to provoke it
SAFE: create two namespaces (or use two drives of one model), compare all identifiers, and check that by-id links resolve uniquely.
D-23Identify returns wrong data for a CNS value it does not really support SilentIdentify
In a PEX trace
Visible The Identify SQE shows CNS in CDW10 bits 7:0. The returned data payload is visible. A controller answering CNS 02h (active namespace list) with the Identify Controller structure, or returning Success with a zero-filled descriptor list, shows up when you compare the payload with what that CNS should contain.
What happens
The controller claims a spec version that includes a CNS value but handles it wrongly: it truncates CNS to one bit (NVMe 1.0 behaviour), so the request is answered as a different structure, or returns Success with an empty structure instead of Invalid Field.
How it shows up
Silent wrong values: missing namespaces, wrong namespace list, garbage descriptors. Sometimes Linux prints "ctrl returned bogus length" for descriptor list entries.
Spec basis
Identify CNS values. NVMe 1.1 widened CNS from one bit to two bits; later versions to a full byte. The Linux comment in nvme_id_cns_ok() explains this history.
Typical causes
Old command decoders kept after raising the reported version. Linux quirks: NVME_QUIRK_IDENTIFY_CNS (only CNS 0/1 handled, QEMU 5845h and Apple controllers in v7.2) and NVME_QUIRK_NO_NS_DESC_LIST (descriptor list not handled despite claiming 1.3).
How to detect / prove
Issue each CNS with nvme admin-passthru --opcode=0x06 --cdw10=<cns> --data-len=4096 -r and compare the structure with what the CNS defines. An unsupported CNS should fail with Invalid Field, not return Success with unrelated data.
Linux v7.2 source
core.c:nvme_id_cns_ok() (CNS ≤ 3 for ≥ 1.1 unless quirk, else ≤ 1), core.c:nvme_identify_ns_descs(), core.c:nvme_process_ns_desc() ("ctrl returned bogus length"), apple.c sets NVME_QUIRK_IDENTIFY_CNS.
Test to provoke it
SAFE (read-only admin commands): sweep CNS 00h–1Fh with NSID 0, 1 and FFFFFFFFh, log status and payload.
D-24Namespace capacity or format mis-reported SilentIdentify
In a PEX trace
Partly visible NSZE/NCAP/NUSE (bytes 0–23), FLBAS (byte 26) and the LBA format table are in the Identify Namespace payload, so inconsistent values (NUSE > NCAP, NCAP > NSZE without THIN, a format index beyond NLBAF) are visible. Whether the drive really has that much usable space is not: the failure shows later as writes beyond some LBA failing or wrapping.
What happens
The reported size is larger than the media really backs (counterfeit or mis-configured drives: writes past the real capacity wrap around and overwrite earlier data), or the LBA data size in the format table is wrong, or NCAP/NSZE disagree after namespace management.
How it shows up
Silent at first. Later: data at low LBAs is overwritten by writes to high LBAs (wraparound), or LBA Out of Range errors appear below the reported size.
Spec basis
Identify Namespace NSZE, NCAP, NUSE, NSFEAT THIN, FLBAS, LBAF[]; Identify Controller TNVMCAP/UNVMCAP for totals.
Typical causes
Fake-capacity firmware; namespace-management bugs; reporting the LBA count for 512-byte format while the namespace uses 4096.
How to detect / prove
Full-capacity write with LBA-tagged data (fio --verify=crc32c headers include offset, or f3-style tools), then full read-verify. Wraparound shows as blocks containing headers of other offsets. Cross-check blockdev --getsize64 with NSZE × LBA size.
Linux v7.2 source
core.c:nvme_update_ns_info_block() computes capacity and calls set_capacity_and_notify(); capacity is set to 0 if metadata cannot be handled (nvme_init_integrity() false).
Test to provoke it
CAUTION: full-drive tagged write and verify. Also create, resize and delete namespaces repeatedly and check the Identify values each time.
D-25SMART / health counters frozen or wrong; bogus temperature SilentLog page
In a PEX trace
Partly visible Each Get Log Page 02h returns 512 bytes of payload over the link, so values that do not change between two captures, or that are impossible (temperature 0 K, Percentage Used decreasing), are visible. Whether a counter is right needs a reference from the same trace: Host Write Commands must rise by the number of Write SQEs you saw in between.
What happens
Counters do not update (Data Units Written stuck), update at the wrong scale, wrap, or reset at power cycle. Composite Temperature is constant, 0, or far from reality. Critical Warning bits never set even when thresholds are crossed.
How it shows up
Monitoring sees a healthy drive. Wear-out or thermal trouble is missed, or alarms fire falsely.
Spec basis
SMART / Health Information log (02h): Critical Warning, Composite Temperature (Kelvin), Available Spare, Percentage Used, Data Units Read/Written (thousands of 512-byte units, rounded up), Host Read/Write Commands, Power Cycles, Power On Hours, Unsafe Shutdowns, Media and Data Integrity Errors, Number of Error Information Log Entries. Temperature thresholds via Feature 04h.
Typical causes
Counters kept in RAM and only saved occasionally; a broken sensor; firmware that reports a fixed value. Linux has quirks NVME_QUIRK_NO_TEMP_THRESH_CHANGE and NVME_QUIRK_NO_SECONDARY_TEMP_THRESH for drives that misbehave with temperature thresholds.
How to detect / prove
Snapshot nvme smart-log, write exactly N × 512,000 bytes with O_DIRECT, snapshot again: Data Units Written must grow by N (± rounding), Host Write Commands by the number of commands sent. Compare temperature with an external thermocouple and with the hwmon value (sensors, /sys/class/hwmon/*/temp1_input). Power cycle and check that counters persist and Power Cycles increments.
Linux v7.2 source
hwmon.c:nvme_hwmon_get_smart_log(), hwmon.c:nvme_hwmon_read(), hwmon.c:nvme_get_temp_thresh()/nvme_set_temp_thresh().
Test to provoke it
SAFE: counted-write test above; heat the drive with a sustained write and watch temperature and Warning Composite Temperature Time; cool it and check the reverse.
D-26Firmware update reports success but the old firmware is still running SilentAdmin command
In a PEX trace
Visible Firmware Image Download (11h) chunks, Firmware Commit (10h) with its Commit Action and slot in CDW10, the CQE status (Success, or 10Bh/110h/111h "activation requires … reset"), any AER notice for firmware activation, and the Firmware Slot log (03h) and Identify Controller FR payloads afterwards are all on the wire. Comparing FR before and after the reset shows whether activation happened.
What happens
The download and commit succeed, the tool says "updated", but the running firmware revision is unchanged: the commit action only stored the image (CA = 000b), activation was deferred to a reset that did not happen (status 10Bh/110h/111h treated as success by a tool), or activation silently failed and the drive fell back to the old slot.
How it shows up
Silent if the tool ignores the status or the slot log. Linux v7.2 logs "Firmware is activated after next Controller Level Reset" when the slot log's next-active slot differs from the current one.
Spec basis
Firmware Commit (CA values: replace, replace and activate at next reset, activate at next reset, replace and activate immediately), status codes Firmware Activation Requires Conventional Reset (10Bh), Requires NVM Subsystem Reset (110h), Requires Controller Level Reset (111h), Requires Maximum Time Violation (112h), Firmware Slot Information log (AFI: active slot bits 2:0, next slot bits 6:4; FRS1–FRS7), Identify Controller FR and FRMW.
Typical causes
Tool or script not checking the CQE status or not resetting; wrong slot; image verification failing in firmware after the commit returned; a read-only slot 1.
How to detect / prove
nvme fw-log /dev/nvme0 (AFI and slot revisions) and nvme id-ctrl /dev/nvme0 | grep -i '^fr ' before and after the activation reset; cat /sys/class/nvme/nvme0/firmware_rev. The running revision is FR after the reset, not what the tool printed.
Linux v7.2 source
core.c:nvme_get_fw_slot_info() (reads log 03h, compares afi & 0x7 with (afi & 0x70) >> 4, updates subsys->firmware_rev), core.c:nvme_handle_aen_notice() (NVME_AER_NOTICE_FW_ACT_STARTING), core.c:nvme_fw_act_work(); status codes NVME_SC_FW_NEEDS_* in include/linux/nvme.h.
Test to provoke it
CAUTION (vendor image required): commit with each supported CA, check status, slot log and FR before and after a controller reset, a subsystem reset and a power cycle. Also try a corrupted image: the drive must reject it, never report success and keep running old firmware silently.
D-27ZNS write pointer does not match the data SilentZNS
In a PEX trace
Partly visible Zone Append CQEs return the assigned LBA in DW0–DW1, and Zone Management Receive (Report Zones) payloads carry each zone's state and write pointer, so a WP that disagrees with the appends you saw complete is visible. Data persisted beyond or below the WP after a power cut is not, until you read it.
What happens
The reported write pointer is ahead of the data actually persisted (reads below the WP return old or unwritten content), or behind it (data written but the WP rolled back, so the host overwrites it with the next append). Usually after a power loss or a reset in the middle of writes.
How it shows up
Silent. Zoned filesystems and applications that rebuild state from the WP (for example to find the end of a log) lose or duplicate records.
Spec basis
Zoned Namespace Command Set: zone states, write pointer, Zone Append (returns the LBA written), Zone Management Send/Receive, errors such as Zone Invalid Write (1BCh) and Zone Boundary Error (1B8h) that Linux names in include/linux/nvme.h.
Typical causes
WP updated before the data is durable; WP recovery after power loss scanning the wrong way; zone state machine bugs on Finish/Reset.
How to detect / prove
Append records with sequence numbers and checksums, cut power or reset, then nvme zns report-zones and read each zone up to and past the WP. All records below the WP must verify; none above it may be valid new data (allowed values above WP per the read rules for unwritten blocks verify in spec).
Linux v7.2 source
zns.c:nvme_zone_parse_entry() (for zones reported FULL, Linux sets wp = start + len instead of the reported WP; non-sequential zone types fail with "invalid zone type"), zns.c:nvme_ns_report_zones(), zns.c:nvme_setup_zone_mgmt_send().
Test to provoke it
EXPERT: append workload across many open zones with power cuts; compare WP with the last acknowledged append per zone and with the data.

IV.4.3 Completion and DMA failures that hide themselves

D-28Completion posted with the wrong CID SilentNVMe queue
In a PEX trace
Visible Every SQE fetch (CplD with the CID) and every CQE MWr (DW3 CID, SQID) is captured, so an analyzer script can match them: a CQE whose CID was never submitted on that SQ, or a CID completed while its own command is still outstanding and another's is missing, is directly visible.
What happens
The controller completes command A but writes the CID of command B. If B is outstanding, the host completes B (with A's status) while B's data is not there yet, and A later times out. Buffers can be reused while the device still DMAs into them.
How it shows up
Partly reported. Linux v7.2 encodes a 4-bit generation counter in the CID upper bits (unless NVME_QUIRK_SKIP_CID_GEN), so a CID with a wrong generation produces "request 0x… genctr mismatch" and "invalid id N completed on queue M". A wrong CID that happens to match another outstanding request with the right generation is silent and completes the wrong request.
Spec basis
CQE DW3 Command Identifier and DW2 SQ Identifier; CID must be unique among outstanding commands on that SQ.
Typical causes
Firmware CQE-assembly bugs under high queue depth; controllers that store only some CID bits (the reason NVME_QUIRK_SKIP_CID_GEN exists: "requires the command_id value be limited").
How to detect / prove
dmesg | grep -E "genctr mismatch|invalid id". Data verification (fio verify) catches the reads that completed early. Analyzer script: build a map SQID/CID → outstanding from SQE fetches and check every CQE against it.
Linux v7.2 source
nvme.h:nvme_cid(), nvme.h:nvme_find_rq() (genctr check), nvme.h:nvme_try_complete_req() (increments genctr), pci.c:nvme_handle_cqe() ("invalid id %d completed on queue %d").
Test to provoke it
SAFE to observe: high-QD mixed fio with verify while capturing. On QEMU, a modified model that corrupts CIDs shows how Linux reacts.
D-29Duplicate completion for one command ReportedNVMe queue
In a PEX trace
Visible Two CQE MWr TLPs with the same SQID/CID and no SQE fetch of that CID in between are directly visible in the capture.
What happens
The controller posts two CQEs for the same command, for example after an internal retry or an Abort race. If the host has already reused the tag for a new command, the second CQE completes the new command early.
How it shows up
Usually reported, not silent, on Linux v7.2: nvme_try_complete_req() increments the request's generation counter on the first completion, so the duplicate CQE (carrying the old generation in CID bits 15:12) fails the check in nvme_find_rq(), is logged as "genctr mismatch" / "invalid id … completed on queue …" and ignored. It becomes silent with NVME_QUIRK_SKIP_CID_GEN, or if the duplicate arrives exactly 16 reuses later, and then it can complete an unrelated new I/O early.
Spec basis
Exactly one completion per command.
Typical causes
Abort handling races, error-recovery paths, CQ-wrap bugs (phase tag not flipped, so the host re-reads an old entry as new).
How to detect / prove
dmesg genctr messages; analyzer CID-pairing script; check CQ phase-tag handling at wrap (the duplicate appears exactly at the CQ wrap point if the phase tag is wrong).
Linux v7.2 source
nvme.h:nvme_find_rq(), pci.c:nvme_cqe_pending() (phase tag check), pci.c:nvme_update_cq_head() (phase flip on wrap).
Test to provoke it
CAUTION: Abort storms (nvme_core.io_timeout lowered on a test system) under load; small CQ sizes to force frequent wrap.
D-30Missing interrupt or completion hidden by timeout polling Timer onlyNVMe queue
In a PEX trace
Visible Two patterns: (a) the CQE MWr is there but no MSI-X MWr follows (missed interrupt), and about 30 s later (the I/O timeout) the host just resumes; (b) no CQE MWr at all for a fetched CID until the host sends Abort or resets. Timestamps between SQE fetch and CQE show the gap.
What happens
The device posts the CQE but the interrupt is lost (masked vector, wrong MSI-X entry, coalescing bug). After the I/O timeout, Linux polls the CQ, finds the completion and finishes the request normally. The application sees a 30-second stall but no error.
How it shows up
Only a warning: "I/O tag N (CID) QID M timeout, completion polled". No error is returned to the application, so monitoring based on I/O errors never sees it.
Spec basis
Interrupt generation for CQ entries (MSI-X table, Interrupt Vector in Create I/O CQ, interrupt coalescing Feature 08h).
Typical causes
Interrupt coalescing or aggregation firmware bugs; MSI-X table programming races; platform interrupt remapping problems. Linux quirks NVME_QUIRK_BROKEN_MSI and NVME_QUIRK_SINGLE_VECTOR exist for related device problems.
How to detect / prove
dmesg | grep "completion polled"; latency histograms with a long tail at exactly the timeout value; /proc/interrupts counts for the NVMe vectors not increasing while I/O completes.
Linux v7.2 source
pci.c:nvme_timeout(): polls the queue ("Did we miss an interrupt?") with nvme_poll() or nvme_poll_irqdisable(), then logs "completion polled" and returns BLK_EH_DONE; otherwise aborts ("timeout, aborting") or resets.
Test to provoke it
CAUTION: run with interrupt coalescing enabled at extreme settings (Feature 08h), CPU hotplug of the CPUs owning NVMe vectors, and watch for "completion polled".
D-31DMA writes outside the data buffer SilentPCIe / DMA
In a PEX trace
Visible Every device-to-host MWr carries its address and length. Comparing them with the PRP/SGL entries in the captured SQE (and PRP list CplDs) shows a write past the end of the buffer, to a page not in the list, or after the CQE. The analyzer sees it even when nothing in the host notices.
What happens
The device writes data beyond the PRP range, to a stale address from a previous command, or after it already posted the CQE (when the host may have freed the buffer). Without an IOMMU this silently corrupts unrelated kernel or application memory.
How it shows up
Without IOMMU: random crashes, corrupted unrelated data, nothing pointing at the SSD. With IOMMU (Intel VT-d, AMD-Vi, Arm SMMU) in translated mode: a DMA fault message naming the device's BDF and the faulting address (wording varies by IOMMU driver, for example "DMAR: [DMA Write] … fault addr …" or "AMD-Vi: Event logged [IO_PAGE_FAULT …]"; illustrative), and the write is blocked.
Spec basis
PRP/SGL data pointer rules (PRP entries and the transfer length NLB × LBA size); Linux also limits addresses for NVME_QUIRK_DMA_ADDRESS_BITS_48 devices.
Typical causes
Off-by-one in PRP list walking (page boundary at the end of a list page), metadata pointer misuse, firmware reusing a stale PRP after Abort, devices that cannot handle DMA addresses above 48 bits.
How to detect / prove
Boot with the IOMMU in translated (not passthrough) mode (intel_iommu=on iommu.passthrough=0 or the AMD equivalent) and watch dmesg for faults naming the NVMe BDF. In the analyzer, check every MWr address against the command's PRPs.
Linux v7.2 source
Driver builds PRP/SGL in drivers/nvme/host/pci.c; DMA mask reduced for NVME_QUIRK_DMA_ADDRESS_BITS_48. IOMMU fault reporting is in the IOMMU drivers (not in the local snapshot).
Test to provoke it
SAFE with IOMMU strict mode: run fio with odd buffer alignments (--iomem_align), transfer sizes that end exactly at PRP-list page boundaries, and Abort under load. Any IOMMU fault is a finding.
D-32DSM range list over-read: device ignores Number of Ranges SilentNVMe command / DMA
In a PEX trace
Visible The device's MRd for the range list asks for 4096 bytes (256 × 16) while the SQE's CDW10 NR is 0 (one range). The MRd length versus NR+1 is in the capture.
What happens
The controller DMA-reads the maximum range buffer instead of (NR+1) × 16 bytes. With a small host buffer this reads memory past the end, and with an IOMMU it faults and the DSM fails. Linux v7.2 hides it by always allocating a 4096-byte, zero-filled buffer, so on Linux the over-read is harmless and invisible. If the device then also processes the extra (zero) ranges, it should be harmless (NLB 0). If the buffer held stale ranges, it would deallocate the wrong LBAs (see D-06).
How it shows up
Silent on current Linux. Historically visible as failing trims: a 2020 Ubuntu kernel SRU ("Prevent fstrim failure so unused blocks can be discarded", Launchpad bug 1856603) restored the larger allocation after "nvme: rewrite discard support" reduced it, because discard requests failed on a non-compliant device with "FITRIM ioctl failed: Input/output error". Search results connected to that bug also mention IOMMU faults during the trim.
Spec basis
DSM CDW10 Number of Ranges (0's based); data length = (NR+1) × 16 bytes.
Typical causes
Firmware using a fixed-size DMA for the range list.
How to detect / prove
Analyzer: compare range-list MRd length with NR. On an OS that allocates exactly (NR+1)×16 bytes (or with a custom passthrough that places the range list at the end of an IOMMU-mapped page), an IOMMU fault proves it.
Linux v7.2 source
core.c:nvme_setup_discard(): alloc_size = sizeof(*range) * NVME_DSM_MAX_RANGES with the comment "Some devices do not consider the DSM 'Number of Ranges' field when determining how much data to DMA"; kzalloc zero-fills it.
Test to provoke it
CAUTION: nvme dsm --ad -s <slba> -b <nlb> with one range while capturing; check the MRd length.
D-33Verify or Compare returns Success without checking the media SilentNVMe command
In a PEX trace
Partly visible Verify (0Ch) moves no data, so the trace shows only SQE and CQE, and the completion time is the only clue (a 1 GiB Verify finishing in microseconds every time did not read the media). Compare (05h) is visible: the device fetches the host buffer (MRd/CplD), and a Success CQE for a buffer you know differs from the media is proof.
What happens
Verify is supposed to read and check the data (and PI) without transferring it. A shortcut implementation returns Success without reading, so "scrubbing" with Verify finds nothing. Compare returning Success when the data differs (or Compare Failure, 285h, when it matches) breaks fused compare-and-write users.
How it shows up
Silent: scrubs report clean drives that later return uncorrectable errors on normal reads.
Spec basis
NVM Command Set Verify (ONCS bit 7) and Compare (ONCS bit 0); Compare Failure status 285h; Unrecovered Read Error 281h expected from Verify on bad blocks.
Typical causes
Firmware treating Verify as a no-op; Compare checking only the first block.
How to detect / prove
Use Write Uncorrectable (04h, ONCS bit 1) on a test LBA, then Verify it: it must fail (with Unrecovered Read Error or similar). For Compare: compare a buffer that differs only in the last byte of the last block. Also time Verify of a large range against a Read of the same range.
Linux v7.2 source
