nvme_check_mdtstransfer length ≤ page size << MDTSInvalid Field in Command with DNR
nvme_create_sqvalid CQID, unused SQID, 0 < QSIZE ≤ CAP.MQES, page-aligned PRP1, PC=1Invalid Queue Identifier / Completion Queue Invalid / Invalid Queue Size / PRP Offset Invalid / Invalid Field
not checkedCID unique among outstanding commands of an SQcommands proceed; nvme_abort would match the first request with that CID

Two lessons follow. First, the controller-side checks are almost all "ignore and maybe tell the host via an AER" — and the AER path only works if the host keeps an Asynchronous Event Request outstanding. Second, several host-side rules (CID uniqueness, monotonic SQ tail progress) are simply not policed by the device; the trace is the only place they can be caught.

7.1.4 How the cards in this part are organised

  • 7.2 queue and doorbell protocol (V-01 … V-12)
  • 7.3 ordering and interrupt rules (V-13 … V-16)
  • 7.4 command format: PRP, SGL, MDTS, FUSE, reserved fields (V-17 … V-25)
  • 7.5 PCIe Transaction, Data Link and Flit layer rules (V-26 … V-37)
  • 7.6 an executable checker over a synthetic CSV trace

The severity label on each card describes how the violation surfaces if nobody runs a checker: Reported if some register, status or log records it; Timer only if the only symptom is a timeout; Silent if nothing records it; Degraded if things keep working, slower.

7.2 Queue and Doorbell Protocol Violations

← 7.1 How a Protocol Checker Thinks7.3 Ordering and Interrupt Violations →

The NVMe queue model is a pair of circular buffers per queue pair with strict producer/consumer ownership: the host produces SQ entries and advances the SQ tail doorbell; the controller consumes them and reports its consumer position in the CQE's SQ Head Pointer (SQHD); the controller produces CQ entries, marking each new pass with an inverted Phase Tag; the host consumes them and returns slots by writing the CQ head doorbell. A queue with N entries holds at most N−1 items: "full" is (tail + 1) mod N == head, "empty" is head == tail. Every card below is a violation of this ownership contract. verified

Synthetic trace — a legal 4 KiB read on I/O queue 1 (queue size 4), for reference
t (ns)TLPDecodedChecker state after
0MWr host→dev, BAR0+1008h, 4 BSQ1 tail doorbell = 1SQ1 tail 1, 1 entry to fetch
310MRd dev→host, 64 B @ SQ1 basefetch slot 0—
620CplD host→dev, 64 BSQE: opc 02h Read, CID 0010h, PRP1 1000_0000h, NLB 7 (8×512 B)outstanding {(1,0010h)}
4900–530016 × MWr dev→host, 256 B eachread data to 1000_0000h … 1000_0FFFhCID 0010h: 4096/4096 B delivered
5400MWr dev→host, 16 B @ CQ1 base + 0CQE: CID 0010h, SQID 1, SQHD 1, status 0, P=1CQ1 tail 1, outstanding {}
5450MWr dev→host to MSI-X addressMSI-X vector 1—
6900MWr host→dev, BAR0+100Ch, 4 BCQ1 head doorbell = 1CQ1 head 1, empty
V-01SQ tail doorbell value beyond queue size ReportedNVMe queue
In a PEX trace
Visible Doorbell MWr (host→device, 4 B) to BAR0 + 1000h + 2y·(4<<DSTRD) whose data ≥ QSIZE+1 taken from the captured Create I/O SQ command; afterwards no SQE-fetch MRd from that SQ. A resulting async event is visible as a 16-byte CQE MWr to the admin CQ only if an AER command was outstanding.
What happens
The host writes an SQ y Tail Doorbell with a value ≥ the number of entries of that SQ (for example tail = 70 on a 64-entry queue). The value cannot be a slot index.
How it shows up
The controller ignores the write. If an Asynchronous Event Request is outstanding it may post an Error-type async event "Invalid Doorbell Write Value" and log an entry in the Error Information log. If no AER is outstanding, nothing is reported — commands placed in the SQ are simply never fetched and later time out.
Spec basis
NVMe Base: SQ Tail Doorbell register semantics; asynchronous event information "Invalid Doorbell Write Value" (Error event type). QEMU quotes the rule from NVMe 1.3d in nvme_process_db: "If host software writes an invalid value to the Submission Queue Tail Doorbell or Completion Queue Head Doorbell register and an Asynchronous Event Request command is outstanding, then an asynchronous event is posted…".
Typical causes
Host driver modulo bug (wrap at 2n instead of queue size); queue resized by a Create I/O SQ with a different QSIZE than the driver uses (QSIZE is 0's based); memory corruption of the driver's tail variable; a user-space driver (SPDK-style) with a stale queue configuration after reset.
How to detect / prove
Checker rule: for each doorbell MWr, decode queue id from offset and compare the value against the QSIZE+1 seen in the Create I/O SQ command (or AQA.ASQS+1 for the admin queue). On Linux, look for nvme_async_event trace events and nvme error-log entries; Linux v7.2 records the result in ctrl->aen_result.
Linux v7.2 source
drivers/nvme/host/pci.c:nvme_write_sq_db writes nvmeq->sq_tail, which nvme_sq_copy_cmd wraps at nvmeq->q_depth; drivers/nvme/host/core.c:nvme_complete_async_event handles NVME_AER_ERROR.
Test to provoke it
On QEMU (SAFE): use a user-space driver or nvme-cli is not enough — write the doorbell with a raw BAR mapping of an emulated device and watch the QEMU trace event pci_nvme_ub_db_wr_invalid_sqtail. On real hardware this is EXPERT: an unbound device, a vfio-based test harness, and an AER posted beforehand.
V-02CQ head doorbell value beyond queue size ReportedNVMe queue
In a PEX trace
Visible Doorbell MWr to BAR0 + 1000h + (2y+1)·(4<<DSTRD) with data ≥ CQ size; later SQE fetches continue but CQE MWr on that CQ stop after N−1 entries — the "device went quiet" pattern.
What happens
The host writes a CQ y Head Doorbell with a value ≥ the CQ size. The controller cannot interpret how many entries were released.
How it shows up
Write ignored; optional Error async event "Invalid Doorbell Write Value". Because the head is not advanced, the controller eventually sees the CQ as full and stops posting completions: all I/O on every SQ that shares that CQ stalls and then times out.
Spec basis
NVMe Base: CQ Head Doorbell semantics; same asynchronous event as V-01.
Typical causes
Host increments head past the end instead of wrapping; head computed in bytes instead of entries; CQ created with fewer entries than the driver assumes.
How to detect / prove
Same checker rule as V-01, against the CQ size from Create I/O CQ (QSIZE+1) or AQA.ACQS+1. Correlate: after the bad doorbell, CQE MWr count on that CQ stops at exactly size−1 outstanding entries.
Linux v7.2 source
drivers/nvme/host/pci.c:nvme_update_cq_head wraps cq_head at q_depth and flips cq_phase; nvme_ring_cq_doorbell writes it.
Test to provoke it
QEMU (SAFE): raw doorbell write of size+2 on an idle CQ; observe pci_nvme_ub_db_wr_invalid_cqhead and, with an AER outstanding, an async event on the admin CQ.
V-03Doorbell write for a queue that does not exist ReportedNVMe queue
In a PEX trace
Visible Doorbell MWr to an offset whose queue id was never created in the captured admin traffic, or written after the Delete I/O SQ/CQ completion; no fetch MRd follows. Requires the capture to include queue creation (start it before the driver loads, or decode CAP.DSTRD and Create commands from an earlier capture).
What happens
The host writes a doorbell offset belonging to a queue id that was never created, was already deleted, or exceeds the number of queues granted by Set Features Number of Queues.
How it shows up
Ignored by the controller; optional Error async event "Invalid Doorbell Register". QEMU's comment notes that the spec defines this code but "nowhere does it specify when to use it", and QEMU uses it for non-existent queues — so other controllers may report it differently or not at all. impl
Spec basis
NVMe Base: doorbell register layout (1000h + (2y)·(4<<CAP.DSTRD)); asynchronous event information "Invalid Doorbell Register".
Typical causes
Wrong CAP.DSTRD (doorbell stride) used by the host, so every doorbell lands on the wrong queue; queue deleted while another CPU still submits; use-after-teardown during reset; SR-IOV VF using PF queue numbering.
How to detect / prove
Checker keeps the set of live SQ/CQ ids from Create/Delete I/O SQ/CQ commands and their successful CQEs; any doorbell outside the set is flagged. A wrong stride shows as doorbells at offsets that are not multiples of 4<<DSTRD apart.
Linux v7.2 source
drivers/nvme/host/pci.c:nvme_create_queue sets up per-queue q_db pointers from dev->db_stride; teardown paths in nvme_dev_disable.
Test to provoke it
QEMU (SAFE): write SQ tail doorbell of queue id conf_ioqpairs+1; QEMU trace pci_nvme_ub_db_wr_invalid_sq. A synthetic example appears as rule DB-NOQ in 7.6.
V-04Misaligned or partial doorbell write SilentNVMe register
In a PEX trace
Visible MWr in the doorbell region with Length ≠ 1 DW, byte enables ≠ Fh, or a 2-DW write spanning SQ tail and CQ head of one pair.
What happens
A doorbell is written with a 1- or 2-byte access, or at an address that is not dword aligned, or a 64-bit write spans two doorbells (SQ tail and CQ head of the same pair).
How it shows up
Nothing is reported. QEMU logs a guest-error trace (pci_nvme_ub_db_wr_misaligned) and ignores the write; real controllers may ignore, latch only some bytes, or update both doorbells. impl
Spec basis
NVMe Base: controller registers are accessed with their natural width; doorbells are 32-bit registers. Accesses of other sizes are outside the defined behaviour.
Typical causes
Compiler merging two adjacent 32-bit stores into one 64-bit store on a write-combining mapping; a user-space driver using memcpy to MMIO; byte-wise BAR access tools.
How to detect / prove
Checker: doorbell MWr whose length ≠ 4 bytes, whose first/last byte enables are not 1111b, or whose address is not 4-byte aligned.
Linux v7.2 source
drivers/nvme/host/pci.c:nvme_write_sq_db and nvme_ring_cq_doorbell use writel (32-bit).
Test to provoke it
QEMU (SAFE): 16-bit write to a doorbell; check QEMU trace output.
V-05SQ tail moves backwards or overruns unfetched entries SilentNVMe queue
In a PEX trace
Visible Sequence of SQ tail doorbell values that implies more than N−1 unfetched entries (or a "backwards" move), compared with the SQE-fetch MRd/CplD count and SQHD in CQEs; re-fetched slots whose 64 bytes equal an already-completed SQE.
What happens
The new SQ tail value implies either a negative number of new entries (tail moved "backwards", i.e. the host withdrew entries) or so many new entries that the SQ would hold ≥ N items — the host has overwritten SQEs the controller had not yet fetched.
How it shows up
Nothing reported: the value is in range, so V-01 does not fire. Modulo arithmetic hides the problem — a backwards move looks like "N−k new commands". Consequences range from duplicated commands (the controller re-executes stale SQEs from a previous pass, e.g. a stale Write re-writes old data) to lost commands that time out.
Spec basis
NVMe Base queue model: the host shall not submit to a full SQ (full = tail+1 == head); entries between head and tail are owned by the controller and must not be modified by the host. The host learns the head from SQHD in CQEs.
Typical causes
Two CPUs submitting to one SQ without a lock; driver uses CQ depth for flow control while CQ is shared by several SQs; SQHD ignored and SQ larger than outstanding-request budget assumed; a reset path that zeroes the driver's tail but not the controller's.
How to detect / prove
Checker: keep host tail T, controller head H (from the most recent SQHD and from observed fetches); for a new tail T', new = (T'−T) mod N; flag if new > (N−1) − ((T−H) mod N). Also flag if the data of a re-fetched slot is identical to an already-completed SQE (stale replay).
Linux v7.2 source
drivers/nvme/host/pci.c:nvme_sq_copy_cmd under nvmeq->sq_lock; nvme_commit_rqs rings only when sq_tail != last_sq_tail. Linux sizes SQ and CQ identically and limits outstanding requests via blk-mq tags, so it does not need SQHD for flow control (it only passes it to trace_nvme_sq).
Test to provoke it
QEMU (SAFE): QEMU does not check this (see 7.1.3) — write tail values out of order and observe re-executed commands; a good negative test for your checker.
V-06CQ head released past the controller's tail SilentNVMe queue
In a PEX trace
Visible CQ head doorbell value ahead of the number of 16-byte CQE MWr written to that CQ since the previous head.
What happens
The host writes a CQ head that releases more entries than the controller has posted. The controller now believes there is free space that actually contains its own future slots; its full/empty calculation is corrupted.
How it shows up
No status. Later the controller may overwrite CQEs the host has not yet consumed (because it thinks they were released), producing lost completions (timeouts) or, combined with phase-tag reuse, stale completions processed twice.
Spec basis
NVMe Base queue model: the host releases only entries it has consumed (entries with the current phase).
Typical causes
Host consumes entries by index without checking the phase tag (polling bug); host and controller disagree on CQ size; a missed wrap in the host.
How to detect / prove
Checker counts CQE MWr per CQ (device tail) and compares every CQ head doorbell: released = (H'−H) mod N must be ≤ (Tail−H) mod N. Rule CQDB-PAST-TAIL in 7.6.
Linux v7.2 source
drivers/nvme/host/pci.c:nvme_poll_cq consumes entries only while nvme_cqe_pending (phase match) and rings the head once, after the loop.
Test to provoke it
QEMU (SAFE) with a test harness: post one command, write CQ head = 3. QEMU will not complain; your checker should.
V-07CQ overflow: head not advancing, or controller posts into a full CQ Timer onlyNVMe queue
In a PEX trace
Visible (a) N−1 CQE MWr then no CQ head doorbell for a long time; (b) a CQE MWr to the slot just before the current head. Timeout is visible only as absence plus timestamps (a fetched command with no CQE within the host timeout).
What happens
Two variants. (a) The host stops advancing the CQ head (interrupt lost, CPU stuck, driver bug); the CQ fills to N−1 entries and the controller must stop posting — I/O stalls. (b) The controller posts while the CQ is full, overwriting an entry the host has not consumed.
How it shows up
(a) Only the host's I/O timeout, often with Linux "completion polled" if the CQE was actually there (see V-15). (b) Nothing; the overwritten completion is lost and its command times out; the overwriting entry may carry the "wrong" phase from the host's point of view.
Spec basis
NVMe Base: CQ full condition (head == tail+1); the controller does not post to a full CQ and the host is responsible for sizing CQs so that the commands that can be outstanding on its SQs fit. QEMU nvme_post_cqes breaks out of its loop when nvme_cq_full.
Typical causes
(a) Missing MSI-X (V-15), interrupt affinity to an offline CPU, softirq starvation. (b) Controller firmware not tracking the CQ head doorbell; several SQs mapped to one small CQ.
How to detect / prove
Checker: keep CQ tail (count of CQE writes) and head (doorbells); flag a CQE write when (tail+1) mod N == head. For (a), flag "CQ head unchanged for X ms while CQ non-empty".
Linux v7.2 source
drivers/nvme/host/pci.c:nvme_timeout polls the CQ first and prints "I/O tag %d (%04x) QID %d timeout, completion polled" when the CQE was present.
Test to provoke it
QEMU (SAFE): issue N commands while never writing the CQ head; verify QEMU stops at N−1 CQEs. On hardware, the (b) variant needs an analyzer to prove.
V-08Command Identifier reused while still outstanding SilentNVMe command
In a PEX trace
Visible Two SQE-fetch CplDs on the same SQ carrying the same CID (DW0 bits 31:16) with no CQE MWr for that CID between them.
What happens
The host submits a command whose CID equals that of a command still outstanding on the same SQ. Completions become ambiguous: the host cannot tell which of the two finished, and Abort (which names SQID+CID) becomes ambiguous too.
How it shows up
Usually nothing. A controller may detect it and complete the new command with Generic status 03h "Command ID Conflict" (Linux NVME_SC_CMDID_CONFLICT); many controllers do not check. QEMU does not check (its nvme_abort would match the first request with that CID). impl
Spec basis
NVMe Base: the Command Identifier together with the SQ Identifier uniquely identifies a command outstanding at the controller; Generic Command Status "Command ID Conflict".
Typical causes
Host reusing a tag before its completion was processed; driver completing a request on timeout and reusing the tag while the controller still owns the original; user-space drivers with fixed CIDs.
How to detect / prove
Checker keeps the outstanding set per SQ: add (SQID,CID) on SQE fetch, remove on CQE. Flag duplicates (rule CID-REUSE in 7.6). Linux encodes a 4-bit generation counter into the top bits of the CID, so a reused tag normally has a different CID — a duplicate in a Linux trace is strong evidence of a real bug.
Linux v7.2 source
drivers/nvme/host/nvme.h:nvme_cid = nvme_cid_install_genctr(genctr) | rq->tag; nvme_find_rq checks the generation counter.
Test to provoke it
QEMU (SAFE) user-space harness: submit two long reads with the same CID; verify the checker flags it; on hardware, check whether the controller returns status 03h.
V-09CQE for an unknown or already-completed CID ReportedNVMe command
In a PEX trace
Visible A CQE MWr whose DW3 CID matches no earlier SQE fetch on that SQ, or matches a CID that already completed. The host's "invalid id" log line is NOT in the trace.
What happens
The controller writes a completion whose CID matches no outstanding command on that SQ — a duplicate completion, a corrupted CID, or a completion for a command the host already aborted/timed out.
How it shows up
Linux v7.2 logs "invalid id %d completed on queue %d" (or "request %#x genctr mismatch (got … expected …)") and drops the entry. Other drivers may complete the wrong request — a silent data-integrity hazard (the wrong buffer is declared ready).
Spec basis
NVMe Base: each command is completed exactly once by one CQE identifying it by SQID+CID.
Typical causes
Controller firmware posting a completion twice (retry path); CQE corrupted in flight (bit flip in DRAM or a poisoned TLP ignored); host timeout handling that freed the tag while the command was still executing.
How to detect / prove
Checker rule CQE-UNKNOWN. In Linux, grep dmesg for "invalid id" and "genctr mismatch". A trace distinguishes "duplicate" (CID seen in an earlier CQE) from "never submitted" (CID never fetched).
Linux v7.2 source
drivers/nvme/host/pci.c:nvme_handle_cqe; drivers/nvme/host/nvme.h:nvme_find_rq.
Test to provoke it
QEMU fault injection is not built in; use a modified QEMU or an FPGA/emulator that duplicates a CQE (EXPERT). In the synthetic example, CID 0x99 triggers it.
V-10Wrong SQID or non-advancing SQHD in a CQE SilentNVMe command
In a PEX trace
Visible CQE MWr whose DW2 SQID differs from the queue the CID was fetched from, or whose SQHD sequence does not advance while SQE fetches proceed.
What happens
The CQE's SQ Identifier (DW2 bits 31:16) names a different SQ than the one the command came from, or SQ Head Pointer (DW2 bits 15:0) moves backwards, beyond the tail, or never advances although commands are being consumed.
How it shows up
With a shared CQ, a wrong SQID makes the host look up the CID in the wrong SQ — wrong request completed or "invalid id". A frozen SQHD makes a host that uses SQHD for flow control believe the SQ is full: throughput collapses to zero without any error. Linux, which does not use SQHD for flow control, is unaffected — so the same SSD "works on Linux, hangs on another OS".
Spec basis
NVMe Base: CQE DW2 SQID and SQHD semantics — SQHD indicates the current SQ head pointer for the SQ named by SQID.
Typical causes
Firmware filling SQHD from a stale variable; CQE template reused across queues; SQHD reported before the fetch actually advanced the head.
How to detect / prove
Checker: SQID must equal the SQ the CID was fetched from; SQHD must satisfy (SQHD − previous SQHD) mod N ≤ number of fetches since, and must never pass the host tail.
Linux v7.2 source
drivers/nvme/host/pci.c:nvme_handle_cqe passes cqe->sq_head to trace_nvme_sq only and uses cqe->sq_id in the "invalid id" message.
Test to provoke it
Use a driver that honours SQHD (e.g. a user-space test harness) and an SQ much smaller than the outstanding-command budget; a broken SQHD will deadlock it quickly.
V-11Phase tag not inverted on CQ wrap Timer onlyNVMe queue
In a PEX trace
Visible CQE MWr to slot 0 after a wrap carrying the same phase bit as the previous pass (decode bit 16 of DW3 / bit 0 of the status half).
What happens
After the controller wraps from the last CQ slot to slot 0 it must invert the Phase Tag (P, bit 0 of the status half of DW3). If it keeps the old value, the host — which expects the new phase — sees the new entry as "old" and does not consume it; if it inverts too early, the host consumes stale entries.
How it shows up
Missing inversion: completions invisible to the host → I/O timeout (Linux may report "completion polled" only if the phase matches; here it does not, so a plain timeout and abort/reset follow). Early inversion: stale CQEs processed twice → "invalid id" messages or double completion.
Spec basis
NVMe Base: Phase Tag "identifies whether a completion queue entry is new"; it is inverted each pass through the CQ; host initialises the CQ memory to zero so the first pass uses P=1.
Typical causes
Firmware wrap logic off by one; CQ size mismatch between host and controller; controller reset without the host re-zeroing CQ memory.
How to detect / prove
Checker keeps tail and expected phase per CQ (start 1, invert at wrap) and compares every CQE (rule PHASE in 7.6). Note that a phase error is often the symptom of an earlier V-07(b) overflow; always report the first abnormal event.
Linux v7.2 source
drivers/nvme/host/pci.c:nvme_cqe_pending compares status & 1 with nvmeq->cq_phase; nvme_update_cq_head flips cq_phase at wrap.
Test to provoke it
Run enough I/O to wrap a small CQ many times (e.g. io_queue_depth=2 module parameter — the minimum Linux accepts — on a test system, SAFE) and verify no phase findings in the capture.
V-12Shadow doorbell buffer out of sync with the MMIO doorbell SilentNVMe queue
In a PEX trace
Partly visible Controller MRd of the shadow-doorbell buffer and the CplD values it returns are visible, as are MMIO doorbells; the host's own writes to the shadow buffer are CPU-to-DRAM and never cross the link. Only a mismatch between returned shadow values and later MMIO doorbells can be shown.
What happens
With the Doorbell Buffer Config admin command (used mainly by emulated/virtual controllers), the host writes doorbell values into a shadow buffer in host memory and only rings the real MMIO doorbell when the controller's EventIdx says so. If the host updates one but not the other, or ignores EventIdx, the controller works from a stale tail/head.
How it shows up
Stalls that recover when any later doorbell is rung; latency spikes; no error. QEMU's nvme_process_db comments that "various drivers including ones that run on Linux, are not updating Admin Queues" in the shadow buffer, so QEMU writes the admin values back itself. impl
Spec basis
NVMe Base: Doorbell Buffer Config command — Shadow Doorbell buffer and EventIdx buffer; QEMU quotes "the host shall also update the controller's corresponding doorbell property to match the value of that entry in the Shadow Doorbell buffer".
Typical causes
Missing memory barrier between the shadow write and the EventIdx read; admin queue excluded from shadowing in the driver; migration of a VM between hosts.
How to detect / prove
In a VM, the "trace" is QEMU's own tracing (pci_nvme_* events) or a vhost/vfio capture. Compare shadow value reads (DMA reads of the shadow buffer) with MMIO doorbells.
Linux v7.2 source
drivers/nvme/host/pci.c:nvme_dbbuf_update_and_check_event, called from nvme_write_sq_db and nvme_ring_cq_doorbell.
Test to provoke it
QEMU (SAFE): enable shadow doorbells (they are used automatically when the controller supports the command) and stress small-queue workloads while tracing pci_nvme_mmio_doorbell_sq.

7.3 Ordering and Interrupt Violations

← 7.2 Queue and Doorbell Protocol Violations7.4 Command-Format Violations: PRP, SGL, MDTS, FUSE and Reserved Fields →

NVMe over PCIe relies on one PCIe ordering guarantee above all others: a posted Memory Write must not pass an earlier posted Memory Write in the same direction unless the later TLP has the Relaxed Ordering (RO) attribute set (and the path honours it). Data MWr TLPs, the CQE MWr and the MSI-X MWr are all posted writes from the device to the host, so if the device sends them in the order data → CQE → MSI-X without RO on the CQE and MSI-X, the host is guaranteed to observe them in that order. The producer–consumer correctness of every NVMe read rests on this. verified

V-13Completion posted before the data writes (ordering) SilentNVMe / PCIe ordering
In a PEX trace
Visible CQE MWr for CID X timestamped before the last data MWr whose address lies in CID X's PRP/SGL ranges (decoded from the SQE and PRP-list CplDs); or RO=1 in the CQE TLP attributes. This proves the order the device sent; whether a switch reordered further upstream needs a second probe.
What happens
For a Read, the controller writes the CQE (or sets RO on data or CQE TLPs in a way that lets the CQE overtake) before all data MWr TLPs for that command have been sent. The host sees "success", hands the buffer to the application, and the application reads stale bytes; the real data arrives microseconds later, after the application has already used the buffer.
How it shows up
Nothing in any log. Symptoms are intermittent data corruption that disappears when tracing is enabled (timing changes) and checksum failures at the application level, typically on the last TLP(s) of a transfer.
Spec basis
PCI Express Base: ordering rules for posted requests (a posted request must not pass another posted request unless RO is set) and the Relaxed Ordering attribute; NVMe Base: a completion indicates the command's data transfer is complete.
Typical causes
Controller DMA engine with several parallel channels and the CQE sent from a different channel; RO set on the CQE write; a switch or root complex that reorders RO TLPs (legally) combined with the device setting RO where it must not.
How to detect / prove
Checker: map each data MWr to its CID (address ∈ the command's PRP/SGL ranges); at each CQE, require delivered bytes == transfer length (rule CQE-BEFORE-DATA in 7.6). Also flag RO=1 on any CQE or MSI-X TLP. Prove at the application level with fio --verify=crc32c --verify_fatal=1 on reads of data written earlier.
Linux v7.2 source
drivers/nvme/host/pci.c:nvme_poll_cq issues dma_rmb() between the phase check and reading the rest of the CQE — this protects against CPU reordering of the CQE fields, not against a device that wrote the CQE too early. Relaxed ordering enable bit: include/uapi/linux/pci_regs.h:PCI_EXP_DEVCTL_RELAX_EN.
Test to provoke it
CAUTION: toggle Device Control "Enable Relaxed Ordering" with setpci on an idle test device and run a verify workload with an analyzer attached; never on a system with data you care about.
V-14MSI-X sent before the CQE it announces DegradedNVMe interrupt
In a PEX trace
Visible MWr to the MSI-X message address (vector identified from the captured MSI-X table writes) with no preceding CQE MWr on a CQ mapped to that vector, or the CQE MWr arriving after it.
What happens
The interrupt MWr reaches the host before the CQE MWr (or there is no new CQE at all). The interrupt handler polls the CQ, finds nothing with the expected phase, and returns.
How it shows up
Spurious interrupts: Linux nvme_irq returns IRQ_NONE; if this happens very often the kernel's spurious-interrupt detector can disable the IRQ line ("nobody cared"), after which completions are found only by the timeout handler — then V-07(a) and "completion polled" messages. Before that point: extra latency, because the real CQE waits for the next interrupt.
Spec basis
NVMe Base: interrupts are generated for new CQ entries; PCI Express Base posted-write ordering ensures the MSI-X MWr cannot pass the earlier CQE MWr if the device sends them in order without RO.
Typical causes
Interrupt sent from a different internal engine than the CQE; interrupt coalescing logic counting submissions instead of completions; RO set on the MSI-X write.
How to detect / prove
Checker rule MSIX-NO-CQE: each MSI-X for vector v must be preceded by at least one new CQE on a CQ mapped to v since the previous MSI-X. On Linux, compare per-vector counts in /proc/interrupts with completions; spurious counts show in /proc/irq/<n>/spurious.
Linux v7.2 source
drivers/nvme/host/pci.c:nvme_irq (returns IRQ_NONE when nvme_poll_cq finds nothing), nvme_irq_check for threaded interrupts.
Test to provoke it
Device-side bug; to validate the checker, use the synthetic trace in 7.6 (line with MSI-X at t=1500 ns).
V-15CQE posted but no MSI-X ever sent Timer onlyNVMe interrupt
In a PEX trace
Visible CQE MWr followed by no MSI-X MWr for that vector; the host's MSI-X table/PBA MMIO writes and reads are on the link too, so a mask bit set by the host is visible. The eventual timeout appears only as a long gap, then Abort or controller reset traffic.
What happens
The controller writes a CQE but never sends the interrupt (vector masked in the MSI-X table, wrong vector programmed in Create I/O CQ, function-mask bit set, or firmware bug).
How it shows up
Linux v7.2: the request times out; nvme_timeout polls the CQ, finds the completion and prints "I/O tag … QID … timeout, completion polled" — the signature of a lost interrupt. Latency equals the timeout (default 30 s for I/O).
Spec basis
NVMe Base: Create I/O Completion Queue Interrupt Vector (IV) and Interrupts Enabled (IEN) fields; PCI MSI-X table and Pending Bit Array semantics (a masked vector sets its pending bit instead of sending).
Typical causes
MSI-X vector masked during CPU hotplug or IRQ migration and never unmasked; IV out of range of the MSI-X table size; interrupt remapping (IOMMU) misconfiguration so the write is blocked.
How to detect / prove
Checker: CQE written, no MSI-X for the vector within a window (e.g. 1 ms) while IEN=1 for that CQ. Host-side: "completion polled" in dmesg; read the MSI-X PBA through the BAR (read-only inspection) to see pending bits.
Linux v7.2 source
drivers/nvme/host/pci.c:nvme_timeout; vector assignment in nvme_create_queue / queue_irq_offset.
Test to provoke it
EXPERT: mask a vector in the MSI-X table of a test device during I/O; expect "completion polled" and recovery.
V-16DMA to a command's buffer after its completion SilentNVMe / DMA
In a PEX trace
Visible Data MWr/MRd into CID X's buffer range after the CQE MWr for CID X. An IOMMU fault caused by it is host-side and not in the trace.
What happens
The controller writes to (or reads from) host memory belonging to a command after it has posted that command's CQE — for example the tail of the data for a read, or a retry of a data read for a write. By then the host may have freed or reused the buffer.
How it shows up
Random memory corruption elsewhere in the system (the page has been reallocated), IOMMU faults if the mapping was torn down (DMAR/AMD-Vi fault messages in dmesg naming the device), or nothing at all.
Spec basis
NVMe Base: posting the completion transfers ownership of the data buffers back to the host; PRP/SGL entries are valid only while the command is outstanding.
Typical causes
Same as V-13 (parallel DMA channels); Abort handling that completes the command while a DMA is still queued; firmware retry after timeout.
How to detect / prove
Checker rule DMA-NOCMD: any data MWr/MRd whose address belongs to a command that has already completed (and no newer command owns that address). With an IOMMU in strict mode, a late DMA produces a translation fault — strong host-side evidence.
Linux v7.2 source
Unmapping on completion in drivers/nvme/host/pci.c:nvme_pci_complete_rq / nvme_pci_complete_batch.
Test to provoke it
Boot a test host with iommu.strict=1 (or the platform equivalent) and run high-QD mixed I/O; any IOMMU fault naming the SSD is a finding to correlate with a trace.

7.4 Command-Format Violations: PRP, SGL, MDTS, FUSE and Reserved Fields

← 7.3 Ordering and Interrupt Violations7.5 PCIe Transaction, Data Link and Flit Layer Violations →

Once the checker decodes each 64-byte submission queue entry (SQE) from the CplD that answers the controller's fetch, it can validate the command format exactly as the controller should. The rules below are all visible in the SQE bytes and in the PRP-list / SGL-segment reads that follow. Byte layout reminders: CDW0 = opcode (bits 7:0), FUSE (bits 9:8), PSDT (bits 15:14), CID (bits 31:16); NSID at bytes 4–7; MPTR at bytes 16–23; DPTR (PRP1, PRP2 or SGL1) at bytes 24–39; CDW10–15 at bytes 40–63. verified

7.4.1 PRP rules a checker can enforce

RuleDetailQEMU evidence
PRP1 may have an offsetOffset into the first memory page; must be dword aligned (bits 1:0 = 0)nvme_map_prp: trans_len = page_size - (prp1 % page_size)
If the transfer fits in PRP1's page, PRP2 is unusedContent of PRP2 is then ignored (reserved)no read of PRP2 when len becomes 0
If the remainder fits in one more page, PRP2 is a data pointerMust have zero offset (page aligned)prp2 & (page_size-1) → NVME_INVALID_PRP_OFFSET | NVME_DNR
Otherwise PRP2 points to a PRP listThe list pointer may have an offset; entries are page alignedcomment "The first PRP list entry, pointed to by PRP2 may contain offset"; each entry checked for zero offset
List chainingWhen more entries are needed than fit in the rest of the list page, the last entry of that page points to the next list pageif (i == nents - 1 && len > n->page_size) → next list
Page size"Page" = CC.MPS memory page size (212+MPS), not the CPU page sizen->page_size
V-17PRP1 not dword aligned, or PRP list entry with an offset ReportedNVMe command
In a PEX trace
Visible SQE CplD with PRP1 bits 1:0 ≠ 0, or the PRP-list read (device MRd from PRP2, answered by CplD) returning entries with non-zero low bits; then either a CQE with status 13h or data MWr at odd addresses.
What happens
PRP1 has bits 1:0 set, or an entry inside a PRP list (other than as allowed for the list pointer) has a non-zero page offset.
How it shows up
A checking controller completes the command with Generic status 13h "PRP Offset Invalid" (Linux NVME_SC_PRP_INVALID_OFFSET), usually with DNR. A non-checking controller DMAs to the wrong address — silent corruption of unrelated memory.
Spec basis
NVMe Base: PRP Entry format (offset field; dword alignment), PRP List rules; Generic Command Status "PRP Offset Invalid".
Typical causes
Host builds PRPs from CPU page size (e.g. 16 KiB or 64 KiB pages on arm64/ppc64) while the controller is configured with CC.MPS = 4 KiB, or vice versa; byte-granular user buffers passed through a passthrough interface.
How to detect / prove
Checker: decode DPTR, fetch the PRP list via the MRd/CplD that follows, and test each entry against the rules in the table above. Host-side: nvme error-log shows status 13h with the CID and SQID.
Linux v7.2 source
drivers/nvme/host/pci.c:nvme_pci_setup_data_prp builds PRP1 from the first segment's offset and list entries with NVME_CTRL_PAGE_SIZE stride; dma_set_min_align_mask(&pdev->dev, NVME_CTRL_PAGE_SIZE - 1) in probe keeps bounce buffers page-offset-preserving.
Test to provoke it
QEMU (SAFE): passthrough command with a crafted PRP list; expect status 13h and QEMU trace pci_nvme_err_invalid_prplist_ent.
V-18Offset in PRP2 when it is a data pointer ReportedNVMe command
In a PEX trace
Visible 8 KiB command with PRP1 = …1000h and PRP2 = …0010h, no PRP-list MRd, then a CQE with status 13h — or, for a lenient controller, data MWr starting at …0010h.
What happens
The transfer needs exactly two pages (the remainder after PRP1's page fits in one page), so PRP2 is a data pointer; it must point at the start of a page but contains an offset.
How it shows up
Status 13h PRP Offset Invalid with DNR (QEMU and checking controllers). A lenient controller writes the second part of the data to PRP2 including the offset and then across the next page boundary — corrupting the neighbouring page.
Spec basis
NVMe Base: PRP Entry 2 semantics — data pointer vs PRP List pointer — and the zero-offset requirement for PRP entries other than PRP1 and the list pointer.
Typical causes
Host confusing "two-page transfer" with "list" case; off-by-one in computing whether the remainder fits in one page (e.g. using < instead of ≤).
How to detect / prove
Checker rule PRP2-OFFSET in 7.6: compute first = page − (PRP1 mod page); if first < len ≤ first + page then PRP2 mod page must be 0.
Linux v7.2 source
drivers/nvme/host/pci.c:nvme_pci_setup_data_prp (the length <= NVME_CTRL_PAGE_SIZE branch places the second page directly in PRP2).
Test to provoke it
QEMU (SAFE): passthrough read of 8 KiB with PRP2 offset 10h; expect pci_nvme_err_invalid_prp2_align and status 13h.
V-19PRP list crossing or chaining rules broken ReportedNVMe command
In a PEX trace
Visible PRP-list MRd that spans a page boundary, or a data MWr to an address that should have been the next-list pointer; compare described bytes (from list CplDs) with the command length.
What happens
The PRP list is laid out so that entries run past the end of the memory page that holds the list without using the last entry as a pointer to the next list page; or the last entry is used as a data pointer when more entries follow; or the list has fewer entries than the transfer needs.
How it shows up
The controller interprets a data page address as a list pointer (or vice versa): DMA to/from wrong memory, a Data Transfer Error (04h) if the access fails, or 13h when the misinterpreted entry happens to have an offset. Often silent.
Spec basis
NVMe Base: PRP List — a list occupies one memory page; when more entries are required, the last entry in the page is a pointer to the next PRP list.
Typical causes
List allocated from a pool not aligned to the controller page; driver computing entries per page from CPU page size; list allocated at an offset with the "entries per page" count not reduced accordingly (QEMU computes nents from the offset precisely because this is legal for the first list).
How to detect / prove
Checker walks the list exactly as nvme_map_prp does and compares the number of data bytes described with the command length (NLB+1 × LBA size, plus metadata if interleaved).
Linux v7.2 source
drivers/nvme/host/pci.c:nvme_pci_setup_data_prp chains when i == NVME_CTRL_PAGE_SIZE >> 3; NVME_MAX_NR_DESCRIPTORS (5) at the top of pci.c bounds the number of list pages per request.
Test to provoke it
QEMU (SAFE) user-space harness: 1 MiB transfer with a PRP list starting at offset FF0h of its page and no chaining; observe misbehaviour and whether status 13h is returned.
V-20Transfer longer than MDTS ReportedNVMe command
In a PEX trace
Visible SQE whose NLB implies more bytes than 2^MDTS × MPSMIN; MDTS is visible if the Identify Controller data (device MWr of 4 KiB to the host buffer) is in the capture. Then a CQE with status 02h/DNR — or the oversize data transfer followed by success.
What happens
A command transfers more data than Maximum Data Transfer Size allows: MDTS (Identify Controller) is a power of two in units of the minimum memory page size (CAP.MPSMIN); 0 means no limit. MDTS = 5 with 4 KiB MPSMIN → 128 KiB.
How it shows up
QEMU and most controllers: Generic status 02h "Invalid Field in Command" with DNR. Some controllers transfer the data anyway (and may truncate silently).
Spec basis
NVMe Base: Identify Controller MDTS field; applies to the data transfer of a command (NVM Command Set defines how it applies to commands like Write Zeroes, which have no data transfer — they have separate limits such as WZSL in the NVM Command Set Identify Controller structure).
Typical causes
Passthrough tools ignoring MDTS; user-space drivers with hard-coded 1 MiB I/O; kernel limits overridden; MDTS reduced by a firmware update while the host cached the old value.
How to detect / prove
Checker rule MDTS in 7.6: (NLB+1)·LBA size (+ metadata if extended LBA) > 2MDTS·MPSMIN. Host: nvme id-ctrl /dev/nvme0 | grep mdts and cat /sys/block/nvme0n1/queue/max_hw_sectors_kb.
Linux v7.2 source
drivers/nvme/host/core.c:nvme_init_identify derives max_hw_sectors from id->mdts via nvme_mps_to_sectors; nvme_init_non_mdts_limits handles commands without data transfer.
Test to provoke it
QEMU (SAFE): -device nvme,mdts=5 then nvme io-passthru a 256 KiB read; expect status 02h and trace pci_nvme_err_mdts.
V-21Reserved fields non-zero SilentNVMe command
In a PEX trace
Visible SQE bytes with reserved bits set (decode against the opcode's field map for the spec revision in VS, which is visible if the host's config/BAR read of VS is captured).
What happens
The host sets bits that are reserved in the SQE (for example CDW0 bits 13:10, CDW2–3 in commands that do not define them, reserved CDW10–15 bits) or in a data structure it passes (feature data, PRP list padding).
How it shows up
Today usually nothing — most controllers ignore reserved bits. Tomorrow, when a newer spec revision gives those bits a meaning, the same host software suddenly enables a feature it never intended (e.g. a bit that later became a "storage tag" or "directive" field). Some controllers return Invalid Field in Command. impl
Spec basis
NVMe Base conventions: reserved fields shall be cleared to 0 by the writer; receivers are generally not required to check. (Verify the exact wording for your revision in the spec.)
Typical causes
Uninitialised SQE memory (stack garbage) in user-space or firmware hosts; copying a command structure from a newer spec header to an older device.
How to detect / prove
Checker with a per-opcode mask of defined bits, generated from the spec revision the device claims in VS; flag any 1 outside the mask. Re-run the check against the masks of the next spec revision to spot "future meaning" hazards.
Linux v7.2 source
Linux builds commands from a zeroed struct nvme_command (e.g. memset(&c, 0, sizeof(c)) in drivers/nvme/host/ioctl.c:nvme_user_cmd), so reserved fields are zero unless passthrough users set them via CDW fields.
Test to provoke it
SAFE on a scratch namespace: nvme io-passthru a read with a reserved CDW bit set; record whether the controller ignores it or returns 02h — a good conformance data point.
V-22FUSE field misuse (fused operations) ReportedNVMe command
In a PEX trace
Visible SQE with FUSE=01b whose partner slot was not made visible by the same doorbell, or is not FUSE=10b; CQEs with status 09h/0Ah.
What happens
FUSE (CDW0 bits 9:8): 01b = first command of a fused pair, 10b = second, 11b reserved. Violations: first without second; second without first; the two not in adjacent SQ slots; a non-fusable opcode (only Compare + Write is defined for the NVM Command Set); fused commands submitted to a controller that does not report support in Identify Controller FUSES; reserved value 11b.
How it shows up
Defined status codes: Generic 09h "Command Aborted due to Failed Fused Command" and 0Ah "Command Aborted due to Missing Fused Command" (Linux NVME_SC_FUSED_FAIL, NVME_SC_FUSED_MISSING), or 02h Invalid Field. QEMU returns Invalid Field (without DNR) for any FUSE value because it does not implement fused operations.
Spec basis
NVMe Base: Fused Operations; Identify Controller FUSES (Fused Operation Support); NVM Command Set: Compare and Write as the fused pair.
Typical causes
Host sets FUSE but the doorbell is rung between the two commands (so the controller fetches only the first); second command placed after a wrap without considering adjacency; garbage in CDW0.
How to detect / prove
Checker: for FUSE=01b at SQ slot k, require FUSE=10b at slot (k+1) mod N in the same doorbell batch; require FUSES bit 0 set; require opcodes 05h then 01h.
Linux v7.2 source
Linux does not issue fused commands (see the comment in drivers/nvme/host/fc.c: "Linux initiators don't send fused"); drivers/nvme/host/ioctl.c:nvme_user_cmd rejects passthrough commands with non-zero flags (-EINVAL), so FUSE/PSDT cannot be set from user space. Strings for 09h/0Ah are in drivers/nvme/host/constants.c.
Test to provoke it
Requires a user-space driver (SPDK-style, CAUTION on a scratch device): submit a lone FUSE=01b Compare; expect 0Ah or 02h.
V-23Admin command placed on an I/O queue (or vice versa) SilentNVMe command
In a PEX trace
Partly visible The SQE with an admin-looking opcode/CDW layout on an I/O SQ is visible, and so is any data or DSM range-list transfer it triggers; whether the device actually wrote or deallocated media is NOT visible — prove that with a read-back.
What happens
Opcodes are interpreted per queue type: SQ 0 carries Admin opcodes; I/O SQs carry I/O command set opcodes. An admin opcode on an I/O queue is not an admin command — it is whatever I/O command shares that opcode value. Admin 01h Create I/O SQ becomes NVM Write; 02h Get Log Page becomes Read; 00h Delete I/O SQ becomes Flush; 09h Set Features becomes Dataset Management (possibly a deallocate!); 06h Identify, 0Ah Get Features, 10h Firmware Commit map to opcodes that are reserved or optional in the NVM set and normally return Invalid Command Opcode.
How it shows up
When the opcode collides with an implemented I/O command: nothing — the controller executes a real I/O with arguments taken from admin fields (CDW10 = PRP/feature data becomes SLBA/NLB…). Otherwise Generic status 01h "Invalid Command Opcode" with DNR.
Spec basis
NVMe Base: Admin command set vs I/O command sets; opcode tables per command set; Commands Supported and Effects log page.
Typical causes
Passthrough tool sending an admin opcode through the namespace I/O passthrough path (e.g. nvme io-passthru with an admin opcode); user-space driver queue-selection bug; test scripts copying opcode tables.
How to detect / prove
Checker: classify each SQE by queue id; for SQ ≠ 0 validate the opcode against the namespace's command set (Commands Supported and Effects log for that CSI); flag admin-only opcodes on I/O queues whose CDW layout looks like an admin command (e.g. NSID = 0 or FFFFFFFFh with opcode 09h). Then read back the affected LBAs.
Linux v7.2 source
QEMU dispatches by queue: nvme_process_sq calls sq->sqid ? nvme_io_cmd(n, req) : nvme_admin_cmd(n, req), and nvme_io_cmd_nvm rejects unsupported opcodes with NVME_INVALID_OPCODE | NVME_DNR. Linux: drivers/nvme/host/ioctl.c:nvme_cmd_allowed gates passthrough by opcode and capability.
Test to provoke it
CAUTION, scratch namespace only: nvme io-passthru /dev/nvme0n1 --opcode=0x06 … should return Invalid Command Opcode; never try opcodes 01h/09h on a namespace with data.
⚠️ Warning

Opcode collisions are the reason a mis-routed "harmless" admin command can destroy data. When a trace shows an admin-looking command on an I/O queue, treat it as a potential write or deallocate and verify the namespace contents.

V-24SGL descriptor rules broken ReportedNVMe command
In a PEX trace
Visible SQE with PSDT ≠ 00b on SQ 0; SGL segment MRd/CplD whose descriptors break the rules (length not multiple of 16, wrong last-descriptor type); CQE status 0Dh/0Eh/0Fh/11h with DNR.
What happens
Typical violations: PSDT selects SGL on an Admin command (not allowed for NVMe over PCIe); SGL used although Identify Controller SGLS reports no support; Segment / Last Segment descriptor length zero or not a multiple of 16; a Last Segment whose final descriptor is not a Data Block; a Segment descriptor inside a segment in a position other than last; total data block length smaller than the transfer, or larger without "excess length" support; reserved descriptor type; SGL Data Block with address + length overflowing 64 bits.
How it shows up
QEMU statuses (all with DNR): NVME_INVALID_SGL_SEG_DESCR (0Dh), NVME_INVALID_NUM_SGL_DESCRS (0Eh), NVME_DATA_SGL_LEN_INVALID (0Fh), NVME_SGL_DESCR_TYPE_INVALID (11h); metadata SGL length problems map to NVME_MD_SGL_LEN_INVALID; SGL on admin → Invalid Field. Linux names for the same generic codes: NVME_SC_SGL_INVALID_LAST 0Dh, _COUNT 0Eh, _DATA 0Fh, _METADATA 10h, _TYPE 11h, _OFFSET 16h, _GRANULARITY 1Eh.
Spec basis
NVMe Base: Scatter Gather List — descriptor types (Data Block, Bit Bucket, Segment, Last Segment, Keyed Data Block, Transport), SGLS field, PSDT; NVMe over PCIe transport: Admin commands use PRPs.
Typical causes
Host chaining segments like PRP lists; byte-granular buffers with SGLS "dword alignment required" bit ignored; descriptor arrays allocated without 16-byte alignment.
How to detect / prove
Checker walks SGL segments as QEMU's nvme_map_sgl does, including the "no forward progress" rule QEMU adds to stop pathological loops, and compares described length with the command length.
Linux v7.2 source
drivers/nvme/host/pci.c:nvme_pci_use_sgls uses SGLs only when nvmeq->qid ≠ 0 and the controller supports them (forced for page gaps, user commands, multiple integrity segments); nvme_pci_setup_data_sgl; module parameter sgl_threshold (default 32 KiB).
Test to provoke it
QEMU (SAFE): QEMU supports SGLs; a user-space harness can send a Last Segment ending with a Segment descriptor and observe 0Dh.
V-25Illegal queue creation parameters ReportedNVMe admin
In a PEX trace
Visible Admin SQE opcode 01h/05h with QSIZE > CAP.MQES (CAP visible as a captured BAR read), unaligned PRP1, PC=0; CQE with SCT=1 and SC 00h/01h/02h/08h.
What happens
Create I/O SQ/CQ with: QID 0 or beyond the granted number of queues, or already in use; SQ referencing a CQ that does not exist; QSIZE 0 or greater than CAP.MQES; non-contiguous queue (PC=0) on a controller with CAP.CQR=1; queue base not page aligned; interrupt vector beyond the MSI-X table.
How it shows up
Command Specific status: Completion Queue Invalid (00h), Invalid Queue Identifier (01h), Invalid Queue Size (02h), Invalid Interrupt Vector (08h); or Generic PRP Offset Invalid / Invalid Field. QEMU nvme_create_sq returns NVME_INVALID_CQID, NVME_INVALID_QID, NVME_MAX_QSIZE_EXCEEDED, NVME_INVALID_PRP_OFFSET, NVME_INVALID_FIELD (PC=0) — all with DNR.
Spec basis
NVMe Base: Create I/O Submission Queue and Create I/O Completion Queue commands; CAP.MQES (0's based), CAP.CQR.
Typical causes
QSIZE passed as 1's based; ignoring MQES on small embedded controllers; physically discontiguous queue memory on a controller without PRP-list queue support.
How to detect / prove
Checker validates Create commands against CAP (read during init — capture from controller enable) and the queue count granted in the Set Features Number of Queues CQE (DW0).
Linux v7.2 source
drivers/nvme/host/pci.c:nvme_create_queue and the adapter helpers it calls; queue depth clamped against MQES during nvme_pci_enable.
Test to provoke it
QEMU (SAFE): nvme admin-passthru Create I/O SQ with QSIZE beyond MQES on an unused QID; expect status 0102h (SCT 1, SC 02h) in QEMU's encoding.

7.5 PCIe Transaction, Data Link and Flit Layer Violations

← 7.4 Command-Format Violations: PRP, SGL, MDTS, FUSE and Reserved Fields7.6 An Executable Checker over an Exported Trace →

Below NVMe, every PCIe link has its own rulebook. The Transaction Layer constrains TLP sizes, address/length combinations, completion splitting and ordering; the Data Link Layer (DLL) guarantees delivery with sequence numbers, LCRC (Link CRC), Ack/Nak DLLPs and a replay buffer; in PCIe 6.0 Flit mode the unit of protection becomes a fixed-size FLIT with FEC (forward error correction) and CRC. Some of these violations are caught by the receiver and logged in the AER (Advanced Error Reporting) capability — Linux v7.2 names the bits in drivers/pci/pcie/aer.c (aer_correctable_error_string, aer_uncorrectable_error_string) — but many are "receiver may check" rules, so only an analyzer sees them reliably.

Configuration valueWhere it livesLinux v7.2 name / toolUsed by rule
Max_Payload_Size (MPS)Device Control bits 7:5 (supported max in Device Capabilities bits 2:0)PCI_EXP_DEVCTL_PAYLOAD, PCI_EXP_DEVCAP_PAYLOAD; lspci -vvv "DevCtl: … MaxPayload"V-26
Max_Read_Request_Size (MRRS)Device Control bits 14:12PCI_EXP_DEVCTL_READRQ; "MaxReadReq"V-27
Read Completion Boundary (RCB)Link Control bit 3 (endpoints); fixed for root ports (reported in Link Capabilities of the root port as 64 or 128 B)PCI_EXP_LNKCTL_RCB; "LnkCtl: … RCB 64 bytes"V-29
ECRC generation/checkAER capability, Advanced Error Capabilities and ControlPCI_ERR_CAP_ECRC_GENC/GENE/CHKC/CHKE; kernel parameter pci=ecrc=V-34
Relaxed Ordering / No Snoop enablesDevice Control bits 4 / 11PCI_EXP_DEVCTL_RELAX_EN, PCI_EXP_DEVCTL_NOSNOOP_ENV-13, V-33
10-bit / 14-bit tagsDevice Capabilities 2 / Device Control 2 (10-bit); Flit mode (14-bit)"10BitTagComp/Req" in lspci -vvvV-31, V-32
V-26TLP payload larger than Max_Payload_Size ReportedPCIe TL
In a PEX trace
Visible MWr or CplD with Length × 4 > the transmitter's programmed MPS (visible from captured config writes to Device Control, or supplied from lspci); typically followed by an ERR_FATAL message TLP from the receiving port.
What happens
Part V card L-18 (Malformed TLP) and L-32 (MPS/MRRS mismatch) covers how the receiver reports this; this card is the trace-checker rule. A transmitter sends a TLP whose data payload exceeds the MPS programmed in its own Device Control register (for the SSD: data MWr for reads, or CplD for a host read of the CMB). A receiver with a smaller MPS setting cannot accept it.
How it shows up
The receiver treats it as a Malformed TLP: uncorrectable AER bit 18 "MalfTLP", fatal by default severity, which on Linux triggers AER recovery (reset of the link / device) or, with DPC, containment of the downstream port. The NVMe controller disappears briefly and I/O is retried or failed.
Spec basis
PCI Express Base: Max_Payload_Size — transmitters must not send TLPs with payload larger than MPS; receivers treat such TLPs as Malformed. All functions on a path must use an MPS no larger than what every element supports.
Typical causes
Firmware ignoring the programmed MPS and using its capability maximum; hot-plugged device behind a switch whose MPS was configured smaller after the device was enumerated; firmware/OS (pci=pcie_bus_perf) choices that set MPS per segment inconsistently.
How to detect / prove
Analyzer: compare each TLP's Length field with the configured MPS of the transmitter (capture config writes at enumeration or read lspci -vvv of every device on the path). Rule TLP-MPS in 7.6. Host: dmesg AER lines naming MalfTLP; /sys/bus/pci/devices/<bdf>/aer_dev_fatal.
Linux v7.2 source
drivers/pci/probe.c:pcie_write_mps, pcie_bus_configure_settings, pcie_bus_configure_set (MPS policy per pcie_bus_config); drivers/pci/pcie/aer.c string "MalfTLP".
Test to provoke it
EXPERT: lower MPS on the root port with setpci below the device's setting on a test box — this crashes I/O to the device; do it only with no mounted filesystems.
V-27Read request larger than Max_Read_Request_Size SilentPCIe TL
In a PEX trace
Visible MRd with Length × 4 > the requester's MRRS (Device Control, from captured config writes or lspci).
What happens
Part V card L-32 covers how the receiver reports this; this card is the trace-checker rule. The SSD (as requester) issues a memory read (to fetch write data, SQEs or PRP lists) with a length greater than its programmed MRRS.
How it shows up
MRRS is a requester-side limit; whether the completer flags an oversized read is implementation-dependent (verify the receiver rules in the PCIe Base spec). Usually the host bridge just services it — so the violation is silent, but it breaks the fairness and buffer assumptions the OS made when it chose MRRS (e.g. for isochronous or peer devices).
Spec basis
PCI Express Base: Max_Read_Request_Size in Device Control — the requester must not generate read requests larger than this value.
Typical causes
Firmware using a fixed 4 KiB read size; MRRS changed by the OS after the device cached it at link-up.
How to detect / prove
Analyzer: MRd Length × 4 > MRRS of the requester.
Linux v7.2 source
drivers/pci/probe.c:pcie_write_mrrs (calls pcie_set_readrq in performance mode); register field PCI_EXP_DEVCTL_READRQ.
Test to provoke it
SAFE observation: capture a large sequential write and check MRd sizes against lspci -vvv MaxReadReq.
V-28Request crossing a 4 KiB address boundary SilentPCIe TL
In a PEX trace
Visible Any MRd/MWr where (address mod 4096) + length > 4096 — a stateless rule the analyzer can evaluate on every packet.
What happens
A memory read or write request whose address + length spans a 4 KiB-aligned boundary (e.g. MWr of 256 B starting at …0F80h).
How it shows up
Receivers may optionally check this rule; if they do, the TLP is Malformed (AER MalfTLP). Many root complexes do not check, so the request is serviced — and the second part may land in a page that belongs to a different IOMMU mapping, causing an IOMMU fault for "half" a TLP or silent access to the wrong page. impl
Spec basis
PCI Express Base: requests must not specify an address/length combination that causes a memory space access to cross a 4 KB boundary.
Typical causes
DMA engine splitting at MPS multiples from the PRP1 offset instead of at page boundaries; PRP1 with an odd offset (V-17) combined with naive splitting.
How to detect / prove
Analyzer rule: (addr mod 4096) + len > 4096 for any MRd/MWr. Cheap and stateless — always enable it.
Linux v7.2 source
Linux cannot see this; IOMMU fault logs are the only host-side hint. dma_set_min_align_mask in drivers/nvme/host/pci.c preserves page offsets, so a correct device never needs to cross.
Test to provoke it
SAFE: send reads with PRP1 offsets such as 0F80h via passthrough and inspect the device's MWr split pattern.
V-29Completions not respecting the Read Completion Boundary SilentPCIe TL
In a PEX trace
Visible For one read request answered by several CplDs, a non-final CplD whose end address is not a multiple of the RCB.
What happens
A completer answering one read request with several CplD TLPs must split only at RCB-aligned addresses (64 or 128 B): each partial completion except the last must end on an RCB boundary, and the data must be returned in increasing address order for a single request. A completer that splits at arbitrary points (e.g. 100 bytes) violates this.
How it shows up
A requester that relies on RCB-aligned splits (to size its completion buffers) may mis-assemble data; a strict requester flags a Malformed TLP. Often silent. impl
Spec basis
PCI Express Base: Read Completion Boundary (Link Control RCB; root ports 64 B or 128 B) and completion splitting rules for memory read requests.
Typical causes
Device-side CMB / PMR completion logic (when the host reads the SSD's Controller Memory Buffer) with an incorrect splitter; RCB register not programmed consistently with the root port.
How to detect / prove
Analyzer: for each request with multiple CplDs, check that each non-final CplD's end address (Lower Address + payload) is a multiple of RCB.
Linux v7.2 source
include/uapi/linux/pci_regs.h:PCI_EXP_LNKCTL_RCB; CMB mapping in drivers/nvme/host/pci.c (nvme_map_cmb).
Test to provoke it
SAFE observation on devices with a CMB: read the CMB region with large reads (e.g. via a test harness or dd on a resource file — read-only) while capturing.
V-30Byte Count / Lower Address inconsistent in completions ReportedPCIe TL
In a PEX trace
Visible Successive CplDs of one tag whose Byte Count does not decrease by the previous payload, or whose Lower Address does not advance accordingly.
What happens
In a completion, Byte Count must equal the number of bytes remaining to satisfy the request (including this completion's bytes), and Lower Address must be the low address bits of the first byte returned in this completion. A completer that reports the wrong values (e.g. Byte Count = payload length on every partial, or Lower Address not advancing) breaks the requester's reassembly.
How it shows up
The requester may treat the completion as malformed or unexpected, or may conclude the request is finished too early and later receive "unexpected" completions — AER "UnxCmplt" (bit 16) or "MalfTLP"; or the read silently returns partial data. impl
Spec basis
PCI Express Base: Completion header fields Byte Count and Lower Address and their rules for split completions.
Typical causes
Completer logic that does not track remaining bytes across splits; BCM (Byte Count Modified) misuse by PCI-X bridges in legacy topologies.
How to detect / prove
Analyzer: for each tag, track remaining bytes; every CplD must have Byte Count == remaining and Lower Address == (next expected address mod 128).
Linux v7.2 source
Only the AER outcome is visible: drivers/pci/pcie/aer.c strings "UnxCmplt", "MalfTLP".
Test to provoke it
Device-side bug; validate with an exerciser that injects wrong Byte Count (EXPERT, lab equipment).
V-31Completion for an unknown tag (Unexpected Completion) ReportedPCIe TL
In a PEX trace
Visible Cpl/CplD whose Requester ID + Tag matches no outstanding non-posted request seen on the probed link (often a late completion after a long gap). If the request went over a different link (e.g. peer-to-peer through a switch), the matching request is not visible.
What happens
Part V card L-16 covers how the receiver reports this; this card is the trace-checker rule. A completion arrives whose Transaction ID (Requester ID + Tag) matches no outstanding non-posted request of the receiver — because the request already completed, already timed out, was never sent, or the completer copied the wrong tag/requester ID.
How it shows up
The receiver logs Unexpected Completion: AER uncorrectable bit 16 "UnxCmplt" (non-fatal by default, often handled as an advisory non-fatal error and reported as correctable "NonFatalErr"). Frequently seen as the second half of a Completion Timeout ("CmpltTO", bit 14): the late completion for a request already timed out arrives and is unexpected.
Spec basis
PCI Express Base: Transaction ID matching of completions; Unexpected Completion error; Completion Timeout mechanism (range in Device Control 2).
Typical causes
Completion timeout set too short (PCI_EXP_DEVCTL2_COMP_TIMEOUT) on a slow path (e.g. through a switch to a busy root port or to a device in a low-power state); tag mismatch after enabling 10-bit tags on only one side; firmware returning completions after FLR.
How to detect / prove
Analyzer: maintain outstanding (Requester ID, Tag) per requester; flag CplD/Cpl without a match; measure request→completion latency to see if a timeout explains it.
Linux v7.2 source
drivers/pci/pcie/aer.c strings "UnxCmplt", "CmpltTO"; per-device counters in sysfs aer_dev_nonfatal, aer_dev_correctable.
Test to provoke it
EXPERT: shorten the completion timeout range in Device Control 2 with setpci on the requester while the completer is slow (e.g. deep power state), on a test system only.
V-32Tag reused while a request is outstanding SilentPCIe TL
In a PEX trace
Visible Second MRd with the same Requester ID + Tag before all CplDs (Byte Count reaching the final value) of the first have arrived.
What happens
Part V card L-40 (tag capability mismatch) covers how the receiver reports this; this card is the trace-checker rule. A requester issues a new non-posted request with a Tag that is still in use by an outstanding request (same Requester ID). The completer cannot tell them apart; completions may be matched to the wrong request.
How it shows up
Silent data mix-up: the SSD receives data meant for a different read (e.g. PRP list bytes delivered as write data, or one write's data in another write). Possibly Unexpected Completion later when the "second" completion for the tag arrives.
Spec basis
PCI Express Base: Transaction ID (Requester ID + Tag) must be unique among a requester's outstanding non-posted requests; 8-bit, 10-bit (optional, Gen4+) and 14-bit (Flit mode) tag spaces.
Typical causes
Tag allocator bug after a completion timeout (tag freed while the completion may still arrive); 10-bit tag requester whose tags are truncated to 8 bits by a component that does not support 10-bit tags.
How to detect / prove
Analyzer: per requester, flag a non-posted request whose tag is in the outstanding set. This is the PCIe twin of V-08.
Linux v7.2 source
Not visible to Linux: tags are allocated by the device's hardware. A grep of v7.2 include/uapi/linux/pci_regs.h and drivers/pci/ finds no 10-bit-tag enable logic, so check the Device Control 2 setting with lspci -vvv rather than assuming the kernel configured it. impl
Test to provoke it
Device-side; observe with analyzer under deep queue sequential writes (many concurrent MRd) — the scenario where tag exhaustion bugs appear.
V-33Posted-write ordering violation SilentPCIe TL
In a PEX trace
Partly visible On one link you see the order the transmitter sent TLPs and their RO/IDO attributes; proving that a switch or root complex reordered them needs probes on both sides of that component, and what the CPU finally observed is not on any link.
What happens
Part V card L-40 (Relaxed Ordering errata) covers how the receiver reports this; this card is the trace-checker rule. A component reorders TLPs in a way the ordering table forbids: a posted write passes an earlier posted write without RO; a completion passes a posted write in the same direction (which would let a read return before an earlier write is visible); a read passes a posted write. In NVMe terms: host doorbell write overtaking the host's earlier SQE write is impossible on PCIe (the SQE is in host memory, not sent to the device), but device-side reorderings of data/CQE/MSI-X (V-13, V-14) and switch reorderings are possible.
How it shows up
Stale reads, stale data, spurious interrupts; never a status code.
Spec basis
PCI Express Base: Transaction Ordering rules (the ordering table for Posted, Non-Posted, Completion), Relaxed Ordering and ID-Based Ordering attributes.
Typical causes
Device setting RO/IDO on TLPs that need strong ordering; a switch or root complex bug; host chipsets that are known to mishandle RO (Linux has quirks that clear RO enable for certain root ports).
How to detect / prove
Two probes (upstream and downstream of a switch) and compare TLP order; on a single link, check that no CQE or MSI-X TLP has RO=1 and that the ordering of device→host MWr matches the NVMe dependency (data → CQE → MSI-X).
Linux v7.2 source
drivers/pci/quirks.c contains relaxed-ordering quirks for root ports (search for PCI_DEV_FLAGS_NO_RELAXED_ORDERING); enable bit PCI_EXP_DEVCTL_RELAX_EN.
Test to provoke it
Analyzer-only; run fio verify with RO enabled vs disabled on a test system and compare.
V-34ECRC mismatch ReportedPCIe TL
In a PEX trace
Visible TLP with TD=1 whose digest does not match the analyzer's recomputation. Without ECRC enabled (TD=0) there is nothing to check; corruption inside the root complex after the probe point is not visible.
What happens
Part V card L-19 covers how the receiver reports this; this card is the trace-checker rule. When end-to-end CRC is enabled, the transmitter appends a 32-bit TLP Digest (TD bit = 1). A receiver with ECRC checking enabled recomputes it; a mismatch means the TLP was corrupted inside a component (e.g. switch internal SRAM) after the link-level LCRC had already been checked and stripped.
How it shows up
AER uncorrectable bit 19 "ECRC"; Linux logs the TLP header from the AER Header Log. Without ECRC enabled (the common default), the same internal corruption is silent.
Spec basis
PCI Express Base: End-to-End CRC (ECRC), TLP Digest, AER ECRC Generation/Check Capable/Enable bits.
Typical causes
Switch or retimer internal memory errors; a component that modifies a TLP header field it is not allowed to modify (some fields are variant and excluded from ECRC); mismatched ECRC enable (TD set by a device whose partner miscomputes).
How to detect / prove
Analyzer recomputes ECRC on every TLP with TD=1 at both ends of a switch; host: lspci -vvv shows "ECRCGenCap/ECRCChkCap" and enables; dmesg AER messages with "ECRC".
Linux v7.2 source
drivers/pci/pcie/aer.c (ECRC policy via kernel parameter pci=ecrc=on|off, string "ECRC"); PCI_ERR_CAP_ECRC_* in pci_regs.h.
Test to provoke it
SAFE: boot a lab host with pci=ecrc=on and capture; an exerciser can inject ECRC errors (EXPERT).
V-35Data Link Layer replay pattern: Nak, replay, missing Ack, REPLAY_NUM rollover DegradedPCIe DLL
In a PEX trace
Visible Nak DLLP followed by retransmission of TLPs with already-used sequence numbers; or the same sequence number sent four times with no Ack, then training ordered sets (Recovery). Physical-layer root causes are in Part V.
What happens
The individual link-level errors (Bad TLP, Bad DLLP, Replay Timer Timeout, REPLAY_NUM Rollover) are covered as AER errors in Part V (L-02, L-03, L-04, L-05). This card is the checker rule view: the receiver discards a TLP with a bad LCRC or an out-of-order sequence number and sends a Nak; the transmitter replays from its replay buffer; if no Ack/Nak arrives before the replay timer expires it replays anyway; after four replays of the same TLP the link retrains.
How it shows up
Correctable AER bits "BadTLP", "BadDLLP", "Timeout", "Rollover" (Linux names) — if software reads them; otherwise only lower throughput and latency bursts.
Spec basis
PCI Express Base: Data Link Layer — sequence numbers, LCRC, Ack/Nak protocol, replay buffer, replay timer, REPLAY_NUM.
Typical causes
Signal-integrity and PHY causes are in Part V; protocol-side causes are a receiver that is slow to return Acks (Ack coalescing too long, firmware stall) or that loses track of its expected sequence number after Recovery.
How to detect / prove
Checker rules: (1) replay count = TLPs whose sequence number was already transmitted; (2) Ack latency = time from a TLP to the first Ack whose AckNak_Seq_Num covers it, compared with the spec's limit for that speed/width (verify the table in the spec); (3) four transmissions of one sequence number → expect Recovery. Report replays per million TLPs per direction.
Linux v7.2 source
drivers/pci/pcie/aer.c:aer_correctable_error_string ("RxErr", "BadTLP", "BadDLLP", "Rollover", "Timeout").
Test to provoke it
Analyzer-only observation under load; exercisers can drop Acks or corrupt LCRC (EXPERT, lab equipment).
V-36FLIT errors in PCIe 6.0 Flit mode (FEC/CRC, replay, sequence) DegradedPCIe Flit
In a PEX trace
Partly visible With a Gen6-capable analyzer and Flit decode: flit sequence numbers, NAKs and retried flits are visible; FEC corrections happen inside the receiver and are visible only as counters the analyzer or device reports (verify for your analyzer version). PHY margins: see Part V.
What happens
At 64 GT/s with PAM4 signalling, Flit mode carries traffic in fixed 256-byte FLITs (vendor overviews: 236 bytes of TLP, 6 of DLP, 8 of CRC, 6 of ECC). A lightweight FEC corrects small symbol errors in-line; a FLIT whose CRC still fails after FEC is retried at FLIT granularity, with flit sequence numbers and standard or selective NAK. Per-TLP LCRC and the classic per-TLP sequence/Ack scheme are replaced by this flit-level mechanism. version
How it shows up
A rising FEC-corrected count costs nothing yet (an early-warning signal); CRC-failed FLITs cause retries (bandwidth/latency loss); persistent failures cause Recovery or link-down. How these are surfaced to software (AER bits, vendor counters, new capability registers) depends on the implementation and spec version — verify in the PCIe 6.x spec and the device's documentation. uncertain
Spec basis
PCI Express Base 6.0 and later: Flit mode, FEC, flit CRC, flit sequence numbers and NAK/retry (names of the specific counters and capability structures: verify in spec).
Typical causes
PAM4 eye margin (reflections, crosstalk, temperature); equalisation; retimers; mixed Flit/non-Flit negotiation issues on links that fall back to lower speeds.
How to detect / prove
Gen6-capable analyzer with Flit decode: count FEC corrections per lane, flit CRC failures and NAKs; correlate with temperature and link speed. Host: lspci -vvv shows speed 64GT/s and Flit mode state when supported by your lspci version.
Linux v7.2 source
Generic AER handling in drivers/pci/pcie/aer.c; link speed decoding in drivers/pci/pci.c:__pcie_print_link_status. No NVMe-driver-specific handling.
Test to provoke it
Lab-only (EXPERT): margining tools / lane margining at the receiver, cable or channel stress, and compare FEC/CRC counters at different temperatures.
V-37Poisoned TLP data accepted as good SilentPCIe TL
In a PEX trace
Visible CplD/MWr with EP=1 (e.g. answering the device's write-data MRd for CID X), later a CQE for CID X with status 0. Whether poisoned data reached the media is not visible — read back to prove it.
What happens
Part V card L-12 and L-38 covers how the receiver reports this; this card is the trace-checker rule. A TLP carries the EP (Error Poisoned) bit, meaning its payload is known to be bad (e.g. a host memory read hit an uncorrectable ECC error). The receiving NVMe controller must not treat the data as valid — e.g. it must not write poisoned write-data to media as if it were good.
How it shows up
Correct behaviour: AER "Poisoned TLP" received (uncorrectable bit 12, shown by Linux as "TLP") and the NVMe command fails (typically Data Transfer Error 04h). Incorrect behaviour: success, and the corrupted bytes are now persistent on media — silent corruption.
Spec basis
PCI Express Base: Data Poisoning (EP bit) and Poisoned TLP Received error; NVMe Base: Data Transfer Error generic status.
Typical causes
Controller firmware ignoring EP on CplD; host DRAM UE during a write command; switch forwarding poisoned data.
How to detect / prove
Analyzer: any CplD/MWr with EP=1 must be followed by a failing CQE for the owning command (or by the device's documented poisoned-data handling). A success CQE after a poisoned CplD is a finding.
Linux v7.2 source
drivers/pci/pcie/aer.c:aer_uncorrectable_error_string bit 12 "TLP"; status 04h string in drivers/nvme/host/constants.c.
Test to provoke it
EXPERT: error-injection (EINJ on servers that support it) or a PCIe exerciser setting EP on completions.

7.6 An Executable Checker over an Exported Trace

← 7.5 PCIe Transaction, Data Link and Flit Layer Violations8.1 Knowing the Ceiling: Link, Queue and Latency Arithmetic →

A PEX capture (the analyzer's native trace file) is read in the analyzer software, not by scripts; what you can script over is an export: most analyzer suites can export the packet view, the transaction (split-transaction) view, or a decoded NVMe command view to CSV or text. Exact menu names, available views and column headers differ by tool and version — treat any specific name as uncertain and check your tool's manual. The practical approach is: export, map the columns to a small neutral event schema (one decoded NVMe/PCIe event per row), and run rules over it. The script below is self-contained Python 3 (standard library only); COLUMN_MAP at the top is where you map your export's headers. It embeds a synthetic 26-event trace that deliberately contains violations, and it implements 15 rules from this part: DB-RANGE (V-01/V-02), DB-NOQ (V-03), CQDB-PAST-TAIL (V-06), CQ-OVERFLOW (V-07), CID-REUSE (V-08), CQE-UNKNOWN (V-09), SQID (V-10), PHASE (V-11), CQE-BEFORE-DATA (V-13), MSIX-NO-CQE (V-14), DMA-NOCMD (V-16), PRP1-ALIGN (V-17), PRP2-OFFSET (V-18), MDTS (V-20), TLP-MPS (V-26).

🧪 Lab

Save as trace_check.py, run python3 trace_check.py to see the synthetic findings, then convert your own export to the same columns and run python3 trace_check.py my_trace.csv --mps 256 --mdts-bytes 131072. The exit code is 1 when findings exist, so it can gate a CI job.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""trace_check.py - rule-based checker for a CSV exported from a PCIe protocol
analyzer capture (e.g. a .pex file opened in the analyzer software and exported
from its packet / transaction / NVMe-command view).

SYNTHETIC example: the embedded CSV below is invented to exercise the rules.
Real export column names, units and row granularity differ between analyzer
tools and versions: edit COLUMN_MAP so each logical name points at the header
your export actually uses, and convert per-TLP rows into one decoded event per row.
Logical columns (one decoded event per row, time-ordered):
  t_ns   event     q  cid  opc  val  len   prp1        prp2        sqid sqhd ph  tlp_len
  event in: CFG_Q (queue created: val=entries), SQDB, CQDB (doorbell writes),
            SQE (device fetched a command), DATA_WR / DATA_RD (device DMA for cid),
            CQE (device wrote a completion), MSIX (interrupt for vector q),
            TLP (any MWr from device; tlp_len = payload bytes)
Usage:  python3 trace_check.py [export.csv] [--mps 256] [--mdts-bytes 131072] [--page 4096]
"""

# logical name -> header in your export (identity for the synthetic sample)
COLUMN_MAP = {k: k for k in ("t_ns event q cid opc val len prp1 prp2 "
                             "sqid sqhd ph tlp_len").split()}
import csv, io, sys

SAMPLE = """t_ns,event,q,cid,opc,val,len,prp1,prp2,sqid,sqhd,ph,tlp_len
0,CFG_Q,1,,,4,,,,,,,
100,SQDB,1,,,1,,,,,,,
400,SQE,1,0x10,0x02,,4096,0x10000000,0,,,,
900,DATA_WR,1,0x10,,,4096,,,,,,
950,TLP,1,,,,,,,,,,256
1000,CQE,1,0x10,,,,,,1,1,1,
1050,MSIX,1,,,,,,,,,,
1100,CQDB,1,,,1,,,,,,,
1200,SQDB,1,,,3,,,,,,,
1300,SQE,1,0x11,0x02,,8192,0x10001000,0x20000010,,,,
1350,SQE,1,0x12,0x01,,4096,0x10003000,0,,,,
1400,DATA_RD,1,0x12,,,4096,,,,,,
1500,MSIX,1,,,,,,,,,,
1600,CQE,1,0x11,,,,,,1,3,1,
1700,DATA_WR,1,0x11,,,8192,,,,,,
1750,TLP,1,,,,,,,,,,512
1800,CQE,1,0x12,,,,,,1,3,1,
1900,CQE,1,0x99,,,,,,2,3,1,
2000,SQDB,1,,,7,,,,,,,
2100,SQDB,1,,,1,,,,,,,
2200,SQE,1,0x13,0x01,,262144,0x10010000,0x30000000,,,,
2250,SQE,1,0x13,0x01,,4096,0x10050000,0,,,,
2300,CQE,1,0x13,,,,,,1,1,1,
2400,CQDB,1,,,6,,,,,,,
2450,CQDB,1,,,3,,,,,,,
2500,SQDB,5,,,1,,,,,,,
"""

def num(s):
    s = (s or "").strip()
    return int(s, 0) if s else None

def check(rows, mps=256, mdts_bytes=128 * 1024, page=4096):
    findings = []
    def flag(row, rule, msg):
        findings.append((row["_line"], row["t_ns"], rule, msg))

    qsize = {}                 # qid -> entries
    sq_tail, cq_head = {}, {}  # last doorbell values
    cq_tail, cq_phase = {}, {} # device-side CQ position and expected phase
    outstanding = {}           # (qid, cid) -> dict(opc, len, data_done)
    completed_since_irq = {}   # qid -> CQEs posted since last MSI-X

    for r in rows:
        ev, q = r["event"], num(r["q"])
        cid = num(r["cid"])
        if ev == "CFG_Q":
            qsize[q] = num(r["val"]); sq_tail[q] = 0; cq_head[q] = 0
            cq_tail[q] = 0; cq_phase[q] = 1; completed_since_irq[q] = 0
            continue
        if ev in ("SQDB", "CQDB"):
            v = num(r["val"])
            if q not in qsize:
                flag(r, "DB-NOQ", f"{ev} for queue {q} that was never created "
                     "(controller may post AEN 'Invalid Doorbell Register')")
                continue
            if v >= qsize[q]:
                flag(r, "DB-RANGE", f"{ev} value {v} >= queue size {qsize[q]} "
                     "(controller may post AEN 'Invalid Doorbell Write Value')")
                continue
            if ev == "CQDB":
                # host must not release CQ slots the device has not filled
                used = (cq_tail[q] - cq_head[q]) % qsize[q]
                adv = (v - cq_head[q]) % qsize[q]
                if adv > used:
                    flag(r, "CQDB-PAST-TAIL", f"CQ head {cq_head[q]}->{v} releases {adv} "
                         f"entries but only {used} were posted")
                cq_head[q] = v
            else:
                sq_tail[q] = v
            continue
        if ev == "SQE":
            key = (q, cid)
            if key in outstanding:
                flag(r, "CID-REUSE", f"CID {cid:#x} reused on SQ {q} while still outstanding")
