            ln, p1, p2 = num(r["len"]) or 0, num(r["prp1"]) or 0, num(r["prp2"]) or 0
            if ln > mdts_bytes:
                flag(r, "MDTS", f"transfer {ln} B exceeds MDTS limit {mdts_bytes} B")
            first = page - (p1 % page)
            if ln > first:                          # PRP2 is used
                if p1 % 4:
                    flag(r, "PRP1-ALIGN", f"PRP1 {p1:#x} not dword aligned")
                if ln - first <= page and p2 % page:
                    flag(r, "PRP2-OFFSET", f"PRP2 {p2:#x} is a data pointer and must "
                         "have zero page offset (status: PRP Offset Invalid)")
            outstanding[key] = {"opc": num(r["opc"]), "len": ln, "data": 0}
            continue
        if ev in ("DATA_WR", "DATA_RD"):
            o = outstanding.get((q, cid))
            if o is None:
                flag(r, "DMA-NOCMD", f"{ev} for CID {cid:#x} that is not outstanding "
                     "(late DMA after completion?)")
            else:
                o["data"] += num(r["len"]) or 0
            continue
        if ev == "TLP":
            if (num(r["tlp_len"]) or 0) > mps:
                flag(r, "TLP-MPS", f"MWr payload {r['tlp_len']} B > MPS {mps} B (Malformed TLP)")
            continue
        if ev == "CQE":
            if q in qsize:
                if (cq_tail[q] + 1) % qsize[q] == cq_head[q]:
                    flag(r, "CQ-OVERFLOW", f"CQE posted into full CQ {q} "
                         f"(tail {cq_tail[q]}, host head {cq_head[q]})")
                exp = cq_phase[q]
                if num(r["ph"]) != exp:
                    flag(r, "PHASE", f"phase tag {r['ph']} at CQ slot {cq_tail[q]}, expected {exp}")
                cq_tail[q] += 1
                if cq_tail[q] == qsize[q]:
                    cq_tail[q] = 0; cq_phase[q] ^= 1
                completed_since_irq[q] += 1
            if num(r["sqid"]) != q:
                flag(r, "SQID", f"CQE SQID {r['sqid']} but command was on SQ {q}")
            key = (q, cid)
            o = outstanding.pop(key, None)
            if o is None:
                flag(r, "CQE-UNKNOWN", f"CQE for CID {cid:#x} with no outstanding command")
            elif o["opc"] == 0x02 and o["data"] < o["len"]:
                flag(r, "CQE-BEFORE-DATA", f"Read CID {cid:#x} completed after only "
                     f"{o['data']}/{o['len']} B of data were written to host")
            continue
        if ev == "MSIX":
            if completed_since_irq.get(q, 0) == 0:
                flag(r, "MSIX-NO-CQE", f"MSI-X for vector {q} with no new CQE posted")
            completed_since_irq[q] = 0
    return findings

def main(argv):
    mps, mdts, page, path = 256, 128 * 1024, 4096, None
    it = iter(argv)
    for a in it:
        if a == "--mps": mps = int(next(it))
        elif a == "--mdts-bytes": mdts = int(next(it))
        elif a == "--page": page = int(next(it))
        else: path = a
    text = open(path).read() if path else SAMPLE
    rows = []
    for i, raw in enumerate(csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(text)), start=2):
        r = {k: raw.get(v, "") for k, v in COLUMN_MAP.items()}
        r["_line"] = i; rows.append(r)
    f = check(rows, mps, mdts, page)
    for line, t, rule, msg in f:
        print(f"line {line:>3}  t={t:>5} ns  {rule:<16} {msg}")
    if f:
        print(f"\n{len(f)} findings; first abnormal event: line {f[0][0]} ({f[0][2]})")
    else:
        print("no findings")
    return 1 if f else 0

if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main(sys.argv[1:]))

Real output of running the script with no arguments (Python 3, this exact file):

line  11  t= 1300 ns  PRP2-OFFSET      PRP2 0x20000010 is a data pointer and must have zero page offset (status: PRP Offset Invalid)
line  14  t= 1500 ns  MSIX-NO-CQE      MSI-X for vector 1 with no new CQE posted
line  15  t= 1600 ns  CQE-BEFORE-DATA  Read CID 0x11 completed after only 0/8192 B of data were written to host
line  16  t= 1700 ns  DMA-NOCMD        DATA_WR for CID 0x11 that is not outstanding (late DMA after completion?)
line  17  t= 1750 ns  TLP-MPS          MWr payload 512 B > MPS 256 B (Malformed TLP)
line  19  t= 1900 ns  SQID             CQE SQID 2 but command was on SQ 1
line  19  t= 1900 ns  CQE-UNKNOWN      CQE for CID 0x99 with no outstanding command
line  20  t= 2000 ns  DB-RANGE         SQDB value 7 >= queue size 4 (controller may post AEN 'Invalid Doorbell Write Value')
line  22  t= 2200 ns  MDTS             transfer 262144 B exceeds MDTS limit 131072 B
line  23  t= 2250 ns  CID-REUSE        CID 0x13 reused on SQ 1 while still outstanding
line  24  t= 2300 ns  CQ-OVERFLOW      CQE posted into full CQ 1 (tail 0, host head 1)
line  24  t= 2300 ns  PHASE            phase tag 1 at CQ slot 0, expected 0
line  25  t= 2400 ns  DB-RANGE         CQDB value 6 >= queue size 4 (controller may post AEN 'Invalid Doorbell Write Value')
line  26  t= 2450 ns  CQDB-PAST-TAIL   CQ head 1->3 releases 2 entries but only 0 were posted
line  27  t= 2500 ns  DB-NOQ           SQDB for queue 5 that was never created (controller may post AEN 'Invalid Doorbell Register')

15 findings; first abnormal event: line 11 (PRP2-OFFSET)

7.6.1 Reading the result: first abnormal event, then cascades

Synthetic trace excerpt — how the findings chain together
CSV lineEventFindingRoot or cascade?
11SQE CID 0x11, 8 KiB read, PRP2 = 0x20000010PRP2-OFFSETroot (host bug — a checking controller would return status 13h)
14MSI-X vector 1MSIX-NO-CQEindependent device bug
15CQE CID 0x11CQE-BEFORE-DATAroot (device ordering bug, V-13)
16DATA_WR CID 0x11DMA-NOCMDcascade of line 15 — same bug seen from the other side
17MWr 512 BTLP-MPSindependent device bug
19CQE CID 0x99, SQID 2SQID + CQE-UNKNOWNroot (corrupted CQE)
20, 25SQDB 7, CQDB 6 on 4-entry queueDB-RANGEroot (host bug)
22SQE 256 KiBMDTSroot (host bug)
23SQE CID 0x13 againCID-REUSEroot (host bug)
24CQE into slot 0 while host head = 1CQ-OVERFLOW + PHASEoverflow is root; the phase finding is its symptom
26CQDB 3CQDB-PAST-TAILcascade — after the overflow the checker's tail count no longer matches the host's view
27SQDB on queue 5DB-NOQroot (host bug)
💡 Senior insight

A checker that reports 15 findings is less useful than one that says "the first abnormal event is line 11; lines 16, 24-PHASE and 26 are consequences". When you extend this script, give each rule a suppression link ("if CQ-OVERFLOW fired on this CQ, downgrade later PHASE/CQDB findings on it to 'cascade'"). The same principle drives the AI workflow in Part IX.

7.6.2 Extending the checker to PCIe rules

The same structure handles the TLP-level rules if your export has the TLP header fields. Add columns type, req_id, tag, addr, len_dw, byte_count, lower_addr, ro, ep, td and implement:

on MRd/MWr:   if (addr % 4096) + len > 4096        -> V-28 4K-CROSS
on MRd:       if len > MRRS[requester]             -> V-27 MRRS
              if (req_id, tag) in outstanding      -> V-32 TAG-REUSE
              outstanding[(req_id, tag)] = len
on CplD:      o = outstanding.get((req_id, tag))   -> None: V-31 UNEXPECTED-CPL
              if byte_count != o.remaining         -> V-30 BYTECOUNT
              if lower_addr != o.next_addr % 128   -> V-30 LOWER-ADDR
              if not last and (o.next_addr + payload) % RCB != 0 -> V-29 RCB
              if ep                                -> V-37 (expect failing CQE later)
on CQE/MSI-X MWr: if ro                            -> V-13 / V-33 RO-ON-CQE
on DLLP Nak / replay of same seq 4x                -> V-35 DLL-REPLAY
📭 What the spec does not say

The specifications define what is legal, not how an analyzer exports it. Column names, timestamp resolution, whether a CSV row is a TLP or a decoded transaction, and whether replayed TLPs appear twice all differ by tool. Always write a short converter and test it on a known-good capture before trusting findings.

Quiz

  1. The checker reports PHASE on a CQE. Why should you look at earlier lines before blaming the controller's phase logic?

    Answer

    Because a phase mismatch is the visible symptom of several earlier problems: a CQ overflow (the controller wrapped past the host's head), a CQ size mismatch, or a missed wrap in the checker's own state (it started mid-stream). Report the first abnormal event (here CQ-OVERFLOW on the same line) as the root.

  2. Why can a controller not detect V-05 (SQ tail overrun) from the doorbell value alone?

    Answer

    Because the value is a slot index modulo the queue size; any in-range value is a legal tail. Only the history (how many entries the controller has not yet fetched) reveals that the host has gone past the head. QEMU indeed does not check it.

  3. An 8 KiB read has PRP1 = …1000h. Is PRP2 a data pointer or a list pointer, and what must its low 12 bits be (4 KiB pages)?

    Answer

    PRP1's page provides 4096 bytes, the remaining 4096 fit in one page, so PRP2 is a data pointer and its low 12 bits must be zero.

  4. Which AER bit would you expect after V-26, and is it correctable?

    Answer

    Malformed TLP (uncorrectable status bit 18, "MalfTLP" in Linux), fatal by default severity.

PART VIII

Performance Failures

A drive that returns correct data at a third of the speed it should is failing — just not in a way any status code describes. Performance failures are "Degraded" by nature: every command succeeds, every log is clean, and the only evidence is a number that is lower (or a latency that is higher) than it should be. This part gives the arithmetic for what "should be" means, then one card per anomaly with the tool that exposes it: fio, iostat, perf, nvme-cli SMART data and lspci link status.

8.1 Knowing the Ceiling: Link, Queue and Latency Arithmetic

← 7.6 An Executable Checker over an Exported Trace8.2 Device-Side Performance Anomalies →

You cannot call a result "slow" without a ceiling to compare it with. Three ceilings matter: the link (how many bytes per second PCIe can carry after encoding and packet overhead), the device (its datasheet sequential/random figures, measured under the vendor's stated conditions), and the queueing law that links IOPS, latency and queue depth.

8.1.1 Link ceiling

BW_raw = rate (GT/s) × lanes × encoding efficiency ÷ 8     BW_data ≈ BW_raw × MPS ÷ (MPS + overhead)
  • rate — 8 GT/s (Gen3), 16 (Gen4), 32 (Gen5), 64 (Gen6)
  • encoding efficiency — 128/130 for Gen3–Gen5; Gen6 Flit mode uses 1b/1b PAM4 encoding with the FLIT carrying 236 TLP bytes per 256 (vendor overviews) version
  • MPS — Max_Payload_Size of the data TLPs (128, 256, 512 B typical)
  • overhead — per-TLP bytes besides payload: ≈ 4 B framing token (carries length and sequence number in 128b/130b) + 16 B header (4 DW, 64-bit address) + 4 B LCRC = ≈ 24 B; +4 B if ECRC is enabled. DLLP traffic (Ack, UpdateFC) costs a few more percent and is ignored here. derived
LinkRaw after encodingMPS 128 B (84.2%)MPS 256 B (91.4%)MPS 512 B (95.5%)
Gen3 x43.94 GB/s3.32 GB/s3.60 GB/s3.76 GB/s
Gen4 x47.88 GB/s6.63 GB/s7.20 GB/s7.52 GB/s
Gen5 x415.75 GB/s13.27 GB/s14.40 GB/s15.05 GB/s
Gen6 x4 (Flit)32 GB/s line; ≈29.5 GB/s TLP share of FLITsTLP header overhead still applies inside the FLIT's TLP bytes; compute per your MPS derived

All values are computed with the formula above (GB = 109 bytes) and are upper bounds for one direction. Real NVMe reads reach 85–95% of the MPS column because command fetches, PRP list reads, CQE writes and MSI-X writes share the link and because DLLPs consume bandwidth. derived

8.1.2 Queueing ceiling: Little's Law

IOPS = outstanding I/Os ÷ mean latency     (QD 32, 80 µs → 400 000 IOPS; QD 32, 400 µs → 80 000 IOPS)
  • outstanding I/Os — the average number of commands actually in flight at the device (not the fio iodepth you asked for, if the host cannot keep up)
  • mean latency — device + host completion latency (fio clat + slat)

Little's Law holds for any stable system. Use it as a lie detector: if fio reports QD 32, 80 µs average latency and only 150 000 IOPS, then the device did not have 32 commands in flight — the host is the bottleneck (P-09).

8.1.3 The measurement discipline

  • State the drive's condition: fresh-out-of-box, after secure erase, or preconditioned (written sequentially twice its capacity, then the random workload until steady state). Performance numbers without condition are meaningless.
  • Run long enough: fio's steadystate option (e.g. ss=iops_slope:0.1% with ss_dur and ss_ramp) stops a job only once the metric has stabilised; use time_based with runtime.
  • Record time series, not only averages: --write_bw_log, --write_lat_log, --log_avg_msec=1000.
  • Record percentiles: --percentile_list=50:99:99.9:99.99.
  • Record the environment at the same time: nvme smart-log before/after, lspci -vvv link status, CPU frequency governor, IRQ affinity.
# Baseline evidence bundle (read-only; reads only, no writes to the device)
lspci -vvv -s 0000:01:00.0 | grep -E 'LnkCap|LnkSta|DevCtl|MaxPayload|MaxReadReq|ASPM'
cat /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:01:00.0/{current_link_speed,current_link_width,max_link_speed,max_link_width,numa_node}
nvme smart-log /dev/nvme0
nvme id-ctrl /dev/nvme0 | grep -E '^(mdts|apsta|wctemp|cctemp|mntmt|mxtmt)'
nvme get-feature /dev/nvme0 -f 0x0c -H     # APST table
nvme get-feature /dev/nvme0 -f 0x08 -H     # interrupt coalescing
cat /sys/module/nvme_core/parameters/default_ps_max_latency_us
fio --name=rr --filename=/dev/nvme0n1 --readonly --rw=randread --bs=4k --iodepth=32 \
    --numjobs=4 --ioengine=io_uring --direct=1 --time_based --runtime=60 --group_reporting \
    --percentile_list=50:99:99.9:99.99
⚠️ Warning

Write workloads (--rw=write, randwrite, preconditioning) destroy the data on the target. Run them only on a scratch device or namespace. --readonly makes fio refuse to write.

8.2 Device-Side Performance Anomalies

← 8.1 Knowing the Ceiling: Link, Queue and Latency Arithmetic8.3 Host, Power-Management and Link Anomalies →
P-01Throughput well below link capability DegradedSystem
In a PEX trace
Partly visible Bandwidth over time, TLP payload sizes, gaps between data bursts and the number of SQEs outstanding are all measurable; whether a gap is the host (no doorbells) or the device (doorbells but slow fetch/CQE) is visible — the root cause inside either is not.
What happens
Large sequential reads (128 KiB–1 MiB, QD ≥ 8) reach, say, 4.1 GB/s on a Gen4 x4 drive whose link ceiling at MPS 256 B is ≈7.2 GB/s and whose datasheet says 7.0 GB/s.
How it shows up
Only in the benchmark number. No error, no log.
Spec basis
PCI Express Base: link rate/width, MPS; NVMe Base: MDTS (limits per-command size), queue model. The ceiling is arithmetic, not a spec field.
Typical causes
Link trained below capability (P-11); MPS 128 B (P-12); I/O split into small commands by MDTS or max_sectors_kb; too few outstanding commands; CPU or single-thread submission limit (P-09); device thermal throttling (P-06); measuring through a filesystem with buffered I/O.
How to detect / prove
Compute the ceiling (8.1.1) from lspci LnkSta and DevCtl MaxPayload; run fio --rw=read --bs=1m --iodepth=32 --direct=1; check iostat -x 1 rareq-sz (average request size actually sent) and aqu-sz (average queue size). If rareq-sz is much smaller than bs, the block layer is splitting.
Linux v7.2 source
drivers/nvme/host/core.c:nvme_init_identify (MDTS → max_hw_sectors); drivers/pci/pci.c:__pcie_print_link_status reports "available PCIe bandwidth, limited by …".
Test to provoke it
SAFE: read-only fio sweep of bs (4k…1m) × iodepth (1…128); plot bandwidth; the plateau should approach the ceiling.
P-02IOPS collapse at high queue depth DegradedDevice / host
In a PEX trace
Partly visible Outstanding-command count (fetched SQEs minus CQEs) and per-command SQE-fetch→CQE time are visible, so the curve can be reconstructed from the trace; why the device slows down (FTL contention) is not.
What happens
IOPS rise with queue depth until the device's internal parallelism is saturated; beyond that they should plateau while latency grows linearly (Little's Law). A collapse — IOPS falling as QD rises (e.g. 800k at QD 64, 450k at QD 256) — means something degrades under contention.
How it shows up
QD sweep curve with a peak and a decline; mean latency growing faster than QD/IOPS predicts.
Spec basis
None; queue depth limits come from CAP.MQES and the host driver's queue depth.
Typical causes
Device: firmware arbitration overhead, internal buffer thrashing, read disturb mitigation, too many concurrent streams for the FTL cache. Host: lock contention when many jobs share one hardware queue, nr_requests limits causing requeue storms, interrupts from all queues landing on one CPU.
How to detect / prove
Sweep --iodepth 1…256 at fixed numjobs; then repeat with jobs pinned to CPUs on the device's NUMA node. If host CPU (fio sys%, perf top) is saturated at the peak, it's the host; if the device-reported latency (or analyzer SQE→CQE time) rises disproportionately, it's the device.
Linux v7.2 source
drivers/nvme/host/pci.c module parameter io_queue_depth (default 1024, "should >= 2 and < 4096"); q_depth clamped to CAP.MQES+1 in nvme_pci_enable.
Test to provoke it
SAFE (read-only): for qd in 1 2 4 8 16 32 64 128 256; do fio --readonly … --iodepth=$qd; done.
P-03Latency outliers at p99.9 / p99.99 DegradedDevice / host
In a PEX trace
Partly visible Per-command device latency (SQE fetch → CQE MWr) is visible exactly, separating device from host; whether a 12 ms outlier was GC, read retry or a housekeeping task is NOT visible.
What happens
Median read latency is 80 µs but one I/O in a thousand takes 5–50 ms. Averages hide it; databases and distributed storage feel it, because a request that touches many I/Os waits for the slowest.
How it shows up
fio clat percentiles; application tail latency; occasionally Linux timeouts if outliers exceed 30 s (then it becomes a timing failure, not a performance one).
Spec basis
NVMe defines no latency targets for ordinary I/O; some features exist to manage it (Predictable Latency Mode, Read Recovery Level, I/O Determinism concepts) — check Identify Controller for support.
Typical causes
Garbage collection (P-05), read retry / soft-decode on worn or long-retention NAND, internal firmware housekeeping (SMART update, table flush), power state exit (P-07), host: interrupt on a busy CPU, softirq delay, CPU frequency ramp-up, SMIs.
How to detect / prove
fio --percentile_list=99:99.9:99.99 --write_lat_log to get each slow I/O's timestamp; bpftrace/biolatency-style histograms; correlate outlier timestamps with SMART temperature samples, APST transitions, and other activity. An analyzer gives the device-only latency (SQE fetch → CQE), separating device from host.
Linux v7.2 source
Trace events nvme_setup_cmd and nvme_complete_rq in drivers/nvme/host/trace.h give per-command host-side latency (enable via /sys/kernel/tracing/events/nvme/).
Test to provoke it
SAFE: long (≥ 30 min) read-only random read at moderate QD on a drive that has been written full; compare a fresh drive.
P-04Write cliff after the SLC cache is exhausted DegradedDevice (FTL)
In a PEX trace
Partly visible A step down in the rate of write-data MRd and a rise in write SQE→CQE time after N GB are visible; the SLC cache itself and folding are device-internal and not visible.
What happens
Many TLC/QLC drives write first into NAND operated in single-bit (pseudo-SLC) mode, which is fast. When that cache fills during a long sequential write, the drive must write to native TLC/QLC — and simultaneously fold the cache — so throughput drops sharply. Reviewers report drops such as from >2.5 GB/s to ≈0.8 GB/s after ≈150 GB on one TLC drive, and to ≈160 MB/s after ≈80 GB on a QLC SATA drive; the cache recovers during idle time.
How it shows up
A bandwidth-over-time plot with a step down; average numbers for short tests look perfect.
Spec basis
Not specified by NVMe; it is FTL design. (Endurance/space reporting fields in SMART do not expose the cache size.)
Typical causes
Dynamic SLC cache sized by free space (shrinks as the drive fills), no idle time to flush, drive nearly full.
How to detect / prove
CAUTION (destructive): sequential write of the full capacity on a scratch drive with --write_bw_log and 1 s averaging; plot GB written vs MB/s. Repeat at 50% and 90% fill to show the cache shrinking.
Linux v7.2 source
Not visible to the driver.
Test to provoke it
CAUTION: fio --name=fill --filename=/dev/nvme1n1 --rw=write --bs=1m --iodepth=32 --direct=1 --write_bw_log=fill --log_avg_msec=1000 on a scratch device.
P-05Garbage-collection stalls in steady state DegradedDevice (FTL)
In a PEX trace
Partly visible Periods where the device stops fetching SQEs although doorbells advanced, followed by CQE bursts, are visible; garbage collection is inferred, never shown.
What happens
After the drive has been fully written (no free blocks left), every new write needs garbage collection to reclaim space. Random write IOPS fall from the fresh-out-of-box value to a much lower steady-state value, with periodic stalls when GC falls behind.
How it shows up
IOPS-over-time plot: high, then decline, then a noisy plateau with dips; write latency p99.9 in the tens of ms.
Spec basis
Not specified by NVMe. Related features that help: Deallocate/TRIM (DSM), Write Zeroes, over-provisioning, Endurance Group / NVM Sets, Flexible Data Placement (reduces write amplification when supported).
Typical causes
No TRIM (filesystem mounted without discard and no periodic fstrim), low over-provisioning, mixed hot/cold data, and see the "deallocate completes but does nothing" silent failure elsewhere in this atlas.
How to detect / prove
CAUTION: precondition (2× capacity sequential, then random 4k writes) and use fio --steadystate=iops_slope:0.1%; record SMART "Data Units Written" before/after to compute host writes; if the vendor log exposes NAND writes, compute write amplification.
Linux v7.2 source
Discard path drivers/nvme/host/core.c:nvme_setup_discard (DSM deallocate).
Test to provoke it
CAUTION: the SNIA-style preconditioning workflow on a scratch drive; compare with and without a full-drive deallocate beforehand.
P-06Thermal throttling DegradedDevice
In a PEX trace
Partly visible Throughput saw-tooth is visible; temperature is visible only if the host reads the SMART/Health log during the capture (Get Log Page 02h data MWr) or sets/reads features 04h/10h — decode those payloads.
What happens
As the composite temperature rises, the controller reduces performance to stay within limits — either its own internal throttling or Host Controlled Thermal Management (HCTM) levels TMT1/TMT2 set by the host.
How it shows up
Throughput saw-tooth that correlates with temperature. Evidence lives in the SMART / Health Information log: Composite Temperature, Warning Composite Temperature Time, Critical Composite Temperature Time, Temperature Sensor 1–8, Thermal Management Temperature 1/2 Transition Count and Total Time. Crossing a temperature threshold can also raise a SMART/Health async event (critical warning temperature bit).
Spec basis
NVMe Base: SMART / Health Information log page fields above; Identify Controller WCTEMP, CCTEMP, MNTMT, MXTMT; Set Features Temperature Threshold (04h) and Host Controlled Thermal Management (10h).
Typical causes
No heatsink or airflow (M.2 under a GPU), Gen5 drives with high controller power, sustained writes, HCTM thresholds set too low by platform software.
How to detect / prove
Sample nvme smart-log /dev/nvme0 every second during the workload (temperature, thm_temp1_trans_count, thm_temp1_total_time, warning_temp_time); the counters increasing during the dips is proof. Linux exposes temperatures through hwmon (sensors).
Linux v7.2 source
SMART fields in include/linux/nvme.h struct nvme_smart_log: warning_temp_time, critical_comp_time, temp_sensor[8], thm_temp1_trans_count, thm_temp2_trans_count, thm_temp1_total_time, thm_temp2_total_time; feature ids NVME_FEAT_TEMP_THRESH (04h), NVME_FEAT_HCTM (10h); mntmt/mxtmt in Identify Controller.
Test to provoke it
CAUTION: sustained sequential write on a scratch drive with airflow blocked for a short, monitored period; stop at WCTEMP. Never exceed the drive's critical temperature.

8.3 Host, Power-Management and Link Anomalies

← 8.2 Device-Side Performance Anomalies9.1 What an AI Can and Cannot Conclude from a PEX Export →
P-07APST / ASPM wake-latency spikes DegradedPower management
In a PEX trace
Partly visible Link L1 entry/exit (electrical idle, then training to L0) and the host's Set Features 0Ch (APST table in the data payload) are visible, as is the delay between the first doorbell after idle and its SQE fetch; the device's internal power state is not.
What happens
After idle, the drive enters a non-operational power state via Autonomous Power State Transition (APST), and/or the link enters L1 / L1 substates via ASPM. The first I/O after idle pays the exit latency (the power state descriptor's EXLAT, plus link L1 exit latency) — from tens of µs to tens of ms.
How it shows up
Latency outliers that occur only after idle periods (bursty workloads, interactive desktops); benchmarks with continuous load never see them. Some drive/platform combinations fail to wake at all (then it becomes a controller-fatal/timeout failure, which is why Linux has quirks).
Spec basis
NVMe Base: Power State Descriptors (ENLAT, EXLAT, non-operational flag), Autonomous Power State Transition feature (0Ch), Identify Controller APSTA, NPSS; PCI Express Base: ASPM L0s/L1, L1 PM Substates, exit latencies in Link Capabilities.
Typical causes
Linux v7.2 default default_ps_max_latency_us = 100000 (100 ms) allows deep states; platform ASPM policy "powersave"; drives with optimistic EXLAT values.
How to detect / prove
Read the APST table: nvme get-feature /dev/nvme0 -f 0x0c -H; the descriptor latencies: nvme id-ctrl /dev/nvme0 -H (power states); ASPM state: lspci -vvv "LnkCtl: ASPM …"; cat /sys/module/pcie_aspm/parameters/policy. Experiment: run fio --thinktime=2s --thinktime_blocks=1 (idle between I/Os) and compare p99 with APST disabled (nvme_core.default_ps_max_latency_us=0) — a clear difference is proof.
Linux v7.2 source
drivers/nvme/host/core.c:nvme_configure_apst, nvme_apst_get_transition_time, module parameter default_ps_max_latency_us (100000); quirks NVME_QUIRK_NO_APST, NVME_QUIRK_NO_DEEPEST_PS in drivers/nvme/host/nvme.h; per-device limit via PM QoS latency tolerance in sysfs.
Test to provoke it
SAFE: read-only fio with think time as above, with APST enabled vs disabled; plot first-I/O-after-idle latency.
P-08Interrupt storm or interrupt-coalescing misconfiguration DegradedHost / NVMe
In a PEX trace
Visible Ratio of MSI-X MWr to CQE MWr and the delay from first CQE to MSI-X; Set/Get Features 08h and 09h commands and their values in the SQE/CQE.
What happens
One interrupt per completion at 1M+ IOPS costs a lot of CPU (storm); conversely, aggressive coalescing (Feature 08h aggregation threshold/time) saves CPU but adds latency up to the aggregation time to every I/O at low QD. Misrouted interrupts (all vectors on CPU 0) create a single-core bottleneck.
How it shows up
High %irq/%soft in mpstat; one CPU at 100%; or a constant added latency (e.g. +100 µs) at QD 1.
Spec basis
NVMe Base: Interrupt Coalescing feature (08h: Aggregation Time in 100 µs units, Aggregation Threshold), Interrupt Vector Configuration feature (09h: Coalescing Disable per vector).
Typical causes
Coalescing set by vendor tools or firmware defaults; irqbalance moving NVMe vectors away from their managed affinity; fewer MSI-X vectors than CPUs.
How to detect / prove
nvme get-feature /dev/nvme0 -f 0x08 -H; grep nvme /proc/interrupts (per-CPU counts per queue); mpstat -P ALL 1; compare IOPS/CPU with poll_queues + --hipri polling.
Linux v7.2 source
Linux v7.2 does not program Feature 08h: NVME_FEAT_IRQ_COALESCE is only defined in include/linux/nvme.h, not used by drivers/nvme/host. Vector setup: drivers/nvme/host/pci.c:nvme_setup_irqs; polling queues via module parameter poll_queues.
Test to provoke it
CAUTION (changes device settings, revert afterwards): nvme set-feature /dev/nvme0 -f 0x08 -v <value> on a test system and measure QD 1 latency before/after.
P-09CPU-bound submission path DegradedHost
In a PEX trace
Partly visible Slow, irregular doorbell writes and shallow SQ occupancy are visible (the device is waiting); CPU utilisation and where cycles go are not — use perf.
What happens
The host cannot generate I/O fast enough: one fio job on one core saturates at a few hundred thousand IOPS with libaio, so a drive rated for 1.5M IOPS appears "slow".
How it shows up
fio cpu: usr/sys near 100% per job; Little's Law mismatch (8.1.2); adding jobs increases IOPS linearly.
Spec basis
None (host software).
Typical causes
Single job; synchronous engine; buffered I/O; per-I/O syscalls; kernel debug options; security mitigations; IOMMU in strict mode (map/unmap per I/O); CPU in a low-frequency state.
How to detect / prove
perf top / perf record -g during the run to see where cycles go; try --ioengine=io_uring --fixedbufs --registerfiles --hipri, more numjobs, --iodepth_batch_submit; check cpupower frequency-info.
Linux v7.2 source
drivers/nvme/host/pci.c:nvme_queue_rq, nvme_commit_rqs (batched doorbells), nvme_poll_cq; block/blk-mq.c for the submission path.
Test to provoke it
SAFE: read-only 4k random read with numjobs=1 vs 8, libaio vs io_uring; record IOPS per CPU.
P-10NUMA misplacement DegradedHost
In a PEX trace
Not visible NUMA placement is a host-internal property; host DRAM latency appears only indirectly (longer CplD latency for device reads of remote memory). Prove with numa_node/local_cpulist and pinned fio runs.
What happens
On a multi-socket (or multi-die) server, the SSD's root port belongs to one NUMA node. Threads and buffers on the other node make every DMA and every MMIO doorbell cross the inter-socket link, adding latency and consuming inter-socket bandwidth.
How it shows up
10–30% higher latency or lower IOPS depending on which CPUs run the benchmark; results that vary run to run as the scheduler moves threads. impl
Spec basis
None (platform topology).
Typical causes
Benchmark not pinned; application threads on the wrong socket; interrupt affinity crossing nodes; memory allocated on the remote node.
How to detect / prove
cat /sys/bus/pci/devices/<bdf>/numa_node and local_cpulist; run fio with --numa_cpu_nodes=N --numa_mem_policy=bind:N (or numactl --cpunodebind=N --membind=N fio …) for local and remote N and compare; perf stat uncore/inter-socket counters where available.
Linux v7.2 source
drivers/nvme/host/pci.c allocates queues with dev_to_node()-based NUMA hints (e.g. the HMB/descriptor allocations pass numa_node).
Test to provoke it
SAFE: read-only fio pinned locally vs remotely.
P-11Link trained below capability (speed or width downgrade) DegradedPCIe PHY
In a PEX trace
Visible Training sequences and the negotiated rate/width at link-up or Recovery; lanes inactive. See also Part V L-25 for the link-layer card.
What happens
A Gen4 x4 drive links at Gen3 or at x2 (or x1). Everything works, at half or a quarter of the bandwidth.
How it shows up
lspci -vvv: "LnkSta: Speed 8GT/s (downgraded), Width x2 (downgraded)" vs "LnkCap: Speed 16GT/s, Width x4"; Linux at enumeration prints "… available PCIe bandwidth, limited by … link at … (capable of …)". Bandwidth-management interrupts may log autonomous speed changes.
Spec basis
PCI Express Base: Link Capabilities (Max Link Speed/Width), Link Status (Current Link Speed, Negotiated Link Width), LTSSM training and Recovery speed changes.
Typical causes
Slot wired with fewer lanes (chipset slot, bifurcation settings), riser cables, BIOS forcing Gen3, signal-integrity problems causing the LTSSM to fall back, thermal or power policy (some laptops lower speed on battery).
How to detect / prove
cat /sys/bus/pci/devices/<bdf>/{current_link_speed,max_link_speed,current_link_width,max_link_width}; check the upstream port's LnkCap too (the link runs at the lower of the two); dmesg | grep 'limited by'. Bandwidth test: sequential read plateau ≈ the ceiling of the downgraded link.
Linux v7.2 source
drivers/pci/probe.c:pcie_report_downtraining → drivers/pci/pci.c:__pcie_print_link_status ("%u.%03u Gb/s available PCIe bandwidth, limited by %s x%d link at %s (capable of …)"); pcie_bandwidth_available; register fields PCI_EXP_LNKSTA_CLS, PCI_EXP_LNKSTA_NLW.
Test to provoke it
SAFE: move the drive between slots and record LnkSta; CAUTION: forcing the target link speed via Link Control 2 with setpci and retraining on a test system.
P-12Small MPS or MRRS limiting throughput DegradedPCIe TL
In a PEX trace
Visible All data MWr exactly 128 B, MRd sizes capped at a small MRRS; config writes to Device Control at enumeration if captured. See also Part V L-32.
What happens
MPS = 128 B costs ≈8% of a Gen4 x4 link versus 256 B and ≈12% versus 512 B (8.1.1). A small MRRS (e.g. 128 B) forces the SSD to issue many more read requests to fetch write data, each needing a tag and a completion; with limited outstanding tags this caps write throughput.
How it shows up
Sequential read or write stuck at ~85–90% of the expected plateau; lspci -vvv "DevCtl: MaxPayload 128 bytes, MaxReadReq 128 bytes".
Spec basis
PCI Express Base: Max_Payload_Size, Max_Read_Request_Size (Device Control).
Typical causes
A device on the same hierarchy that supports only 128 B forcing the "safe" MPS for all; firmware defaults; kernel MPS policy (pci=pcie_bus_safe, pcie_bus_perf, pcie_bus_peer2peer, pcie_bus_tune_off).
How to detect / prove
lspci -vvv for every device from root port to SSD (DevCap MaxPayload vs DevCtl MaxPayload); compare sequential bandwidth; analyzer shows TLP payload sizes directly.
Linux v7.2 source
drivers/pci/probe.c:pcie_bus_configure_settings, pcie_bus_configure_set, pcie_write_mps, pcie_write_mrrs; pcie_bus_config values PCIE_BUS_TUNE_OFF, PCIE_BUS_SAFE, PCIE_BUS_PERFORMANCE, PCIE_BUS_PEER2PEER.
Test to provoke it
CAUTION: boot with a different pci=pcie_bus_* policy on a lab machine and compare; never lower MPS on one end only (that is V-26).
P-13Misaligned or sub-sector writes causing read-modify-write DegradedHost / device
In a PEX trace
Partly visible SLBA/NLB values not aligned to the preferred granularity are visible in SQEs; the read-modify-write inside the device is not.
What happens
A namespace formatted with 512-byte LBAs on a drive whose internal mapping unit is 4 KiB (or larger) receives writes that are not 4 KiB aligned or not 4 KiB multiples. The FTL must read the rest of the unit, merge and rewrite: more latency, more NAND writes.
How it shows up
Small-write IOPS far below datasheet; higher write amplification; nothing in logs.
Spec basis
NVM Command Set: LBA formats (Identify Namespace LBAF, "Relative Performance" field), and optimal I/O hints: NPWG (Preferred Write Granularity), NPWA (Preferred Write Alignment), NOWS (Optimal Write Size) when reported.
Typical causes
Partitions not 1 MiB aligned; databases with 512 B or 2 KiB pages; namespace formatted with a non-preferred LBA format.
How to detect / prove
nvme id-ns /dev/nvme0n1 -H (LBA formats with "Relative Performance", npwg/npwa/nows); cat /sys/block/nvme0n1/queue/{physical_block_size,optimal_io_size,minimum_io_size}; fio with --bs=4k --offset=512 vs aligned on a scratch device.
Linux v7.2 source
drivers/nvme/host/core.c derives physical_block_size/io_opt from NPWG/NOWS when the namespace reports them (search for npwg in nvme_update_disk_info-related code).
Test to provoke it
CAUTION (writes): aligned vs misaligned 4k random write on a scratch namespace.
P-14Flush/FUA-heavy workload on a drive without (or with disabled) volatile write cache DegradedHost / device
In a PEX trace
Visible SQE opcode 00h (Flush) or FUA=1 writes after each write, and the long SQE→CQE time of each Flush; VWC is visible in captured Identify Controller data.
What happens
Applications that call fsync after every write generate Flush commands (or FUA writes). On consumer drives with a volatile write cache, each Flush forces cached data to NAND — sync-write latency jumps from tens of µs to milliseconds. Enterprise drives with power-loss protection can acknowledge flushes quickly.
How it shows up
Database commit latency high; iostat shows low throughput but high w_await; nothing in logs.
Spec basis
NVMe Base / NVM Command Set: Flush command (00h), Force Unit Access bit in Write, Volatile Write Cache feature (06h) and Identify Controller VWC.
Typical causes
Workload design; drive class (no power-loss protection); volatile write cache disabled by a tool (each write then becomes write-through).
How to detect / prove
nvme id-ctrl /dev/nvme0 | grep vwc; nvme get-feature /dev/nvme0 -f 0x06; cat /sys/block/nvme0n1/queue/write_cache; fio with --fsync=1 vs none on a scratch device; count Flush commands with the nvme_setup_cmd trace event.
Linux v7.2 source
drivers/nvme/host/core.c:nvme_setup_cmd (flush and FUA paths); write-cache reporting set from VWC.
Test to provoke it
CAUTION (writes): fio --rw=randwrite --bs=4k --fsync=1 on a scratch namespace, compared with --fsync=0.

8.3.1 Triage table: which tool answers which question

SymptomFirst commandWhat proves itCard
Sequential bandwidth lowlspci -vvv LnkSta, DevCtlLnkSta below LnkCap; MaxPayload 128P-11, P-12, P-01
IOPS low, latency OKfio CPU%, perf topLittle's Law mismatch; CPU saturatedP-09, P-10
IOPS fall at high QDQD sweeppeak then declineP-02
Tail latencyfio --percentile_list, lat logoutliers correlated with idle / temp / GCP-03, P-05, P-07
Throughput drops over time (writes)--write_bw_logstep after N GB; recovers after idleP-04, P-05
Saw-tooth throughputnvme smart-log every 1 sthermal counters increasingP-06
High CPU in IRQ/proc/interrupts, mpstatone CPU saturated; MSI-X:CQE ratioP-08
Slow sync writesiostat -x w_await, VWCFlush per writeP-14
💡 Senior insight

Most "the SSD is slow" escalations end at P-09, P-11 or P-12 — the host or the slot, not the drive. Collect the baseline evidence bundle (8.1.3) before opening a vendor case; it answers the vendor's first five questions.

PART IX

Using AI (Claude) on a PEX Trace Export

An AI assistant cannot plug into an analyzer, cannot see the wire and cannot look inside an SSD. What it can do is read the text you export from a PEX capture — packet lists, transaction lists, decoded NVMe commands — together with logs and register dumps, apply every rule in this atlas to it, line up timelines, explain status codes, and write the checker scripts that make the conclusions reproducible. This part is a practical workflow: how to export, what to hand over, which prompts work, what the AI may conclude, and the guardrails that keep it honest.

9.1 What an AI Can and Cannot Conclude from a PEX Export

← 8.3 Host, Power-Management and Link Anomalies9.2 Exporting from the Analyzer and Handing It Over →
🧒 Kid analogy

Imagine giving a very fast, very well-read detective a printed list of everything that went through a door: who, when, what they carried. The detective can spot that the same person came in twice without leaving, or that a parcel was delivered before it was ordered. The detective cannot tell you what happened inside the house — nobody wrote that down.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

A human detective knows when they are guessing. A language model can produce a fluent, confident explanation for something the list does not show. The workflow in this part exists to force every conclusion back to a row in the export.

9.1.1 Three levels of conclusion

LevelMeaningExampleCan an AI state it?
ObservedDirectly in the export, a row or a set of rows"Row 1843: CQE for CID 0x0013 written at 12.004 ms, but the last data MWr for that command is row 1851 at 12.019 ms."Yes — with row citations; you can verify in seconds
Rule violationObserved rows + a protocol rule"That is completion-before-data (V-13): posted-write order was violated by the transmitter."Yes, if the rule is one of the well-established rules in this atlas and the AI names it; verify the rule wording yourself
HypothesisA cause that is not in the trace"The controller probably sends CQEs from a different DMA engine."Only explicitly labelled as hypothesis, with the experiment that would test it

9.1.2 Question by question

Question you might askFrom the export alone?What else is needed
"Which command failed and with which status?"Yes — CQE DW3 status field; the AI can decode SCT/SC/DNR/More and name the codeCross-check the name against include/linux/nvme.h or the spec
"What is the first abnormal event?"Yes, for every rule in Part VII that is marked VisibleCapture must start early enough (queue creation) or the AI must be told the starting state
"Was the doorbell value legal?"Yes, if queue sizes were captured (Create I/O SQ/CQ) or providednvme id-ctrl, CAP value
"Did the drive time out?"Partly — a request with no completion within N is visible as an absence with timestampsThe host timeout value; dmesg for what the host did
"Did the deallocate really unmap the LBAs?"No — only that a DSM command with the deallocate attribute and its range list was sent and completedRead-back test, Get LBA Status / vendor log, capacity counters
"Is the data on media correct?"No — the export shows payloads crossing the link, not the mediafio verify / checksums on read-back
"Why is throughput low?"Partly — bandwidth, payload sizes, gaps, outstanding count, link width/speed at traininglspci -vvv, fio results, CPU profile, SMART temperatures
"Did an AER error happen?"Only if ERR_* messages or config reads of the AER registers are on the probed linkdmesg, sysfs aer_dev_* counters
"Is this a host bug or a device bug?"Often yes — the direction of the offending TLP tells who broke the ruleFor host-memory effects, the host source or a second capture
💡 Senior insight

The single most valuable thing an AI does with a trace is not "finding the bug". It is finding the first abnormal event among hundreds of thousands of rows, and separating it from the cascade that follows. A human engineer then spends their time on one row instead of a million.

9.2 Exporting from the Analyzer and Handing It Over

← 9.1 What an AI Can and Cannot Conclude from a PEX Export9.3 A Concrete Workflow with Prompt Templates →

A PEX capture file is a binary, analyzer-specific format. An AI assistant should not be expected to parse it directly; the analyzer software decodes it, and you export the decoded view as text. The menu names and options below are deliberately generic — they vary across tool versions. uncertain Check your analyzer's manual for exact names.

9.2.1 Which view to export

View (generic name)GranularityBest forWatch out for
Packet / TLP listone row per TLP or DLLP (optionally ordered sets)PCIe rules (V-26 … V-37): sizes, tags, Byte Count, EP/TD/RO bits, Nak/replayLarge; replayed TLPs appear twice; include both directions
Transaction / split-transactionone row per request with its completion(s)latency per read, Unexpected Completions, tag reuse, completion timeoutsHow unmatched completions are shown varies
NVMe command / queue decodeone row per SQE / CQE / doorbell, sometimes per command with bothPart VII queue and command rules (V-01 … V-25), status codes, per-command latencyNeeds the analyzer to know BAR0 and queue bases — usually learned from captured enumeration and queue creation; start the capture early
Link / LTSSM eventstraining, Recovery, power-state transitionsP-07, P-11, link context for Part VPhysical-layer analysis belongs to Part V

9.2.2 Export settings that matter

  • Timestamps with their unit stated (ns, µs) and absolute or relative origin. Keep the analyzer's timestamp column unmodified.
  • Both directions (upstream and downstream) in one file, time-ordered, with a direction column.
  • Raw fields as well as decoded text: TLP type, length, address, requester ID, tag, attributes (RO, NS, IDO), TD, EP, Byte Count, Lower Address; for NVMe: opcode, CID, NSID, PRP1/PRP2 or SGL, CDW10–15, CQE DW0–DW3.
  • Payload bytes for SQE fetch completions, CQE writes, PRP-list reads and Identify/log-page data (these are where NVMe decoding comes from). Data payloads of bulk I/O can be truncated to save space.
  • Time window: from controller enable (or at least queue creation) to a few seconds after the failure. If the file is too big, export two pieces: the setup phase (enumeration, CAP/CC writes, Identify, Create I/O queues) and a window around the failure.
  • Filters: filtering out DLLPs and ordered sets is fine for NVMe questions; keep them for link questions. Say which filters you applied.

9.2.3 Evidence checklist — what to hand over

✅ Evidence checklist
  • The export file(s) (CSV/text), with the analyzer tool name and version, the view exported, filters applied, and the timestamp unit.
  • Where the probe sat (root port ↔ SSD, switch downstream port ↔ SSD, …) and the link speed/width.
  • Configuration context: lspci -vvv of the SSD and every port above it (MPS, MRRS, RCB, ASPM, LnkCap/LnkSta, AER capability); nvme id-ctrl (MDTS, SGLS, FUSES, VWC, APSTA, power states); nvme id-ns; CAP/VS if a register dump is available.
  • Host logs for the same period: journalctl -k / dmesg -T, with a note on how host time maps to analyzer time (e.g. "the doorbell at analyzer t=12.000 ms corresponds to the nvme_setup_cmd trace event at 1739.512301 s").
  • Device logs after the event: nvme error-log, nvme smart-log, vendor logs if available.
  • The workload: exact fio job or application, start time, what was expected vs observed.
  • Known-good comparison: the same export from a passing run, if you have one.
  • A statement of what was redacted (serial numbers, host addresses) — so the AI does not "find" artefacts of redaction.
⚠️ Warning

Exports can contain real data payloads (file contents, keys in memory buffers) and system identifiers. Truncate data payloads you do not need, and follow your organisation's rules before uploading anything to any external service.

9.2.4 Size strategy

A busy Gen5 link produces millions of TLPs per second; a full export will not fit in any conversation. Use this order: (1) give the AI the column header and the first 200 rows so it can write a parser for your format; (2) run that parser (or the checker from 7.6) locally on the whole file; (3) hand back only the findings and a few hundred rows around the first abnormal event. With an agentic tool such as Claude Code, step (2) can be done by the assistant itself on your machine — it reads the file and runs the script, and you see every command before it runs.

9.3 A Concrete Workflow with Prompt Templates

← 9.2 Exporting from the Analyzer and Handing It Over9.4 Guardrails: Where AI Help Ends →

9.3.1 Template A — describe the export and get a parser

I captured a PCIe trace with a protocol analyzer (probe between the root port and an
NVMe SSD, Gen4 x4) and exported the <packet | transaction | NVMe command> view to CSV.
Tool and version: <...>. Timestamp unit: <ns>. Filters applied: <none | DLLPs removed>.
Here are the header and the first 200 rows: <paste>.
1. Explain what each column means; say "unknown" if you cannot tell - do not guess.
2. Write a Python 3 script (standard library only) that maps these rows to the event schema
   t_ns,event,q,cid,opc,val,len,prp1,prp2,sqid,sqhd,ph,tlp_len  (events: CFG_Q, SQDB, CQDB,
   SQE, DATA_WR, DATA_RD, CQE, MSIX, TLP).
3. List any rows you could not map and why.

9.3.2 Template B — find the first abnormal event

Here is my CSV export (or: here are the findings of trace_check.py plus rows N-200..N+200).
Context: lspci -vvv <paste>; nvme id-ctrl <paste>; dmesg for the same period <paste>.
Expected behaviour: <e.g. fio 4k randread QD32 should run 60 s without errors>.
Task: find the FIRST abnormal event.
Rules for your answer:
- Cite every claim with row numbers from the export.
- Label each statement OBSERVED, RULE (name the rule; no spec section numbers), or HYPOTHESIS.
- Separate the root event from its cascade (what follows from it).
- If the export does not contain enough to decide, say exactly which extra evidence you need.

9.3.3 Template C — explain a status code or async event

Row 5521 is a CQE: DW0=00000000 DW1=00000000 DW2=00010023 DW3=8027A00C (raw hex, little-endian
fields already decoded by the analyzer as shown).
Decode SQHD, SQID, CID, phase, SCT, SC, CRD, More, DNR. Name the status code and say which
command (by CID) it answers. Point to the SQE row for that CID. If the code name depends on the
command set or spec revision, say so.

9.3.4 Template D — timeline correlation

Analyzer time 0 = <host timestamp> (anchor: the SQ1 doorbell at analyzer 12.000 ms is the
nvme_setup_cmd event at 1739.512301 s in the attached ftrace).
Merge the analyzer findings, the ftrace nvme_setup_cmd/nvme_complete_rq events and dmesg into one
timeline. For each dmesg line (timeouts, resets, AER messages) show the nearest preceding
abnormal trace row and the time difference. Do not assume causality from proximity alone.

9.3.5 Template E — generate a new checker rule

Add a rule to trace_check.py: "every MRd with Length*4 > MRRS (given on the command line) is a
finding V-27". Write a unit test with two synthetic rows (one legal, one violating) and show the
test output after running it. Do not change existing rules.

9.3.6 Template F — performance from a trace

From this NVMe command export compute: per-second read bandwidth, average payload size of data
MWr TLPs, mean and p99.9 of (SQE fetch -> CQE) per opcode, average outstanding commands, and the
ratio of MSI-X writes to CQEs. Compare bandwidth with the link ceiling for Gen4 x4 at MPS 256 B
using rate x lanes x 128/130 / 8 x MPS/(MPS+24). Show the arithmetic. Then list which Part VIII
anomalies are consistent with the numbers and which extra evidence would confirm each.

9.3.7 Worked example (synthetic)

Synthetic exchange — Template B applied to the 7.6 sample
StepContent
InputThe 15 findings printed by trace_check.py in 7.6, rows 2–27 of the sample CSV, and "queue 1 was created with 4 entries; MPS 256 B; MDTS 128 KiB".
Answer, part 1OBSERVED: row 11 is the first abnormal event — SQE CID 0x11, 8 KiB, PRP1 0x10001000, PRP2 0x20000010. RULE: PRP2 is a data pointer here (the remainder after PRP1's page fits one page), so its offset must be zero (V-18). A checking controller would complete it with status 13h; the sample export has no status column, so whether it did is unknown — ask for the CQE status field (DW3) of row 15 before concluding. HYPOTHESIS: data for the second page landed at 0x20000010 and overran into the next page; verify with a read-back into a guarded buffer.
Answer, part 2OBSERVED: row 15 CQE for CID 0x11 precedes the 8 KiB DATA_WR at row 16. RULE: completion before data (V-13); row 16 is the same defect seen as DMA after completion (V-16) — a cascade, not a second bug.
Answer, part 3OBSERVED: row 24 CQE posted into slot 0 while host head is 1 → CQ overflow (V-07b). The PHASE finding on row 24 and CQDB-PAST-TAIL on row 26 follow from it.
Answer, part 4Independent host-side findings: rows 20, 25 (doorbell values ≥ 4), 22 (256 KiB > MDTS), 23 (CID 0x13 reused), 27 (doorbell for non-existent queue 5). Independent device-side: rows 14 (MSI-X without CQE), 17 (512 B TLP > MPS), 19 (CQE with SQID 2 and unknown CID 0x99).
NeedNot in the export: whether the host saw corrupted data (needs application checksums), and whether the device reported any of this in its Error Information log (needs nvme error-log).

Notice the shape of a good answer: every sentence starts from a row, rules are named, the cascade is separated, and the "Need" line lists exactly what the export cannot show.

9.4 Guardrails: Where AI Help Ends

← 9.3 A Concrete Workflow with Prompt Templates

Language models can produce plausible but wrong root causes. Research on LLM-based log analysis reports exactly this: models invent root causes when evidence is ambiguous, and simply instructing a model to use only the supplied evidence does not reliably prevent it; grounding the model in structured, pre-computed evidence helps. Treat the AI as a fast junior analyst whose every claim must be checked against a row.

RiskWhat it looks likeGuardrail
Invented spec citations"Section 4.2.3.1 requires…"Ask for rule names and field names, not section numbers; verify wording in your copy of the spec
Status-code mix-upsWrong name for a code, or a command-specific code read as genericDecode SCT first; cross-check names against include/linux/nvme.h / drivers/nvme/host/constants.c or the spec
Claims about device internals"The FTL failed to unmap", "the SLC cache filled"Must be labelled HYPOTHESIS with an experiment (read-back, SMART deltas, long-run bandwidth log)
Proximity = causality"The AER at 12.3 ms caused the timeout"Require the mechanism (which rule) and a second occurrence, or a provoked reproduction
Parsing errorsMisread column, wrong endianness, hex vs decimalRun the AI-written parser on a known-good capture first; spot-check 10 rows by hand
Sampling biasLooking only at the rows you pastedRun checks on the full file with a script; paste only windows around findings
Missing stateCapture started mid-stream: "CQE for unknown CID" everywhereTell the AI where the capture started; let the checker learn state and suppress early findings
Destructive suggestions"Run nvme format / sanitize / setpci to test"Only on scratch hardware; an agentic tool must ask before running anything that writes; review every command
📭 What the AI cannot see
  • The wire itself — only what your export contains.
  • Anything on a link the probe was not on, or inside the root complex, switch or SSD.
  • Host memory contents that never crossed the probed link.
  • Whether a command did its job inside the device (deallocate, write to media, firmware activation) — the "completes but does nothing" class needs read-back evidence.
  • Analyzer-specific decode errors — if the analyzer mis-decoded a packet, the AI will faithfully reason about the wrong data.

9.4.1 Acceptance test for an AI conclusion

✅ Before you put an AI conclusion in a bug report
  • Every observed claim points to row numbers, and you have looked at those rows yourself.
  • The rule is named, and you checked its wording in the spec or in this atlas's card.
  • The finding is reproduced by a script run over the full export, not only by reading pasted rows.
  • The first abnormal event is identified, and the later findings are explained as cascade or as independent.
  • Hypotheses about device internals are labelled and paired with an experiment.
  • Context the AI did not have (probe location, redactions, filters) has been considered.

Quiz

  1. An AI says "the trace proves the drive did not deallocate the last 5 GB". What is wrong with the claim?

    Answer

    The trace can prove only that a DSM command with the deallocate attribute and its range list crossed the link and completed with a given status. Whether the device unmapped those LBAs is device-internal (marked Not visible); proof needs read-back behaviour, Get LBA Status or capacity/utilisation counters.

  2. Why give the AI the setup phase of the capture (enumeration, CAP/CC writes, queue creation) even if the failure happens later?

    Answer

    Many rules are stateful: queue sizes, doorbell stride, BAR addresses, MPS/MRRS and the MSI-X table come from that phase. Without it the AI must guess state, which creates false findings (e.g. unknown CIDs) or missed ones (doorbell range).

  3. What is the minimum you should paste into a conversation for a multi-gigabyte export?

    Answer

    The header and a few hundred rows so the AI can write a parser; then run the parser/checker locally on the full file and paste only the findings and windows around the first abnormal event.

Interview questions

  1. Intermediate How would you use an AI assistant to triage a 2 GB analyzer export of an NVMe timeout?
    Model answerExport the NVMe-command and transaction views to CSV; give the AI the header plus sample rows and the configuration context; have it write a mapper and a rule checker; run them locally on the full file; give back the findings and a window around the first abnormal event; require row-cited, rule-named conclusions; verify the root event by hand and with a reproduction.
  2. Senior What can a PEX trace not tell you about a "successful" command that did nothing?
    Model answerIt shows the command, its data/range list and a success CQE; it cannot show media state. You need functional evidence: read-back, Get LBA Status, utilisation counters, or a device log — and only then can you call it a silent failure.
